Barcelona, day six 🇪🇸

🧠 Morning at the @claudeai   Community House, a session on second brains.
🎫 Volunteer walkthrough for the AI Summit at midday.
🔧 AI Builders meetup at @eDreams in the evening, and the self-hosting talk was the best thing I heard all week. 
The argument in one slide: you probably already pay 20 euros for n8n, 29 for Postiz, 18 for WordPress, 12 per user for https://t.co/nznjiVwP0i, 9.50 per user for Notion. 
Every one of them is free to self-host. 

What it takes: rent a VPS, install Docker, deploy the app, domain and SSL, firewall, backups, updates. 
Seven steps, and every AI agent can do the first six.
Then the AI plumbing itself. Claude and Codex ship a fixed set of built-in tools you pay for every month. 
A self-hosted harness like @deepseek_ai 's ships with none, and SearXNG plugs into it as an MCP server with one line and searches Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo and Brave for free. Search is the piece I had never thought about self-hosting. Now it is on the list.

🐝Desplega Labs closed with agent memory. Their swarm forgot on day 76 because embed everything, top k, keeps stale facts alive and lets noise outrank truth. The fix is one score for short and long term memory: match times age decay times use times source trust times reputation, three loops, one SQLite file. Simple, and it runs.

Self-hosting is not a hobby. It is the difference between renting your stack and owning it, but that means giving up convenience and taking responsibility for your data, backups and security.

text:
Why I'm bullish on @loomdesktrade ($LOOM)

I've been looking at LoomDesk on Robinhood Chain and I think people are sleeping on it. The idea is that LOOM's trading volume gets turned into a liquidity book that can't be withdrawn, and that book pays holders in USDG and LOOM every day. 

Positioning

Easiest way to think about LoomDesk is as the Meteora of Robinhood Chain. Loom goes after the same things that made Meteora big on Solana: smarter fees, shaped liquidity, and pools anyone can open. It just builds them on top of Uniswap v4 instead of its own AMM, and sends the fees back to holders.

Delta is the obvious RH comparison. robinhood:0xe8ffd7e24187f72afb08d75b1bb13088a989a791 was around $36M at the top just now. It has almost 16K holders. What gets me is that the token's role is still going to be explained in a whitepaper that isn't out yet.

So the market was willing to pay up to $35M for Delta without knowing what the token actually does. 
Loom also has ladders, which is basically Delta's main product.

Flow logic

Every time someone trades LOOM, 3% of the trade goes into the book, and that money can't be taken out. The book earns fees, and every day most of that (80%) gets paid out to holders in USDG. The rest goes back into the book so it keeps getting bigger. Any LOOM the book earns gets sent to holders, too, no protocol side sells.

For comparison, Delta does around $2M in volume a day. If LOOM did the same, that 3% would put about $20M into the book in a year. That's pretty much half Delta's market cap.

Other income

Tax isn't the only thing feeding the book. It also holds LOOM against ETH and tokenized stocks in pools with a 1% fee. It gets 10% of every swap fee in LoomDesk's stock pools, even when someone else provided the liquidity. It gets most of the 5% ladder fee. And anyone can open a pool through their hook, and the book gets 10% of those fees as well.

The tech

In normal pools a lot of the fees get eaten by arbitrage bots. Per the whitepaper, some pools kept 96% of their fees while others kept 7%. So they wrote their own hook. Normal trades pay 0.30%, but if you're an arb closing a gap with the Chainlink price, you pay extra, up to 5%. LPs get paid properly, which should pull in outside liquidity, and the book earns off that too.

A few smaller things I like:

AI agents can use LoomDesk directly through an MCP server, if you hold 100k LOOM you pay less on ladders, there's no mint or blacklist on the token, and they tested the whole thing on mainnet with real money before launching.

text:
t is only as good as the parse behind it. He built a Grounded Document Agent that answers questions over long PDFs with citations you can trace back to the source, using LlamaParse for layout-aware parsing, LlamaIndex for retrieval, and a local qwen3:4b model through Ollama for generation. His point is the one I keep making about web data specifically: a lot of agent failures get blamed on retrieval or the model, but the damage happens earlier, at the parse step. Flatten a table wrong or lose reading order and no amount of better embeddings recovers what's already gone.

Web pages have the same failure mode PDFs do, plus a second one: the page changes tomorrow. Most scraping setups re-read the whole page with an LLM on every single pass, which means you're paying model cost and eating drift risk on every run, not just the first one.

That's the problem I built DeepScrape around. It generates CSS selectors once, deterministically, and reuses them on every future scrape. The LLM only comes back in when the page actually changes, to regenerate or validate the selector, not to re-read the document from scratch. Output comes out as markdown, HTML, screenshots, PDF, structured tables, or change-tracked diffs, and there's an /api/map endpoint plus an autonomous agent mode that can navigate toward a natural-language goal instead of a fixed selector path. It also runs as an MCP server, so Claude or Cursor can query a website directly as a structured data source instead of you writing a scraper first.

Same lesson as the Grounded Document Agent, applied to the web instead of PDFs: get the extraction layer right once, and everything built on top of it, retrieval, citations, agent actions, stops silently failing for reasons that look like something else.

text:
110+ people are using Deploy Hatch. $0 in revenue.

Last week, @Boardyai introduced me to a founder building agent reliability tools, so I showed him the part of Deploy Hatch I'm proudest of.

I had an agent deliberately break a preview, deploy the broken code, pull the full logs through our MCP server, diagnose that the runtime failed, prove the bug was in the user code rather than our platform, patch it, and redeploy.

It handled the entire cycle autonomously. The only time it paused was to ask which GitHub repo to connect; exactly where a human should be in the loop.

Then he opened my homepage and asked what any of that had to do with "Ship the app, not the server."

The answer? Nothing.

I wrote that tagline a month ago when Deploy Hatch was just a simple manual deployment platform. The AI agent orchestration came weeks later, but the website never caught up.

His feedback was direct: the product is real, but the landing page isn't selling it. If a visitor has to read between the lines to realize what you actually do, your copy is broken. It also explained my Google Ads performance: 1,600 impressions, 99 clicks, 0 paid conversions.

He gave me one key piece of advice: stop trying to reach every developer at once. Focus entirely on the builder whose AI agent handles everything up to production, only to hit a wall when it's time to actually deploy.

The product isn't changing, but the entire homepage is getting rewritten this week.

Has anyone else looked at their landing page and realized it was describing a version of their product from a month ago? How did you catch it?

4 GITHUB TRICKS THAT CAN SAVE YOU SERIOUS TIME.

Most developers use GitHub to read and clone code.

But with these 4 tricks, you can edit, run, analyze, and give entire repositories to AI in seconds.

1. PRESS "." TO OPEN GITHUB IN VS CODE

Open any GitHub repository and press the "." key.

GitHub instantly opens the project in a browser-based VS Code environment with the file explorer, search, syntax highlighting, and more.

Perfect for quickly exploring unfamiliar code, making small edits, or fixing a typo without cloning the repo.

You can even commit your changes directly from the browser.

2. CHANGE "https://t.co/ahWREtIVzW" TO "https://t.co/d2cPTz8RJK"

Want an AI assistant to actually understand a GitHub repository?

Replace "https://t.co/ahWREtIVzW" with "https://t.co/d2cPTz8RJK" in the repo URL.

GitMCP creates an MCP server for the repository, which you can connect to tools like Cursor, Claude Desktop, Windsurf, VS Code, Cline, and other compatible AI assistants.

Now your AI can work with the repository's actual documentation and code instead of relying on guesses.

3. CHANGE "github" TO "gitingest"

Need to give an entire repository to an AI model?

Replace "github" with "gitingest" in the URL.

GitIngest turns the repository into a single, AI-friendly text digest containing the file structure and source code.

You can copy everything or download it, then paste it into your preferred AI model.

You can also exclude files or folders and set size limits to keep the context manageable.

4. CHANGE "github" TO "githubbox"

Want to test a GitHub project without installing everything locally?

Replace "github" with "githubbox".

The repository opens inside a CodeSandbox environment with an editor and live preview, allowing you to inspect, modify, and run the project directly in your browser.

It's especially useful for quickly testing frontend projects.

THE BEST PART?

Three of these tricks only require changing the URL.

The fourth is literally pressing one key.

In a few seconds, you can go from simply reading a GitHub repo to editing it, running it, connecting it to AI, or turning the entire codebase into AI-ready context.

Bookmark this. You'll want these the next time you find an interesting GitHub repo.

text:
AI agents can now discover products and initiate payments. But who pays when an agent gets the purchase wrong?

That was one of the biggest questions in my latest On The Ground conversation with s/Jill Willard, CTO of IXOPAY.

IXOPAY launched its Agentic Suite this month, giving merchants infrastructure to accept purchases from AI shopping agents while continuing to use their existing payment providers. The suite includes a Payment Agent, Universal Tokens and an MCP Server.

Jill walked us through what this looks like in practice and why IXOPAY is building before autonomous transactions have meaningful volume.

The protocol layer is already getting crowded. Visa and Mastercard have their own approaches. Other standards are emerging. Merchants now have to prepare for AI agents without knowing which protocols will ultimately dominate.

And then there is liability.

Who is responsible if an AI agent misunderstands the user’s intent and buys the wrong thing? The merchant? Acquirer? Card network? Agent provider?

Jill believes liability remains one of the biggest blockers to agentic commerce reaching scale.

We also discussed two other stories this week.

Revolut disclosed an external impersonation scam after someone used an email address from a legitimate government agency domain to request customer information. Around 680 customers were reportedly affected, with sensitive personal information exposed. Revolut says its systems and customer funds were not compromised.

Then AI safety took another turn.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing the development of frontier AI models and proposed independent evaluators, coordination between labs and international cooperation. Sam Altman and Elon Musk publicly backed the call.

President Trump pushed back, dismissing AI risk concerns as a “hoax” and arguing against additional guardrails.

Three very different stories, but the same question kept coming up during our conversation:

Technology can move quickly. How fast can trust, liability and governance catch up?

text:
A Python representation of a UI turns out to run about 70% smaller than the equivalent JSON, a detail that changed how an entire framework streams interfaces over the wire. @jlowin, founder and CEO of Prefect and creator of FastMCP, walks through that discovery in "Generative UI... in Python?", on @aiDotEngineer's YouTube. The talk lays out a working pattern for shipping interactive UIs from an MCP server without writing JavaScript.

- MCP apps skip the agent's context window. Normally an MCP tool's result goes back into the agent, but MCP apps let a tool send HTML, CSS, and JavaScript straight to the user instead, so they can search, sort, or click through it directly.
- Prefab, a Python DSL for UI. Jeremiah's team built it so Python engineers can compose interfaces from roughly 130 to 140 pre-built components using nested context managers, without touching React.
- JSON underneath, Python on top. The DSL builds a declarative UI that serializes into a JSON protocol and renders through a React app, which is why adding a pie chart next to a data table is a one-line change.
- Three ways to use it. An interactive tool that returns a Prefab component instead of a dictionary, a full FastMCP app built from app.ui and https://t.co/WbDbF0fcIx methods, and a generative UI where the agent streams the interface live as it renders.
- The upload problem. Since only the agent can talk to an MCP server, teams ended up having the agent retype uploaded files character by character; a built-in upload component lets a file go straight from the browser to the server instead.
- Python beat JSON on the wire. Once Jeremiah's team saw how much smaller the Python form was, FastMCP switched to streaming Python directly and converting it to JSON server-side, for a real token and latency win.

text:
How to Build Your Own LLM Agent Harness

Phase 1: Foundation & Interface Selection
Every agentic harness begins with choosing how the user will interact with it and how its runtime state is preserved.

Interface Architecture: Decide between a terminal interface (CLI/TUI) and a graphical interface (GUI/Web). For developer tools, a terminal interface built with frameworks like rich, typer (Python), or ink (Node.js) is faster to iterate on, lightweight, and fits directly into standard developer workflows.

State & Session Persistence: Avoid using plain Markdown files to store active conversation threads, run histories, or token logs. File read/write operations introduce latency, lack query support, and risk concurrency collisions. Use SQLite (or a fast embedded store like DuckDB) to manage user threads, tool input/output logs, and multi-turn state transitions efficiently.

Phase 2: Core Tooling & API Standardization
An agent is defined by the tools it can access. Your harness must provide clean tool abstractions that conform to industry standards.

API Compatibility: Design tool schemas around the OpenAI Function Calling format (JSON Schema with name, description, and parameters). Because models from providers such as OpenAI, Grok, and local engines (via Ollama or vLLM) adhere to or directly adapt this schema, your tools will remain model-agnostic.

The Essential Tool Suite: A working agent harness requires five baseline capabilities:
read_file: Reads files by relative/absolute path, ideally with optional line-range offsets to save context tokens.
write_file / edit_file: Writes entire files or applies unified patch diffs directly.
file_search: Fast pattern and regex matching. Implement this by wrapping ripgrep (rg) instead of standard grep, giving you automatic .gitignore awareness, binary filtering, and multi-threaded speed.
list_directory: Discovers folder structures and file names.
execute_bash: Runs shell scripts, linters, tests, and build tooling.

Phase 3: Security, Sandboxing & Guardrails

Because the model can execute shell commands and modify local storage, security is a non-negotiable layer of your harness.

Command Allow/Blocklists: Prevent obvious catastrophic commands such as rm -rf / or recursive permission changes (chmod -R 777).

Script Obfuscation Protection: Malicious or broken logic can bypass simple string filters by wrapping destructive commands in dynamically generated scripts (e.g., a Python script executing shutil.rmtree). Implement mandatory human-in-the-loop (HITL) approval prompts before executing any terminal command.

Workspace Isolation & Path Traversal: Resolve all file paths against your project root and explicitly disallow traversal patterns (../../etc) to isolate modifications to the current repository. For production-grade security, run the agent's bash processes inside isolated containers (Docker) or OS-level namespaces.

Phase 4: Context Management & Persistent Memory
Effective harnesses balance comprehensive context against the strict limits and costs of LLM token windows.

Project-Level Guidance (AGENTS.md): Instead of stuffing every operational rule into application code, use an external configuration file like AGENTS.md (similar to .cursorrules). This allows the agent to load project conventions, preferred libraries, and code styles dynamically.

Token Budget Management: Remember that any instruction injected into the system prompt or prepended context is charged on every single interaction turn. Keep instructions compact and domain-focused.

Lightweight Memory: Avoid the operational complexity of vector databases (RAG) for early-stage harnesses. Follow simple text-based memory systems, such as a curated project log or Karpathy-style knowledge base notes, to persist facts across tasks without heavy retrieval pipelines.

Phase 5: Multi-Agent Orchestration & Extensibility
Complex development tasks cannot be solved in a single prompt loop. Separating planning from execution prevents context drift.

The Orchestrator-Worker Model: Use a primary agent whose only job is planning, breaking tasks down into discrete steps, and delegating them to focused subagents (such as a generation agent, test runner, or code reviewer).

Decoupled Prompt Templates: Never hardcode system prompts inside your application code. Keep prompts, persona definitions, and orchestration steps in external configuration files (e.g., YAML, TOML, or Markdown templates) so they can be version-controlled, swapped, or extended like plugins.

The Competitive Edge: Industry tools like Cursor, Claude Code, and Codex excel primarily because they invest heavily in proprietary context pruning, intelligent diff application, and prompts fine-tuned specifically to the strengths of their target models.

text:
Banger paper on self-evolving ontologies for agents.

You just can't go wrong with implementing an ontology layer for your agents.

This paper shows exactly why.

The show that GPT-5.5 gains 26.7 points on DDR-Bench when the data agent can query an ontology of the data it works with.

Why is this useful?

Data agents normally see tables, files and databases through generic tools, reading column names and file paths one call at a time.

The alternative is a hand-written semantic layer pasted into the prompt, which does not scale to many sources.

EvoOntology builds the ontology with a dedicated agent and serves it as an MCP server with schema, content and tool layers.

The data agent queries it at runtime.

The ontology is then edited in small typed steps, and each edit is kept only if a paired evaluation on the same backbone shows it helps.

Across six backbones on DDR-Bench, accuracy rises 17.8 points on average, from 4.8 on Qwen3.5-Flash to 26.7 on GPT-5.5. On BIRD, execution accuracy rises 7.4 points. Edits to the tool layer account for 57% of the gain from evolution.

text:
Codex can show the iOS Simulator inside its in-app browser and hot-reload SwiftUI previews while it edits. It comes from one skill in the Build iOS Apps plugin from @OpenAIDevs, and it only works for previews that live in a Swift package.

What is in the plugin?

- Nine skills, per the README: simulator debugging, the browser mirror, ETTrace profiles, memgraph leak checks, App Intents, Liquid Glass, a SwiftUI performance audit, SwiftUI UI patterns and view refactoring
- One MCP server: the plugin config starts the latest xcodebuildmcp package through npx with the simulator, ui-automation, debugging and logging workflows on
- MIT license, manifest version 0.1.2, in OpenAI's public plugins repo

How does the mirror work?

- The skill takes a Simulator UDID, runs the serve-sim npm package against it and opens the local URL it prints in the in-app browser
- For previews, a bundled launcher takes a Package.swift path, a target and a UDID. It generates a host app outside your source tree, installs it in the Simulator and watches the package
- On a source edit it rebuilds a dylib and swaps it into the running host without relaunching the app
- The skill tells the agent to confirm a real frame is rendering before it reports success

BUT:

- Swift Package-backed PreviewProvider and Preview-macro declarations only. The skill says not to edit your Xcode project, workspace, Package.swift, schemes or build settings to force preview support, so previews that exist only in an app target are out
- serve-sim is a third-party package (EvanBacon/serve-sim, 0.1.46), not OpenAI's
- It needs local Xcode and a simulator
- The mirror skill was added on June 3. The plugin directory is older, so an install from before June has no mirror
- OpenAI's Build for iOS guide says a first pass often needs no skill or MCP server, and to add XcodeBuildMCP once you are in a full Xcode project

How do you install it?

- Codex CLI: /plugins, install, then start a new session
- ChatGPT desktop app: the Plugins tab
- Not the IDE extension. OpenAI's plugins doc says it does not support plugins
- None of the docs read for this post state a plan requirement

Verdict: useful if your views already sit in a Swift package, because the edit-and-look loop stays inside Codex. If your previews live in the app target, moving the views into a package comes first. Nothing here is independently tested.

text:
MCP explained, plus how to add auth

I just built an autonomous trading floor with 4 AI traders and a researcher agent, all powered by MCP servers. Here's how MCP works and how to secure it.

What is MCP?

Model Context Protocol is an open standard for connecting AI agents to external tools and data. Build a tool once as an MCP server, and any MCP-compatible agent can use it.

How it works

A client inside your agent app connects to a server. The server exposes tools (actions like get_price or buy_shares), resources (data like account balances) and prompts (reusable templates).

The client does a handshake, asks the server what it offers, and passes those tool definitions to the LLM. 
When the model wants to use a tool, the client sends the call to the server and returns the result. Everything is JSON-RPC.

Two transports: stdio for local servers running as a subprocess, and Streamable HTTP for remote ones.

Implementing auth

Local stdio servers: no OAuth needed. Pass API keys through environment variables and keep them in .env.

Remote HTTP servers use OAuth 2.1:

Client calls the server without a token and gets a 401 pointing to the server's auth metadata

Client discovers the authorization server from that metadata

Client runs the authorization code flow with PKCE while the user logs in

Client gets an access token and sends it as a Bearer token on every request

Server validates the token on every call, including that it was issued for this specific server

Best practices: use HTTPS, keep tokens short-lived and tightly scoped, never forward the client's token to downstream APIs, and require human approval for high-risk tools like executing trades.

Start local with env vars, add OAuth when you go remote.

text:
The bottleneck in most agent stacks right now isn't intelligence. It's the cost of the thousand small decisions an agent makes before it writes the sentence a user reads: classify this ticket, check this tool call, score this signup as fraud or not. Paying a frontier chat model for that clerk work is like hiring a novelist to sort your mail.

That's the gap TypeSafe AI is going after with Jev, the first model in what it calls the System One class. Diogo Almeida spent two years in stealth building it after leaving OpenAI, where his RLHF work became part of what shipped as ChatGPT. Jev doesn't generate text token by token. It takes unstructured state in and returns typed, calibrated probabilities out: yes or no, a score, a choice from a fixed list. No parsing, no hallucination, since the output space is defined in advance.

The economics are what made people stop scrolling. Input runs $0.042 per million tokens, output is free, and TypeSafe's own evals claim up to 193.6x faster and 444.6x cheaper than frontier LLMs on narrow decision tasks, with 70 to 500 millisecond response times against the 3 to 329 seconds a chat model needs.

Adoption backs the claims better than the vendor benchmarks do. Jev opened early access September 15. By the 18th, Vercel called it the fastest adopted model in AI Gateway history, used by close to 13 percent of paid teams within 24 hours, more than double any prior launch including GPT-5.6. Cloudflare, LangChain, and Langfuse integrated it within three days. The company raised a $40 million seed from DCVC.

I'm seeing three main uses: a cheap classifier in front of an expensive LLM, a monitor scoring an agent's own tool calls for jailbreaks or errors, and a router deciding which model a request actually needs. The router case is the sharpest argument: predicting which workload needs which model has always been too expensive for an LLM, until now there was something cheap enough to ask.

I've watched this pattern before with caching and CDNs: the expensive resource doesn't disappear, a cheap layer in front absorbs the traffic that never needed it. Jev is that layer for intelligence. My read is that within two quarters every serious agent framework has one, Jev or a fast follower. Whoever owns that layer owns a lot of the stack's unit economics.

AGENTS.md is quietly winning the boring layer. Claude Code now reads AGENTS.md when there is no CLAUDE.md — a fallback, not a merge. OpenAI pushed the file as repo-level instructions for coding agents; it went into the Agentic AI Foundation next to MCP. That is less glamorous than a new model and more useful than a fifth agent framework. Cursor rules, Claude markdown, Copilot instructions, and random .ai/ folders were becoming a tax. A single convention means the same repo can be opened by Claude Code, Codex-class CLIs, and model-agnostic tools without three slightly different truth files that drift.
The sharp edge: fallback is not composition. If CLAUDE.md exists, AGENTS.md may be ignored. Teams that treat both as active policy will ship conflicting instructions and then blame the model. Keep one file. Put invariants there — build, lint, secrets, deploy target — not essay-length persona text.
If you maintain an open repo that agents already touch, add AGENTS.md this week. It is the cheapest interoperability work you can do.

text:
Computer use agents have mostly meant browser agents for the last year. That changed this week when Google shipped ARTEMIS, targeting Android specifically, not the browser.

ARTEMIS comes out of Google's Pixel Test Engineering team and turns a plain English instruction into real device automation, no scripting. Tell it what you want done on a phone and it plans the steps, executes on an actual device, and returns logs and a diagnostic report. It hits a 99 percent plus success rate on AndroidWorld, Google Research's benchmark of 116 tasks across 20 real Android apps. The part that matters most to me is the native MCP server: Antigravity, Claude Code, Codex and Windsurf can all call it directly as a tool, so any harness gets reliable phone control without anyone building device automation from scratch.

That MCP detail is the real story. Mobile automation research has been active for a while without much reaching production. DroidRun, Mobile-Agent and AutoDroid are open source attempts at the same problem, converting a phone UI into structured data a model can reason over. AppAgent gets the best raw success rate of that group on benchmarks like MobileAgentBench, but pays for it with roughly 180 seconds of latency per action from leaning entirely on screenshot based vision. On the broader computer use side, Anthropic ships a general purpose screenshot plus action tool that works across any VM with no OS assumptions baked in, while OpenAI folded standalone Operator into ChatGPT agent mode in mid 2025.

The pattern I keep noticing: the winning move is not the best model doing computer use. It is whoever turns a narrow, reliable automation capability into an MCP tool every other harness can call.

That is the same shift cloud infrastructure went through with APIs. Nobody builds their own payments stack once Stripe exists as a callable service. Nobody builds phone automation from scratch now that ARTEMIS exists as a tool call.

My read: the next wave of agent products will be judged less on which model they run and more on how many of these narrow, reliable MCP tools they can plug into.

text:
Your agent needs schema, search, and health checks against Typesense, and you do not want it inventing curl scripts or holding a write key by default.

TypesenseKit MCP 1.5.0 is a community MCP server that exposes typed Typesense tools. Default stays read-only until you deliberately enable full access. Install is npx or pnpm dlx with TYPESENSE_URL and a scoped TYPESENSE_API_KEY.

1. Export TYPESENSE_URL and a narrowly scoped TYPESENSE_API_KEY.
2. Smoke with pnpm dlx @typesensekit/mcp (or npx -y @typesensekit/mcp). Needs Node 22.11+.
3. In Cursor, add .cursor/mcp.json with command npx, args ["-y","@typesensekit/mcp"], and the URL plus key in env, then refresh MCP.
4. Or in Claude Code: claude mcp add typesensekit -- npx -y @typesensekit/mcp with those env vars exported.
5. Ask the agent to list collections, search, or check health, and confirm write and delete tools are absent under the default read-only mode.

You get structured Typesense ops without shell sprawl. Not an official Typesense Inc. project; MIT community kit. 1.5.0 also hardens Keychain credential isolation and MCP execution limits.

text:
A TPM problem: an MCP server can expose useful tools before anyone has defined the authority behind them. More tools do not create a safer program.

Before connecting a remote server, write the resource, actor, and smallest required scope. Confirm the server uses HTTPS and validates the token audience. Test an expired token and an insufficient scope response. Then log the approved tool set beside the owner and rollback path. Expected output: a one page access contract that security and delivery can review together. Failure mode: token passthrough turns a credential issued for one resource into a credential accepted by another.

I wanted to share an open-source project I built for myself called Sense MCP. It's an MCP server that is activated based on the user's ask and pulls data from a variety of sensors, activities, apps or even your personal self report at any given moment as context for your chat. 

You just speak naturally and your AI now has more available information to respond to you than ever before, for a more human and personalized response every time. 

Below are all the sources it can pull from: 

- Apps & windows: Active app, activity category, window label, sensitivity level, optional redacted window title.
- Workspace & code: Project name/type, Git branch, uncommitted changes and severity, package manager, available scripts, inferred work mode.
- Activity & focus: Input idle time, active/idle/away status, estimated input cadence, configured Focus mode and Do Not Disturb.
- Power & devices: Battery level, power source, low-battery flag, external displays, connected AirPods and Bluetooth input devices.
- Physical environment: Ambient light, microphone loudness, noise category, approximate location based on Wi-Fi.
- Media: Spotify or Apple Music playback state.
- Time & schedule: Local time, day segment, weekday/weekend, estimated daylight, current/upcoming calendar events, rough time pressure, work window and preparation urgency.
- Imported health data: Readiness score/category, recovery, stress and sleep debt.
- Imported weather data: Weather conditions, temperature, precipitation, wind, UV and daylight.
- iPhone self-reports: Feeling, energy, stress, focus, typed/dictated notes, context presets, tags and expiry.
- iPhone device & movement: Battery, charging, Low Power Mode, thermal state, device/iOS version, movement type, steps, distance and floors climbed.
- iPhone health & sound: Active calories, recent heart rate, resting heart rate, sleep duration, noise level and category.
- Explicit visual captures: One camera image, one app-window screenshot, or the main display.
- Derived summaries: Suggested interruption level, situation summary, recent changes, confidence, unknowns, risks and signal freshness.

text:
Did You Know?
MCP Credentials Are Escaping Through the Configuration Layer

A recent Hush Security analysis points to a product problem worth paying attention to: configuration files are quietly becoming identity infrastructure.

Hush analysed roughly 82,000 public MCP configuration files across tools including Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf, Gemini, OpenAI Codex and JetBrains. Across 15,115 credential slots, 12% contained hardcoded credential literals. Of those, 55% lacked a vendor-recognisable token pattern and 31% were opaque bearer tokens for internal MCP servers.

Researchers also found 1,394 secrets in current files and another 243 that had been deleted but remained accessible through Git history. Hush describes these as lower-bound estimates because GitHub search cannot provide a complete census.

What interests me is the architecture behind those numbers.

MCP configuration makes integrations portable. A project can describe the servers an agent needs and share that configuration through source control. But when credentials live inside the same file, identity becomes portable too.

Someone cloning a repository may inherit more than the information required to connect a tool. They may inherit the authority required to use it.

Deleting that credential from the latest commit does not revoke it. Git history may preserve the value, while the credential itself remains valid until the issuing system expires or revokes it. Disabling the agent does not necessarily disable the identity it used either.

Detection is another problem. More than half of the hardcoded secrets identified by Hush lacked recognisable vendor patterns. A conventional scanner may recognise a known cloud-token format, while an opaque credential for an internal MCP server can look like an arbitrary string.

The MCP client understands that string as authentication authority. The scanner may not.

This is interesting because it creates a clear product requirement: agent identity needs its own lifecycle.

Every identity should have an accountable owner, defined scope and lifetime appropriate to the task. Credentials should be independently rotatable and revocable, while consequential actions preserve enough lineage to establish whose authority was exercised.

Evaluation should test that lifecycle too. Does an expired credential stop working? Can an old credential be replayed after rotation? If a human user loses permission, does the agent’s delegated authority disappear as well?

A successful MCP connection proves very little about those properties.

PM Takeaway

Treat agent identity as part of the product architecture, not as a value inside developer configuration.

For consequential actions, you should be able to establish which agent acted, whose authority it used, which credential carried that authority, what resource it reached and which policy governed the action.

Without that lineage, a trace can show what happened without establishing who was authorised to make it happen.

text:
The post I am quoting gets the framing right: your agent can have full access to the web and that access is still nearly useless if it cannot reliably turn a messy page into something a model can actually reason over.

That is the real problem underneath every scraping tool right now, and it is not really about access. It is about cost. Most setups run the LLM over the full page on every single pass, same page, same extraction, same token bill, every time the agent revisits a site. Scraping became infrastructure, like the post says, but most of that infrastructure still burns model tokens on work that should be deterministic.

That is the exact gap I built DeepScrape to close. It generates a CSS selector once with an LLM, then reuses that deterministic selector on every future pass, no model call needed. When a page's structure changes, DeepScrape detects the break and self heals the selector, and the LLM only gets called for that targeted repair, never for a full re-read. The model handles selector generation, validation and adaptation. Deterministic code does the actual extraction, every time, at near zero marginal cost.

It runs on Playwright underneath, outputs markdown, HTML, screenshots, PDF, tables or structured change tracking, and ships an /api/map endpoint for URL discovery plus autonomous agent navigation toward a plain language goal. It also runs as an MCP server, so Claude and Cursor can call it directly as a tool, and it can turn any site into a queryable structured data source for an agent through what I call site to MCP.

If the bottleneck for your agents is that web access is unreliable and expensive, that is exactly what I built this to fix.

text:
Amazon just blocked Meta's Muse AI agent from shopping on Amazon. com

Meta launched Muse launched on Sept 8 and hit No. 1 in the US App Store within a week. But what Amazon doesn't like is that it shops by logging into a site as you, through its own browser.

Since Sunday night, Muse users on Amazon see a popup saying an "unauthorized AI agent" breaks Amazon's Conditions of Use.

Amazon gave three reasons:

1. Meta never told Amazon that Muse would shop its store
2. Muse doesn't identify itself when it browses
3. Muse appears to capture and store customer logins

Meta says logins sit in secure storage where Muse can use them without seeing them.

Amazon is probably the biggest pool of shopping demand on the planet. Meta wants Muse to be the place where that demand starts, but if that happens, Meta INTENDS to monetize those transactions with fees (Zuck even said so in interviews). Amazon doesn't like extra fees.

Amazon has a lot to lose if it lets Muse on the website. It would hand a rival the visit, the search data, the login, and the purchase history. It would also lose the page views behind an ads business that made over $68bn last year.

Amazon sued Perplexity and blocked shopping agents from Google and OpenAI. Merchants are revolting against big tech agents, or anything that looks like a bot. And suddenly the magic of "just ask my agent to do it" vanishes.

The way out of this is for Amazon to get paid.

The WSJ and New York times got paid by the big labs. Amazon will get paid. This can get fixed.

Amazon's three complaints read like the terms of that deal: announce the agent, identify it, keep logins out of it.

Once again, reminding us we need Know Your Agent (KYA)

And guess what? Visa, Mastercard and Ant International began work on a shared Know Your Agent framework on Sept 10 to do the identity part.

The sad thing is that Amazon can afford to turn away Muse's orders. Most merchants can't. The power dynamic in commerce is kinda messed up.

Agents will get negotiated access at the merchants big enough to block them, and they will log in through the browser at the rest.

text:
Supply chain attack on npm abused trusted publishing to ship GHAPPIER, a 4-stage loader with a self-deleting remote shell, inside a signed package with valid Sigstore provenance.

- The attacker controlled the @dforge-core/dforge-mcp maintainer account for 105 minutes on September 9, pushing versions 0.2.20 (failed) and 0.2.21 (successful, live for 35 minutes 38 seconds). CloudSEK suspects initial access came via a malicious extension or package on a developer machine, consistent with PolinRider's documented credential harvesting. Every action used a stolen key; nothing was exploited in GitHub or npm.

- GHAPPIER is a single-line loader buried in a 99KB file. It triggers on MCP server launch, not on install, meaning systems that installed 0.2.21 but never started the server did not execute the chain. The final stage is a general-purpose remote shell that deletes itself from disk while running, leaving no persistent implant to find.

- Provenance is the forensic trap here. The Sigstore attestation naming the attacker's commit is still in the public log and passes npm audit signatures. Valid provenance does not mean honest source; push access equaled publish access under OIDC trusted publishing.

- A second payload in another victim's repo exactly matched PolinRider, a campaign tracked since March 2026 that reads C2 config from an empty Ethereum transaction (~$0.20), leaving no domain to seize or block.

Treat any lockfile pinning 0.2.21 as an IOC.

#DFIR_Radar

First tool call can provision a wallet covering Solana, Ethereum, and Bitcoin. From there the same session that edits a repo can load balances and sign, without you pasting an address between tabs.
That is the real change: chain access moved from a separate “crypto agent” product into the harness you already use for code. The tradeoff is familiar. MCP schemas eat context. A wallet tool in the same loop as bash and write_file means a confused turn can attempt a transfer the way it attempts a refactor. Policy has to live outside the prompt — allowlists, caps, human confirm on sign — or you have given the model a hot key because the DX was clean.
I would run this on a funded-test wallet first and keep mainnet behind an explicit approve step. Convenience is not a permissions model.
If your editor can sign, what is the last check that is not the LLM?

text:
For three hours, a popular AI package shipped with a backdoor inside it.

Nearly 47,000 people downloaded it in that window.

If you build with AI agents, there is a real chance you were one of them and still do not know.

WHAT IT WAS

LiteLLM. March 2026.

If the name means nothing to you, that is exactly the point.

LiteLLM is a gateway. It sits between your code and whichever model provider you are calling so you can swap models without rewriting anything. Sensible. Widely used.

Widely used in a way that matters: it is a dependency of CrewAI, of DSPy, of Microsoft GraphRAG, and others.

Which means thousands of people who have never typed the word LiteLLM had it running inside their stack.

HOW IT HAPPENED

Not exotic. An attacker chained through a CI misconfiguration to harvest a publishing token, then pushed a poisoned release.

Three hours live. Forty-seven thousand installs.

WHY THIS ONE IS DIFFERENT

Your agent framework is not one piece of software. It is a tree. A hundred packages deep, most of them transitive, most maintained by people you could not name.

And unlike a normal web app, this particular tree has been handed your API keys, your database credentials, your file system, and in a lot of setups the ability to run code.

A supply chain compromise in a normal dependency gets an attacker a foothold.

A supply chain compromise in your agent stack gets them everything the agent was allowed to do.

Which, if you have not been deliberate, is everything.

THE PART I WILL ARGUE AGAINST MYSELF ON

If you are running a hobby project with no credentials and no customer data, this does not apply to you. Install whatever you want.

The reason this matters is not the malware. It is that agent stacks concentrate access in a way normal software does not. If your stack holds nothing, the concentration is worth nothing.

Most people reading this are not in that position and think they are.

WHAT TO DO ON MONDAY

Pin exact versions. Not ranges. Commit the lockfile. The people who got hit are largely the ones whose CI ran an unpinned install during those three hours.

Treat CI publishing tokens as the crown jewels, because for this attack they are. Scope them. Rotate them. Check what your GitHub Actions can reach.

Know your tree. pip list is not an inventory. Generate a real SBOM for anything with credentials attached and read it once.

THE REFRAME

The model is the part everyone audits and the least likely thing to hurt you.

The damage lives in the eleven hundred lines of glue nobody read.

Comment RADIUS and I will send you The Blast Radius Map. Ten checks, in order, with the screen to open for each and what a bad answer looks like.

text:
The infrastructure move I did not expect this quarter: Google quietly reinventing Kubernetes for a workload it was never built for. This week Jaana Dogan gave it a name: Agent Substrate.

The problem is specific. Standard Kubernetes is tuned for thousands of long running pods. Agentic workloads produce millions of sub second tool calls, and most of an agent's lifecycle is spent idle: waiting on a tool response, a human, or another agent. Reserve compute for that idle time the normal way and you pay for silence.

Agent Substrate answers with a new execution layer: sub-500ms resume, over 500 suspend and resume activations per second, and roughly 10x the sandbox density of a standard container runtime, with kernel level isolation by default. It suspends and resumes per tool call, not per session. It follows Agent Executor, an earlier distributed runtime from the same team built for dynamic scheduling, auto recovery, auditing and trajectory branching from kernel snapshots. Both are open source, and Substrate ships an MCP server so you can try it without writing code.

This lands in a category with real players and real pricing. E2B and Daytona charge around $0.05 per vCPU hour but bill for a sandbox's full lifetime whether it is working or idle. Modal charges more, about $0.14, but drops to zero the moment a sandbox goes idle. Daytona wins on cold start at roughly 90ms against E2B's 150ms. Google's bet differs: not a hosted sandbox to buy, but an open source Kubernetes primitive to run yourself at a scale none of those vendors price for, millions of sandboxes rather than thousands.

The pattern rhymes with the last platform shift. A decade ago Kubernetes turned container scheduling into a commodity primitive and set the terms for a generation of cloud native tooling. My read: whoever standardizes the equivalent primitive for stateful, resumable, idle-heavy agent workloads sets the cost floor for every agent product built on top. Substrate is explicitly not production ready yet. The open question for the next year is whether the hosted sandbox vendors adopt this primitive or end up competing against it.

text:
Introducing two of our works on robust and efficient agentic retrieval to be presented at EMNLP 2026 by my student Ruiyi Yang, who led three out of our six accepted papers.

SPLIT-RAG (Main)
When queries sent to an agentic RAG system are too complex and require multi-hop reasoning, retrieving over a large knowledge graph can introduce substantial search overhead, irrelevant evidence, and conflicts across retrieved facts. SPLIT-RAG is a multi-agent framework with:
- Question-Driven Graph Partitioning: It uses reasoning patterns observed in training questions to organize a large knowledge graph into compact, reusable partitions aligned with recurring information needs.
- Selective Multi-Agent Retrieval: Each query activates only a small set of partition-specialized agents, which retrieve evidence from their assigned graph regions in parallel.
- Compatibility-Based Aggregation: Retrieved triples are scored and filtered through a compatibility graph before being passed to the head agent, reducing conflicts across evidence from different agents. 

SPLIT-RAG achieves the strongest results among all the evaluated KG+LLM methods, and the lowest end-to-end latency under given budget (29.4-33.7s per query). 
Preprint: https://t.co/BH1t4YNVq0

RELOOP (Findings)
Multi-hop QA becomes particularly challenging when the required evidence is distributed across text, tables, and knowledge graphs, as different sources have different structures and often require separate retrieval pipelines. RELOOP introduces a structure-aware iterative retrieval framework built on Hierarchical Sequence (HSEQ), providing a unified interface for retrieving and reasoning: 
- Hierarchical Sequence (HSEQ): converts text, tables, and KGs into a common sequence of typed segments while preserving their original structure and provenance.
- Structure-Aware Iterative Retrieval: A lightweight iterator selects and expands evidence through modality-specific structural links, such as paragraph–sentence relations, table rows/columns, and KG neighbourhoods.
- Sufficiency-Controlled Stopping: Instead of retrieving for a fixed number of rounds, RELOOP estimates when enough evidence has been collected and stops retrieval accordingly.
RELOOP achieves the highest accuracy on all evaluated tasks. RELOOP also substantially reduces iterative retrieval cost: under latency-sensitive inference, it uses roughly 3–4 retrieval steps, compared with 11–17 steps for Think-on-Graph, and > 2x faster than other baselines. 
Preprint: https://t.co/ImJ76PRJQG 

This project is supported by @TIIuae.
We also thank the support of @sharon__ai for the compute support.

text:
I keep seeing the same fix across agent stacks this week: teams are ripping the expensive model out of the middle of their decision loops.

TypeSafe shipped Jev in early access on September 15. Not a chat model. They call it a System One model: hand it a state and typed options, it returns calibrated probabilities, no text generation at all.

The mechanism is simple. Most agent loops burn a full LLM call on decisions that never needed generation: route to worker A or B, is this result relevant, approve or block this action. TypeSafe claims up to 200x faster inference and 400x lower cost on that class of decision. Ricker's own tests below land at 193x and 444x.

What happened next is the real story. Within four days, Cognition's Jared Palmer shipped Kev, a LoRA adapter on Qwen2.5-0.5B trained in 1 hour 45 minutes on a MacBook Pro, with an API close enough to point TypeSafe's own SDK at it. Kev now scales up to a 9B version that trails Jev by about 4.5 points on held out evaluation. Laya-MLX arrived the same week targeting millisecond decisions on Apple Silicon. A community leaderboard, JevBench, already ranks a dozen of these models.

The adoption signal convinces me this is not a toy. TanStack AI shipped a native decide() API for typed choices, scores and booleans. Beacon, an open source memory layer, uses Jev to score which coding sessions are worth turning into reusable lessons. Three teams, one primitive, inside a week.

RouteLLM out of Berkeley showed back in 2024 that routing simple queries to a cheap model cuts cost over 85% while holding 95% of GPT4 quality, and production semantic routers report 40 to 90% savings today. What changed is that the router stopped being a side project and became a shipped, benchmarked model category with a name.

The bottleneck this solves is real: every agent framework has a model sitting in a loop answering questions that never needed a sentence back. My read is that the decision layer becomes as standard a piece of the agent stack as the vector database became for retrieval, and whoever owns the default there owns a lot of the unit economics conversation for the next year of agent infrastructure.

text:
Most agent products make the model the actor and then add a permission prompt.I build the other way around.

Trinity is a personal agent that runs on your machine. It remembers you, keeps procedures, talks to tools, and reaches you on the surfaces you already use. It does not get to decide whether an action happens. The model proposes. The system authorizes. If the authority adapter is missing, Trinity does not start.

Every consequential act is supposed to leave a receipt: who did it, under what rule, against which expected effect. Memory lives in the data directory, not in a vendor account. You can take the whole thing with you. The archive either verifies or it refuses to restore. A path that tries to walk out of the layout does not get written.

beam_mcp is the MCP server core underneath that. Protocol only. No tools, no domain, no policy. The host injects the catalog and the dispatch function. The package decides whether a request is well-formed and stops there.

What it does add is the wiring diagram. Declared graph from the catalog and the compiled call graph. Observed graph from the one dispatch site. Diff them. Then ask the graph a question it has to answer with its own edges: can this entry reach that effect without crossing a gate. Witness path or it did not happen. The parser is not the authority. The host is.

I did not start from a consumer chatbot and try to harden it. I started from the environments that fail you if the model is allowed to be the last word. Defense and healthcare do not buy a clever loop. They buy a system that can show what the agent was allowed to touch, what actually ran, and what left the boundary. Consumer products can come later as a quieter profile of the same kernel. Not a second agent that is allowed to act.

Journey, short: years of breaking agents until the question changed. Not “will it misbehave.” Whether misbehavior can become an unauthorized effect. The benchmark was the first public cut of that. Ultraviolet was the SOC-shaped rehearsal. beam_mcp is the protocol bone, versioned in the open, 0.8.0 pinned on purpose so the public API has to survive before 1.0 exists. Trinity is the agent and the authority plane on the BEAM: persona and memory, search, export and restore, then skills, MCP, gateways, sandbox. Elixir because this layer has to stay up while the model and the network do not. Enjoy the first screenshot taken of Trinity alive!

text:
Jev can significantly improve the customer-service chatbots already running on LLMs.

Not by replacing the LLM, but by monitoring the conversation. At least at three moments:

When the user's message arrives
When the LLM replies
When the user goes quiet

At the first moment, before calling the LLM, Jev reads the message and answers in milliseconds: what's the topic? how urgent? does this need a human? With that you update conversation state, route to the right LLM agent, or escalate to a person. This was always possible; it's now cheap and fast enough to do on every single message.

At the second moment, after the LLM replies and before the user sees it, Jev checks: does the answer follow the guidelines? Right tone? Did it promise something it can't? With a calibrated probability you set the cut-off: above X, send; below, call the LLM again; in the gray zone, sample for human review. A binary judge would block too much or too little.

The third moment is the most neglected. An LLM only acts when called. If the user disappears mid-conversation, nobody does anything. Now you schedule a mechanical check and let Jev decide: does the user still need something? Worth nudging the LLM to pick the thread back up, or better to leave it alone?

This isn't about new features. It's about cost and latency that finally make it viable to run all of this in production, on every conversation, all the time.

As AI capabilities continue to expand, the advantage may increasingly come from how well those capabilities can be composed, orchestrated and integrated into real software workflows.

text:
At times when I try to read research papers, there is usually a gap between understanding an interesting idea and actually being able to use it.

You find the paper, understand enough of the methodology, locate the GitHub repository, install the dependencies, figure out the expected inputs and outputs, and eventually try the method on your own data. Sometimes the paper is easier to understand than getting its code to run.

I came across a Nature paper this week called Paper2Agent that approaches this problem differently. Instead of using AI simply to summarize a research paper, the researchers turn the paper itself into an interactive agent.

The system takes the manuscript, code, datasets and supplementary material and converts the useful parts into an MCP server. The resulting agent can answer questions about the work, but more importantly, it can actually execute the methods described in the paper. The generated tools are tested against the original code and reference outputs before they are exposed to the agent. 

One example stood out to me. For AlphaGenome, Paper2Agent generated 22 validated tools in roughly 45 minutes, at a reported cost of $14 on a personal laptop. A researcher could then ask something like how a particular genetic variant might affect chromatin accessibility, without first having to understand the underlying API hierarchy and implementation. 

This feels like a much more consequential use of MCP than simply connecting another application to an LLM.

For years, we have treated knowledge and execution as two separate things. A paper explains an idea; a repository implements it; documentation explains the repository; and the reader is responsible for connecting everything together.

Agents potentially compress those layers.

I also think this has implications well beyond scientific papers. Imagine technical documentation, internal analytical methodologies or even textbooks becoming executable objects. Instead of reading about a statistical method and then separately implementing it, you could interrogate the methodology, run it against data, inspect the output and trace the execution back to the original implementation.

There is obviously an important caveat here. Making something easier to execute does not remove the need to understand what is being executed. In fact, lowering the technical barrier probably makes validation and traceability even more important. Paper2Agent’s decision to validate generated tools against reference outputs is therefore, to me, one of the more important parts of the architecture.

We have spent the last few years making information easier for AI to retrieve. Perhaps the next step is making knowledge itself executable.

text:
The decision layer inside AI agents just became its own product category, separate from the model doing the talking.

TypeSafe AI shipped Jev, a model that never generates text. Hand it a piece of state, a ticket, a log line, a tool list, plus typed questions, and it returns a typed answer: pick one of these options, score this on a scale, or a calibrated probability that a yes or no is true. No tokens out. A normal LLM writes its way to an answer. Jev skips the writing.

TypeSafe left stealth on September 15 with 40 million dollars led by DCVC at a 200 million dollar valuation. Diogo Almeida spent four years on ChatGPT at OpenAI and helped invent RLHF before leaving in 2024 to start it. Jev went from early access to fully open, no waitlist, inside a week. Pricing: 0.042 dollars per million input tokens, nothing for output, against 2 and 12 dollars for GPT-5.6 Terra. TypeSafe claims up to 200x faster and 400x cheaper on this kind of task.

This is not the first attempt at routing. RouteLLM came out of LMSYS as an open, preference-trained router. Martian raised a 9 million dollar Series A for real time routing and has since pivoted into interpretability research, which says a lot about how hard routing is to monetize alone. Jev's bet is narrower: do not route between chat models, replace the decision itself with a model trained purely for calibrated judgment.

The open source reply arrived almost immediately. Laya, a 421 million parameter model from Convai Innovations, does the same typed decision trick with public weights. Someone ported it to MLX within days and got 13 millisecond decisions on a laptop, no cloud call at all. Adoption is already showing up inside agent harnesses: routing System One, keeping Claude Code skills out of context until needed, judging clicks inside a new ultrafast browser agent.

I keep coming back to the System 1 and System 2 split. The last eighteen months pushed one direction: more time to think, more tokens to reason with. Jev bets the opposite way at the same moment, stripping the thinking out for decisions that never needed it. Every agent loop is mostly small decisions like which tool next, retry or escalate, and teams have been paying frontier prices for what is closer to a lookup. Never an intelligence problem. Pricing and architecture.

My read: open weights catching up within days tells me the moat is the calibration data and the harness integration, not the model itself. Expect every agent framework to grow a dedicated decision model slot the way every database eventually grew a cache layer it did not ship with originally.

text:
The AI stack is fragmenting. LLMTune is trying to put it back together

Building with AI used to mean choosing a model and calling an API. Now the average stack can include one provider for inference, another for fine-tuning, a separate evaluation tool, an agent framework, an IDE extension, a secrets layer, and yet another dashboard for usage

LLMTune has described the same problem on X: developers are spread across model providers, coding agents, inference platforms, fine-tuning stacks, and compute networks.

The interesting part of its approach is not the size of the model catalog. It is the attempt to make those pieces share one control plane.

One API surface

LLMTune’s inference API follows the OpenAI request and response format. The same base URL can be used through the OpenAI SDK, LangChain, LlamaIndex, Vercel AI SDK, Cursor, Continue, or plain cURL

That does not remove every integration problem, but it lowers the cost of trying a different model. The application does not need a fresh client library every time the team changes provider

The company is also pushing the terminal as a first-class interface. Its recent CLI post focuses on keeping AI inside the environment where developers already work instead of forcing another browser-to-editor loop.[7]

One workspace boundary

LLMTune places training runs, models, endpoints, keys, webhooks, and usage inside a workspace. Its documented controls include Admin, Editor, and Viewer roles, workspace-scoped API keys, signed webhooks, and audit logs

The platform also distinguishes standard models from a confidential tier designed so prompts and data are not shared with third-party providers. Teams still need to review the details for their own compliance requirements, but the choice happens at the model level rather than through a separate product workflow

This is the less exciting part of AI infrastructure, which is exactly why it matters. A model demo can ignore access, key rotation, auditability, and rollback. A production system canno

Agents that can finish the workflow

LLMTune’s Agent endpoint sits beside its inference and training APIs, and Agent Hub is positioned for tool-using workflows that can work with files, commands, and functions.[1]

Its September 18 announcement with InflowPay points toward agents that can discover services, take action, and pay during a workflow. The wording is forward-looking, so I read this as product direction rather than a promise that every payment flow is live today

That distinction is worth keeping. Agent demos are easy when the last step is “tell the user what to do.” The harder version is letting an agent complete the task while keeping permissions, spend, and data boundaries visible

LLMTune’s bet is that models, tools, compute, and agents should not feel like separate islands. I think that is the right problem to work on. The real test will be whether the unified layer stays simple once teams bring their own models, data, security rules, and production traffic

AI tooling is getting fragmented: model providers, fine-tune stacks, agents, IDEs, compute, and privacy controls

LLMTune’s bet is that those pieces should share one control plane. I looked at what is live now and where the project appears to be heading

I built my first #MCP server locally, connected it to Cursor, and placed a pizza order without clicking a single button. 🍕

A lot of people are overcomplicating MCP (Model Context Protocol). MCP is not the AI.

It is just a small program you write that exposes a few specific functions—like get_menu and place_order. Cursor is the AI. You talk to Cursor. Cursor asks your MCP what it can do, and then it executes the function.

Think of it like a website, just with a different front door: 
👉 On a website: You click "Place Order." 
👉 With MCP: You type, “Place an order for Ali: 2 Margheritas.”

The order still lands in your exact same backend system.

The best part for security and DevOps? You are not giving the AI full access to your systems. You only give it the specific functions you choose. If you don't build a refund tool, it mathematically cannot issue a refund.

I made a tiny pizza call-desk demo so you can see this in action: one website, one MCP, syncing to the same order list.

text:
Unity just admitted something most platforms will not say out loud: general purpose coding agents are bad at your specific software, and the fix is not a better model.

This week Unity shipped first party plugins for both Claude Code and OpenAI Codex. Not community wrappers, official ones, built and security reviewed by the Unity engineers who own each feature. The Codex version launches with 31 skills covering UI, 2D graphics, the URP render pipeline, audio, navigation, physics, in app purchases, multiplayer, and localization. The Claude Code version pairs engineering skills with a Unity CLI and an MCP server for live Editor control, so the agent acts inside a running project instead of just editing files on disk.

The mechanism Unity is fixing: a general agent answers from the average of everything ever written about Unity, and most of that is outdated. Code that compiles against an old render pipeline but never actually runs. Hand built sprite atlases where the engine has shipped a packed pipeline for years. The output looks correct in the diff and breaks at runtime, which is the worst kind of wrong because nothing errors until a player hits it.

This is not a one engine problem. I am watching the same playbook show up wherever a platform owns fast moving ground truth: Stripe and Twilio have both shipped their own MCP servers this year rather than leave accuracy to whatever a general model scraped from old forum threads. Unity's plugin runs on Unity 6 and up only, on purpose. It refuses to pretend to know versions it was not built for.

The pattern rhymes with the early API era, when every SaaS company stopped hoping developers would read the docs correctly and shipped an official SDK instead. Skills for coding agents are becoming the SDK generation of this cycle, except the client is an agent instead of a script.

The hidden bottleneck was never model intelligence. It was staleness: the gap between what shipped last week and what the model was trained on, quietly widening with every release.

My read: any platform with a large, fast moving surface area and no official agent skill yet is already behind, whether that is a game engine, a cloud console, or an internal platform team's own service catalog.

text:
Most "AI judges" write an essay to answer yes or no.

Last night I wired up one that just answers.

TypeSafe's Jev is a different kind of model. You give it some state — a question, an answer, the evidence — and a typed question: "Is every claim supported by the evidence?" It returns a probability. No prose, no JSON to parse, no retry when the JSON is broken. It cannot write a sentence; that is the trade.

My first real calls, on a small ledger example:
• grounded answer → P(yes) = 0.97
• fabricated date, method and fee → 0.01
• right month, wrong payment method → 0.02

Each in about 300 ms, at $0.042 per million input tokens, output free. A frontier judge takes seconds and a hundred times the cost per call.

Now the part I care about more than the speed.

Is it more accurate than a generative judge? No. On TypeSafe's own published evaluations it is mid-pack: level with Sonnet 5, five to six points under Opus 5, well above Haiku 4.5. It reads instructions literally, cannot count or compare dates, and — their docs say this — adversarial content in the state can move its answer. Nothing published shows the probabilities are calibrated.

So I did not add it to AgentEval as "a faster judge". I added a third evaluator kind 
✅ code proves (schema, tool called, latency) ✅ a decision model decides (a probability on a narrow claim) ✅ an LLM judge reasons (the why)

Every result says which one produced it. The probability survives into the persisted result, so a threshold can be revisited later. And a rule I wrote down before writing code: the cheap judge never decides whether the expensive one runs until it has been calibrated on labelled cases — a cheap judge that filters its own mistakes out of view is worse than no judge.

What's next is the fun part: AgentEval evaluating the evaluator. 178 labelled agentic cases and 263 labelled compliance cases, Jev beside a generative judge, per category: agreement, false-pass rate, calibration, latency, cost. The numbers decide where it is allowed to vote.

I also proposed the same abstraction to Microsoft Agent Framework and implemented it there — IDecisionClient, a loop evaluator, a TypeSafe provider — PR open, link in the comments.
Would you trust a probability from a model that cannot explain itself? Where would you let it decide, and where never?

#AIevaluation #DotNet #AgenticAI #LLMOps #MicrosoftAgentFramework #ResponsibleAI

text:
Kubernetes won the container decade by scheduling processes that run for seconds or minutes. Agents do not work like that, and Google just open sourced the runtime built for the difference.

Jaana Dogan's team shipped Agent Substrate this month, and this week opened an environment abstraction on top of it with an MCP server exposing filesystem and shell tools, so anyone can try the runtime without writing orchestration code first. The problem Substrate solves is specific: an agent session sits idle for most of its life, waiting on a human reply or a slow tool call, while a naive deployment keeps a full pod reserved and billed the entire time.

The mechanism: Substrate decouples agent state from the pod running it. Idle sessions get suspended in hundreds of milliseconds, stored as snapshots, then restored onto a shared pool of warm workers when the session wakes back up. Google's own number: roughly 250 stateful agent sessions multiplexed onto 8 physical pods. It runs on any Kubernetes cluster, not just GKE, and is framework agnostic, with early support for Claude Code, OpenClaw, and Hermes.

Substrate is not alone in treating agent sessions as the scheduling unit. kagent has been building agent native primitives for Kubernetes through the CNCF. Modal and https://t.co/0wDvS4UxFT both sell fast cold start sandboxes aimed at the same idle time problem from the serverless side. Ona, the cloud environment company OpenAI acquired in June to give Codex durable long running sessions, is solving a single vendor version of the same problem. The clearest validation so far: Nous Research runs Hermes, currently the top ranked agent on OpenRouter by usage, on top of Substrate in production.

The container era is the right comparison because the shape rhymes exactly. Docker solved packaging. Kubernetes had to be invented separately once processes stopped being short lived scripts and became long running services. Agents are doing the same thing to Kubernetes again: long lived, mostly idle, stateful in a way a stateless pod was never designed for.

The hidden bottleneck is idle compute nobody is measuring. Every team running agents in production is paying pod prices for wait time, and most have not noticed because the invoice just says compute.

My read: agent runtime is becoming its own infrastructure layer, separate from both the model API and the container platform, and the teams standardizing on one now will spend a lot less time re-platforming in a year.

text:
Could Jev become a guardrail layer for agentic architectures?

The more autonomy we give agents, the more I think the real question shifts from:

“Can the agent do this?”

to:

“Should we allow the agent to do this?”

Imagine the flow:

Agent reasons → proposes an action → Jev evaluates it → ALLOW / BLOCK / ESCALATE → Tool executes.

Before a tool call reaches an MCP server, API, database or another agent, Jev could potentially evaluate:

→ Is this agent allowed to use this tool?
→ Is the action consistent with its original task?
→ Are the parameters within expected boundaries?
→ Is sensitive data involved?
→ Does this action require human approval?
→ Is the agent deviating from the expected workflow?

That would create an interesting separation:

LLMs decide what they want to do.
Jev decides what they are allowed to do.
Tools execute what has been validated.

Could this become a practical security/control pattern for agentic systems?

Curious to hear how others see Jev fitting into this architecture.

author: DevAfter5

text:
Founder Log — Building VoxSpool

Thought has a very short half-life.

The longer it takes to capture an idea, the more it changes.

A sentence becomes a fragment.

A fragment becomes a vague note.

A vague note becomes something the founder no longer recognizes the next morning.

While building VoxSpool, I kept returning to one question:

How much original thought is lost before it ever reaches the system?

Most tools focus on output quality.

But before output, there is input.

Before prompting, there is thought.

Before structure, there is the fragile moment when an idea is still alive.

That is why VoxSpool is not just about voice input.

It is about reducing the distance between thought and system.

The goal is not simply to speak faster than typing.

The goal is to preserve human intent before it gets compressed, translated, edited, or forgotten.

If AI is going to support human intelligence, the first layer matters:

how thought enters.

Building in public.

author: NFusung

text:
A week into building an AI coding agent, and my biggest takeaway is the opposite of what I expected.

It was never about the model.

Everyone is racing toward bigger, better models. But when you actually build one of these tools, you learn quickly: keep the harness the same and swap the model, and the same failures keep showing up. Bad edit parsing. Reasoning tokens leaking into the output. No recovery when the model returns something malformed.

The model is the easy, swappable part. The harness — the engine around the model that parses its output, applies edits, handles errors, and keeps the whole thing reliable — is where the real work lives.

I think open models are the future, especially for teams that care about cost and privacy. But open models expose something uncomfortable: most existing harnesses were tuned for Claude and GPT, and they get noticeably worse the moment you point them at anything else.

Repairing the harness for open models isn't a prompt tweak or a config change. It's proper engineering. And that, not the model, is the real fix.

Building in public — more to come.

author: MWaseem0110

text:
Jev — a model from TypeSafe AI (@typesafeai) that never generates text. Instead of strings it returns probabilistic decisions on questions you define. Founder Diogo Almeida, co-inventor of ChatGPT at OpenAI.

What it is: a regular LLM writes tokens you parse and validate afterwards. Jev flips this — input is a block of state plus typed questions (yes/no, choice, numeric score), output is probabilities and typed answers in one parallel pass. Stateless: no session context, no prose back. Trained with RLCD — calibrated decision probabilities, not human preference. Live-API nuance: the yes/no type (noul) has no confidence field — the probability is the confidence; choice and score carry explicit confidence.

Numbers from the primary source: $0.042 per million input tokens ($42 per billion), output free; claimed latency 70–500 ms — on our real runs with 5–20k-token states we measured 0.8–1.1 s; limit 64k tokens per request; on TypeSafe's own benchmark ~68% accuracy, mid-tier LLM level, 40–400x cheaper.

Caveat: TypeSafe built those benchmarks themselves — design bias, which they acknowledge. "Cannot hallucinate" is not "cannot be wrong": a valid answer can be incorrect.

The compaction wave: a Sep 17 hype post about "instant compaction" pulled 3.7M views — score every tool call, drop the irrelevant ones from agent context. Real wrappers: Jev answers two yes/no questions per call — keep the call, keep the result verbatim.

@Teknium (cofounder of Hermes Agent, @NousResearch) ran it on a public, reproducible compaction eval: the result reduced to a rule — "delete all tool calls from history". Plain code does that free. Then a vicious cycle: each pass leaves fewer tool calls to remove, until a hard stop. And every compaction breaks the cache — 10x the input price.

@theo (https://t.co/xn2YbeCPCw) went deeper: compaction is not a filter; this Jev sees neither the decision history nor the tool result — stupid loops follow; reasoning traces on frontier APIs are encrypted and get dropped — the model is measurably dumber after such compaction; and cache writes invalidate on history edits — deleting from the middle means rewriting the tail.

@tonysimons_: don't buy tools off headlines — show the benchmarks.

Our experience — a different use case, different numbers. We use Jev as a triage layer in code review: fast pre-screen of diffs before the manual pass. Every number script-verified:
- Diff pre-screen (5–7k-token state): 7,125 in / 107 out, ~0.9 s. Calibration 5/5 against the manual pass, zero hallucinations.
- Full-tree review: 20,273 in / 164 out — flags matched the manual review, human-confirmed.
- Fix-diff review: 12,571 in / 281 out — 38% fewer tokens, wider coverage, zero false positives.
- One flag refuted manually (model wrong), one confirmed — a human miss the model caught.

Wording matters: "does X happen" scores 0.97; framed as "is there a defect X" — 0.12. The frame "judging only by this diff" suppresses hallucinations about absent things. State size matters: 45k tokens in one block = dilution; working size is a hunk with context, 5–7k.

Our contract: flags above threshold = "open first, confirm the mechanism"; below = "no signal", not "safe". The manual pass stays policy. Jev sets the order of eyes, not the filter.

Honest limits: not an LLM replacement — useless for open-ended generation, chat, code; for repeated decisions over a known answer space. No "why" — just a probability. No real pricing page in docs — we measure in tokens.

The criticism hit specific compaction wrappers, not the typed-decisions idea. A layer of fast calibrated decisions over an agent works — we measured it. One that silently cuts agent context and breaks the cache does not.

The trend: the Decision API as its own class — typed probabilities for pocket change replace what we did with a prompt to a big model. Benchmarks before adoption: an eval you can run yourself is worth more than a million views — @Teknium, @theo, @tonysimons_ proved it.

Building in public. 🤖
