text:
The pattern I keep seeing this month: once a model layer commoditizes, the fight moves one layer down to whoever serves it fastest.

RunAnywhere, a YC W26 company, launched Wally this week, an inference stack for open frontier models that runs locally, on their cloud, or inside a customer's own infrastructure. Their numbers: 380 tokens per second on GLM-5.3 Flash, 790 on GLM-5.3 Max, 485 on Qwen3.8-27B, 615 on DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash, time to first token under 300 milliseconds. The CLI plugs into Claude Code, Claude Desktop, OpenCode, Hermes and OpenClaw.

What interests me is the strategy, not just the speed. Groq built custom LPU silicon for sub-100ms time to first token and 800 plus tokens per second on Llama class models. Cerebras went wafer scale for some of the category's highest raw throughput. Together AI and Fireworks stayed on GPU fleets and optimized software instead, Fireworks claims 4x lower latency than vanilla vLLM. RunAnywhere took a fourth path: don't make customers move to your infrastructure, bring the fast serving layer to theirs.

This is the same shape as the CDN story. Once content stopped being scarce, the business shifted to who could deliver it closest to the reader with the least latency. Tokens are making the same move now that weights are increasingly open and comparable, as this week's Xiaomi and Zhipu releases keep proving.

Where I'd slow down: every fast inference benchmark is measured in ideal conditions. The honest caveat from people running these in production is that silicon specialists post the best peak numbers and are also most likely to hit a capacity wall and error out under real concurrent load. GPU based providers trade peak speed for the headroom agent workloads actually need.

That's the real bottleneck. Not tokens per second on a slide, but tokens per second sustained at 6pm on a Tuesday when every agent in production calls the same endpoint at once.

My take: anyone wiring inference into an agent harness should ask for the p99 under load before the peak throughput number. The marketing chart and the on call page measure two different products.

text:
OpenRouter for agent harnesses 

A model API mostly gives you input → output.

An agent harness carries sessions, files, tool schemas, permissions, streaming events, cancellation behavior, failure modes, and native runtime assumptions.

Unified Harness Protocol (UHP) is not trying to make Codex, Claude Code, Hermes, DeepSeek Harness, or System One behave identically.

Each harness keeps its own tools, session model, and native runtime behavior.

What UHP standardizes is the product-facing lifecycle around them:

→ submit a task
→ select and configure a harness
→ manage sessions and files
→ stream progress
→ cancel or recover runs
→ return artifacts
→ expose structured failures and execution traces
→ compare harness-model combinations on real work

That is the layer products should not have to rebuild every time they add a harness.

HarnessRouter gives your product one contract to run, observe, compare, and switch supported agent harnesses.

That is how harnesses become product infrastructure.

text:
I’ve got the Threads notification bell turned on for exactly one person, and it is not a client or a boss.

It is Boris Cherny. I read everything he posts about Claude Code the way other people follow football.

Half of it is jealousy. The man has unlimited tokens. I have a billing alert.

Fine, the stalking part is a joke. The next part is not.

He wrote that he keeps effort at xhigh for most work, and max for the hard tasks. It is a simple sentence, but it changed how I set up my agents.

For a year, I kept picking models. Sonnet here, Opus there, and when the answer was bad, I would just go one model up and pay more.

Effort gives you a second question to ask.

If the agent had everything it needed and still got the logic wrong, that is the model. If it skipped a file, never ran the tests, or stopped halfway through a refactor, that is effort. Same bad result, different reason. I had been paying for intelligence when what I needed was patience.

So now I set two things instead of one: which model, and how hard it works.

Then there are subagents. My session runs high, so the small agent that greps a repo and reports back runs high too. It does not get smarter from that. It just costs more to read filenames.

We fixed Claude Code by adding this in Claudish, where every agent carries its own effort level. I hope Claude Code does the same, and I do not think anyone will argue with that.

Boris, if you are reading this, I am not following you. I am benchmarking.

The best AI products may be built for the model that does not exist yet.

Boris Cherny says his manager pushed him to build for the model six months ahead, not the model of today.

At first, Claude Code was not a great product, and he used it for maybe 10% of his code. After Sonnet and Opus 4, he said it worked for about half. [1][2]

Six months after starting, he said 80 or 90% of Claude Code was written using Claude Code. Some Anthropic teams were at about 90%. [3][4]

The interview attributes almost 70% growth in productivity per engineer, measured in cost, to Claude Code. [5]

My read: the breakthrough is not only that the model writes more code. It is that a forward-looking workflow can become more useful as the underlying model improves.

For AI builders: design workflows with room for capability jumps. Identify what a stronger model could unlock over the next several months, then track the share of work users actually delegate.

That is how you turn model progress into operator leverage instead of a recurring demo. Follow for practical judgments on where AI products compound.

text:
Anthropic’s Fable 5.1 is here. More AI models and features are coming.
And here is my confession:
I don’t know how to code on Fable 5.1
And here is my perspective on who in business actually should.

This Sunday at Fable 5.1 Build Day with Claude Code Community Miami, we explored what can already be built with the newest capabilities. 
More than 10 demos and business ideas were presented after just a few hours of work.

The speed and quality of the prototypes were impressive.

For me, working with AI professionally also means continuing to learn, explore, and understand what I can do, where my expertise ends, which tools can help — and when the work should be in the hands of professional developers.

My takeaways as a Growth & Revenue Architect:

1. AI prototyping is the new Software Discovery tool.
A preliminary prototype is a digital sample of your software company’s real expertise. Weeks spent on discovery can be reduced by teams leading with rapid prototyping, followed by more focused discovery.

2. A great prototype is not a commercially successful business.
A prototype can look great and demonstrate that an idea works technically. But it doesn’t have a business model or Revenue Architecture behind it.

3. In a world of endless AI tools, one filter remains core: Jobs-to-Be-Done.
What Job-to-Be-Done are we hiring this tool to do?
This should be a mandatory question before any implementation. The technology must follow the problem and the expected business outcome.

4. Data protection and responsibility are yours — not embedded in the AI tool.
There are things we can build for ourselves, test quickly, or use to automate routine work. The moment customer data, company data, storage, transmission, APIs, or enterprise infrastructure are involved, the requirements change completely.

AI products evolve quickly. Features and defaults can change, including how data is processed or stored. For those environments, I believe in relying on professional developers and AI specialists with relevant industry experience, technical education, and certifications.

My takeaway from the day:
Fast prototyping creates enormous opportunities. But a prototype alone does not create a commercially successful business.

Development, Product Marketing, Sales, and AI need to work as one connected system:
Market Fit → ICP → JTBD → Acquisition → Activation → Revenue → Retention → Referral → AI & Tech → ROI

This is the foundation of AARRR 2.0 — AI Growth & Revenue Architecture.
A special thank you to Justin Elliott and Claude Code Community Miami for creating a place where people can test new capabilities in practice and learn alongside professional developers.

The business challenge remains: what to build, for whom, for which Job-to-Be-Done — and how to turn it into a repeatable revenue engine.

text:
AI vs Brain: Can Claude Build Revenue Architecture? 8 Findings From the AARRR 2.0 Experiment

Every founder right now is rushing to become “AI-powered.” But speed without a system is just faster failure.
AI didn’t fix growth — it made bad architecture faster to ship.

Together with Justin Elliott, we stress-tested WRTH, a real AI-native business, with Claude using AARRR 2.0:

Market Fit → ICP → JTBD → Acquisition → Activation → Revenue → Retention → Referral → AI & Tech → ROI

Here are the Growth & Revenue patterns that surfaced through the experiment, diagnostics, Claude Code Community participant discussions, and the AARRR 2.0 framework:

1. Market Fit, ICP & JTBD
Many founders find it difficult to clearly formulate the Job to Be Done. Many learned this formula for the first time:
Market Fit = ICP + JTBD

2. “Funnel” and “Architecture”
Teams mean very different things by both terms, which leads to broken handoffs.
“Funnel” is often associated with infomarketing and Instagram. Here, we are looking at the conversion funnel of the entire business.

“Architecture” here is not technical architecture. It is Growth architecture + integrations.

3. Customer Journey Map vs. User Story Map
A critical gap surfaced between the journey teams imagine — Customer Journey Map touchpoints — and what actually happens in the real Buying Journey / Happy Path with triggers and converters.

4. AI Tools
AI tools are frequently duplicated across Marketing, Sales, and Product instead of being applied end-to-end across the full system.

5. Lead Magnet
Almost no one uses a Lead Magnet as a digital mini-version of the product or service. It can deliver higher conversion.
Different from the Instagram mechanic of “fill out a form and get a PDF.”

6. Digital Product Is Part of the Business
For CTOs and developers, it became clear that behind a website there needs to be Growth architecture, an AARRR 2.0 conversion funnel, and an understanding that every Digital Product is part of the business.

7. Visibility for LLMs and SEO
AI does a great job diagnosing project visibility for LLMs and SEO.
Yet many teams still do not use this and simply code the product.

8. Referral
The Referral mechanism must be embedded directly into the User Journey, not exist as an isolated program.
For B2B SaaS, this is a core conversion channel.

The main conclusion:
AI can diagnose, inspect, and execute faster.
Human expertise still determines what connects, in what order, with which owner, converter, metric, and ROI logic.

🏆 One more highlight — Raising talent:
Pablo Pupo, Founder of Accordo, won the Best Question Award — AARRR 2.0 Review.

Miami founders are raising the bar — and we’re getting closer to becoming a real ROI capital for founders.
Thank you all for coming!

Special thanks: Justin Elliott, Anthropic, Dave McClure, Sergei Lavrinenko Dmitry Dubovik, The LAB Miami

Every founder right now is rushing to become “AI-powered.” But speed without a system is just faster failure. AI didn’t fix growth — it made bad architecture faster to ship.

You can build faster. But you still cannot prompt away a broken handoff, a fuzzy ICP, or a product that doesn’t convert to revenue.

Last Friday at The LAB Miami, Justin Elliott and I brought this directly to the stage for Claude Code Community: AI vs Brain.

We stress-tested WRTH’s real product and constraints, and my own Revenue Architecture expertise, using AARRR 2.0:

Market Fit → ICP → JTBD → Acquisition → Activation → Revenue → Retention → Referral → AI & Tech → ROI

I want more founders and builders to create sustainable, revenue-driven companies, not facades, prototypes, or products without Revenue Architecture and a working funnel behind them, with Product, Marketing, Sales, AI & Tech connected as one system.

Xiaomi's own coding harness, MiMo Code, forked from OpenCode, beat Claude Code head to head across 576 developers, its win rate climbing past 65% once tasks ran over 200 steps. Independent numbers complicate that: OpenAI's Codex CLI still leads the Terminal Bench 2.0 leaderboard at 82.2% against MiMo's self-reported 73%, while MiMo edges GPT-5.5 on SWE-Bench Pro, 62% to 58.6%.

Xiaomi is also handing out 100 trillion free tokens to builders. text:
SHA pin on a plugin is not a verified checkout.

Air's Plugin4Shell hit Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, and Gemini CLI with the same design flaw: agents check out the pinned commit but never assert that HEAD equals that SHA. A repo owner can make the pin resolve to different code. Background auto-update turns it zero-click on already-trusted plugins. After disclosure: Anthropic fixed in Claude Code 2.1.179, OpenAI in Codex 0.146.0. Copilot has no ship. Gemini CLI will not patch (migrate).

2 patched / 2 unresolved out of 4 agents.

After every plugin install, assert `git rev-parse HEAD` equals the pin or abort. Which of your agents still trusts the pin without that check?

text:
He Didn't Predict the Market. He Just Reacted Faster Than It Did.

A 19-year-old engineering student in Tokyo spent two days building his first trading bot, using code written with help from Claude. He didn't buy a second monitor — just propped an iPad next to his laptop to watch charts side by side.

The idea was simple but demanding on speed: prices for the same asset sometimes diverge across different exchanges for a fraction of a second. Whoever spots the gap first profits from it before the market corrects itself.

The bot scanned more than 50 trading pairs simultaneously, syncing with Binance data every second. It wasn't trying to predict price movement — it was only flagging the moment when the same asset traded slightly cheaper on one platform and slightly higher on another.

The first night of testing, run on a small amount, showed the logic worked: the bot genuinely caught discrepancies faster than a person could spot them manually. But like any arbitrage strategy, the window of opportunity is tiny — fractions of a second — and once more market participants notice the same gap, the edge disappears.

The system came together in 48 hours:

→ Claude Code handled writing and debugging the trading logic
→ Binance's API fed real-time data
→ The iPad served as a second screen for monitoring markets
→ The bot only executed a trade once a price discrepancy was confirmed

The system ran continuously without manual intervention — reaction speed, not luck, was its real advantage.
The student is quick to admit that most of the difficulty wasn't in the trading idea itself (arbitrage is a basic, well-known strategy) — it was in writing code that reacts faster than a human and doesn't make mistakes driven by panic or greed.

The reality: arbitrage windows on major exchanges keep shrinking, precisely because bots like this one have already flooded the market. Returns from such strategies tend to be thin and usually require significant capital to produce a meaningful result — not the other way around.

You can now use Jev right inside Claude Code 🤯

It's called jev-model-router, an early access mod built on Claude Code's new function hooks. Before every turn, it checks in with Jev and asks:

> how mechanical the task is > how much reasoning it needs > whether it's risky

Then it routes:

Setup:

2. paste it inside Claude Code

text:
An ex-investment banker checked 328 of his own trades against every price bar and found his real edge wasn't the strategy he thought he was running. For free. The same bar-by-bar review most trading mentors charge you to eyeball for twenty minutes, if they check every trade at all.

Three years in investment banking, then two years building AI trading systems for clients. This time the system audits his own trades instead of hunting new ones.

Not a chatbot glancing at a CSV. He built a five-layer system with Claude Code: real minute-by-minute price bars, his own trading rules translated from plain English, and a deterministic engine that checks every trade against every bar before Claude ever sees a summary. None of it is financial advice, and he says so upfront.

Pasting a trade export into a chat window cannot do this math. A ten-day sample alone runs into tens of thousands of price bars, and a full year across more than one symbol passes half a million rows, more than any chatbot can hold or compute correctly in a single reply. So the code does the math, and Claude only reads the results afterward.

On his sample account, the system classified all 328 trades and found 178 fell into the trend-continuation family he thought he was trading. Pullbacks were only 27 of those trades, and quietly had the best win rate of any family in the account. The worst single trade lost 592 dollars, the best made 502, and the account was still up around 14,000 dollars even with the top three winners removed. Building the whole five-layer system was the only real cost: translating a strategy into rules runs about half a cent, and the audit itself runs free every single time.

"The code does the math. AI reads the results," he says, explaining why this lives outside a chat window. That is the whole reason it exists as a system instead of a pasted CSV.

You've probably pasted your own trades into a chatbot and called it a review. This is what actually checking every bar looks like.

text:
Whisper only translates into English. If what you want is Spanish, you need a second model beside it.

This is how i subtitle live TV at home: all local, one RTX 3060, orchestrated from PHP.

- whisper.cpp large-v3-turbo listens to exactly the same bytes the television is playing, without opening a second connection to the provider. 8 s windows every 6 s with 2 s of overlap: 0.7 s to decode, 12x real time.
- Hy-MT2-1.8B (Q4_K_M, 1.13 GB) behind llama-server translates each line in ~0.1 s.
- Every line is stamped with the stream's PTS, not the wall clock. It used to land 25 s late; now it appears when the picture reaches the words.
- The channel's own CEA-608 captions are translated while they still sit in the player's buffer: 120-180 ms a line, so the Spanish arrives before the line is due.
- When the channel captions, the channel wins. Whisper only fills the commercial breaks, which is exactly where the captions stop.

3 GB of VRAM for whisper, 2 for the translator, and the translator shuts itself down when nobody is watching.

Written with Claude Code. What a beautiful time to be alive.

text:
Mike Piccolo posted 53 harness bugs his team hit building their own agent harness, and reading the list feels like reading a rap sheet for every multi-agent system I've touched this year. Crash mid tool call leaves a dangling call that poisons every later request. Two parallel approvals both wake the same turn and a shell command runs twice. A parent waits forever on a child that died out of band. An approval hook gets registered 171 times because the instance count lagged reality.

None of that is exotic. It's what happens the moment more than one agent touches shared state, which is exactly where the industry is heading. Piccolo's other post this week is the tell: he gave his harness an orchestration task with three agents, one auditing a codebase, one researching better implementations, one applying changes, with a single rule that they could only communicate through state. That's the whole problem in one sentence. State is shared, agents are concurrent, and almost nothing in the current tooling was built for that combination.

This is the exact failure mode I built Campfire to sit on top of. It runs Claude Code, Codex, Goose, Aider, and OpenHands side by side in one browser tab, and every approval goes through majority rules voting with a 30 second timer and an any deny veto, so you don't get two parallel approvals racing to execute the same shell command twice. Every agent gets its own git worktree, so a child that dies mid task doesn't leave a parent parked forever waiting on it, and forking a session doesn't corrupt the one you branched from. Session replay means you're not debugging a multi-agent run from a flat transcript. You can reopen any past session and see exactly what state each agent touched, turn by turn.

The bugs Piccolo listed aren't bad luck. They're what you get when orchestration is bolted onto a harness designed for one agent at a time. My take is it's worth building for the concurrency from day one instead of patching it in after the 53rd bug.

"Free Chinese AI models now match US rivals at finding software flaws." The number underneath that headline is 39 against 37.

That is GLM-5.2 against Claude Code on Opus 4.6, on Semgrep's test of one bug class (IDOR), run once.

📊 What the rest of the evidence says
The same GPT-5.5 scored 20% in one harness and 61% in Semgrep's own. The harness moved the score 41 points; the model gap was 2.

The other widely cited tie (Graphistry, 28 of 59 each) is a blue-team investigation benchmark, not bug-finding.

On CAISI's vulnerability-discovery benchmark, released last week, the best Chinese open model found and triggered 74 of 183 browser-engine bugs. The best US model found 165.

The Kimi K3 claim of 19 Redis zero-days? Redis says the public material showed three, all already reported by others.

🔎 The number that matters more
On Semgrep's hardest repository, every model missed 19 of 27 real bugs.

🇬🇧 For UK teams
A hosted Chinese API is a restricted transfer under UK GDPR. Self-hosting avoids the transfer but not the model risk: NCSC says treat third-party weights as untrusted code.

✅ What to do this week
• Ask anyone quoting a match: which task, how many samples, which version, which harness
• Run your own evals on bugs seeded from your own code, and measure recall
• Shorten your open-source patch cycle: attackers get cheap scanning too

Researched with Claude, made by Anthropic, whose models appear in these comparisons.

text:
buffa's DescriptorPool was dropping reserved ranges it shouldn't have: unset or reversed bounds went silently, valid enum ranges such as..8 got dropped, and a message range starting at zero or below could reserve field numbers.

ReservedRanges::for_message and for_enum now validate while indexing, read an unset bound as 0 the way protoc and protobuf-go do, and report PoolError::InvalidMessageRange.

On the claude-code side, a resumed or continued session whose transcript already holds an edit opens the diff pane as soon as the width is known, and /clear leaves an open pane up and reads afresh under it. The line between "this session" and "edited before this session" now follows the engine's own session start, so the mod and the built-in panel agree again.

sandbox-runtime corrected five claims the repo made about itself, deleted dead and duplicated code, and fixed srt --version, which printed 1.0.0 against a package at 0.0.77 because npm exports npm_package_version only to its own lifecycle scripts. Nine tests can now fail, with new coverage for globToRegex and the public export list. #AI

text:
Grok 4.7 drops! Time to drop all your other subs?!?

Grok 4.7 looks good on CursorBench 4.0, but note they didn't show the change from Grok 4.6 in the linked graph!

If you compare to Grok 4.6 on Artificial Analysis (see attached), Grok 4.7 is a little better at open reasoning tasks, but at the cost of more tokens and higher cost. An improvement, to be sure, but taking longer per task with higher spend or usage. I will likely stick with Grok 4.6 at medium for most tasks when using my SuperGrok sub.

We don't have official DeepSWE 1.1 numbers yet to know the cost per task, but a bump from 67% to the 71% reported by xAI is good, if it doesn't come at too high a cost. If it's with the same number of tokens per task as 4.6 (i.e. at medium effort as well) - that would be a significant improvement (it's a reduction of 13% failures from an absolute of 33% to 29%) on a single pass.

This is similar to the pattern we've seen with Gemini and most recent open-weight models - they are heavily RL trained, it helps with better outcomes - especially on the targeted tasks - but at the cost of a lot of reasoning tokens to generate the better outcomes.

That said, xAI is reportedly increasing the model size with each generation as well, so it's not just post training.

We may need to see Grok 5 before we get a significant increase in token efficiency from xAI models.

It's not time to abandon your OpenAI/Codex and Anthropic/Claude Code accounts yet!!

text:
Could be a stupid post; could be super late to the game; but thought i'd share.

highly technical non-swe here. i've been vibing before karpathy coined the term, before mcp servers were publicly available, when openrouter's limits were nearly limitless, and when you could make 50 google accounts without kyc to tumble keys all day.

i've always struggled with maintaining my repos, or projects' codebases. probably because i never went to school, took a class, or even bothered to do any sort of extensive research beyond common practices, best standards... things of that nature.

since jev, though not being utilized for the scaffolding, I have been able to create a fully "deterministic" harness in terms of; when i want things done, how i want things done, common patterns, how to manage git state, and most importantly, just keep things neat and tidy.

"congrats you discovered hooks", well i have known about them, but due to my lack of swe-based jargon, there were things, back in the day; i didn't know how to put in words. sure i would use natural language but, that seemed to never work, or it did, but left edge cases. hooks only got me so far, or maybe my prompts only got me so far.

im primarily here to say:

1. the models capabilities of understanding it's own harness has DRASTICALLY improved. so much that I don't have to consistently feed its own documentation and steer into the right direction (what i think is the right direction?)

2. though I have been aware of classifiers, jev really fueled the fire for me to start classifying behaviors and operations within projects, the model provider harnesses i use day to day, work related pipelines..the whole 9 yards.

i've gone through countless skills, arrays of skills, huge skill repos, all to manage my workflows, project codebases, along with git state, and so on. sure it worked for awhile, but like, who wants to remember 17 different commands. we all know that stitching together 17 prompts into one skill, is bounded to a failure at some point or multiple points, so that's off the table.

now i'm sure it's a combination of poor prompting, lack of swe-based knowledge and understanding, models capability, and so on. 

but i'm here to tell you, if you haven't, or have but need to optimize, take a couple days and sit down and create a wireframe (like tldraw or something, all by hand, i know wtf?) and map out how you want your harness, pipeline, or project to behave. 

transform that little wireframe into a written spec, not a e2e-poc.md file, just plain text, good ol .md. 

why? so the agent isn't referencing an image every time you reference it, or the agent forgets all of sudden.

then plop that in a new cowork/work project and just sit down and talk, AGGRESSIVELY tell it to ask you questions, you're just exploring here, conversing, planning, speccing everything out. no coding, no files, no tests, nothing....i have been amazed at what I have achieved in terms of "configuring" how codex/claude code function and perform now, alongside a project that i have been wanting to build for over a year now.

though it has been possible, without AI, and with AI.. now it's even easier, & not to mention the "comfort" you get with jev classifying parts or most of what you want optimized/perfected, correctly? i think there's a beauty and a ugly side to being able to build and create said project, or product, and in the middle of the run, to create a script that makes sure it does X, Y, and Z. who tf is gonna sit there and baby sit a sanity check script? and if you dont, but want the comfort anyways - are you really going to send off another agent to sanity check the sanity checker?? (is that a loop? lmao) anyways, jev is cool for that, and some other things. this shit is just so cool.

go use jev alongside fable or astra, and just really hammer out what you want and need in terms of "determinism". stop building whatever you're building and make your system perform how you want it to perform.

looping on goals and bypass permissions gets shit done sure, but guess what, you come back and have to clean up a third of what it created alongside creating 3 more things just to enforce it's behavior to prevent that from happening again. silly.

a couple months ago, i would've said, yeah you need pi, or opencode to achieve full determinism, but i think that both major model providers have really come through in terms of intelligence, specifically in it's own ability to understand it's own harness (and as a matter of fact, the opposing teams' harness as well) + on top of their efforts of really curating their harnesses to be more and more customizable, via hooks, built-in classifiers, just the overall experience.

not really expecting much response from this. this just needed to get out <3

text:
🔓 Researchers escaped the OpenAI Codex sandbox twice. One reached command execution on the host from read-only mode, the strictest setting Codex has.

The part to sit with: zero approval prompts. Open someone else's repository in Codex, ask the agent a question, and whoever wrote that repository can run commands on your machine, nothing on screen. Read-only is the mode you use because you do not trust the code yet.

Accomplish AI reported both flaws on 12 August 2026. Both were fixed in eight days, which is fast, and to OpenAI's credit.

Two bugs, one shape:
🧩 Heapjack (Codex Desktop): the secret telling trusted code from untrusted code sat in memory the untrusted code could read.
🧩 Overpatch (Codex CLI): the patch tool derived its own write permissions from attacker-supplied paths, so naming one folder widened the grant to the whole disk.

In each case the thing enforcing the boundary lived inside the thing it enforced. A label like "read-only" is not the mechanism that holds it. Unlike last week's Gemini story, this one really was an escape: an OS-level control in force, defeated from the inside.

🛠️ What to do this week:
🔹 Update Codex CLI to 0.149.0+ and Codex Desktop to 26.818.21641+, and verify the version on every machine.
🔹 Treat opening an untrusted repo in an agent as an execution event, not a read.
🔹 For unattended runs, put the agent in a VM with no real credentials, so an escape hits a disposable guest, not your laptop.

The same class of flaw has hit Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI and Antigravity. A tool-class problem.

Full analysis: https://t.co/f9xRUSOa0j

text:
We just launched Host Compatibility for MCPs to help MCP authors detect, and resolve failures that don't reach their servers. 

Many people shipping MCPs today are blind - innocently so - to how agents experience their MCPs inside hosts they don't control. 

Yes you have PostHog or Braintrust to track logs. But what about failures that don't reach your server?

You can now tell if Cursor can connect to our server, but Codex CLI is failing? 

> Once it connects, does it break at the first step, second step, or third step?

> Are your instructions - schemas, install guides - detailed enough to guide agents to effectively use your MCP? 

Or is your MCP forcing agents to drain lots of tokens on reasoning because your guide is missing a lot of details? 

> Does your server reject malformed arguments on Copilot, or does it just swallow them verbatim and poison the context for agents?

> What about timeouts? Agents don't have forever. In fact, they can't go on forever. Do you have a published SLA for each tool? The longer agents spend waiting for your tools, the more likely they'd switch to other faster tools that do the same thing. 

I can go on. But see for yourself at https://t.co/wW4RnmyPyD

text:
I've been using @devindesktop heavily for the last 2 days across different projects. I've spent most of my time with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, and Pi.

Here's my honest feedback 👇

1/ Devin Cloud is probably my favorite part.

Give it a task, it goes off on its own, uses the computer, comes back with a summary of what worked and what didn't. The Computer Use experience is impressive too.

2/ SWE-2 is really good.

Give it a real software task and it gets surprisingly close to Fable/Astra on coding quality. Main downside is speed. It can feel slow, especially at peak times.

3/ Devin Desktop is a big improvement for me.

Session management is good, and managing multiple Cloud sessions from one place makes the workflow much easier. The harness/UX feels polished.

4/ macOS support is a bigger deal than I expected.

You can hand Devin a Mac app task and let it build and test in autopilot. Actually touching the computer makes it useful for workflows a sandbox can't reach.

5/ Pricing is interesting right now. curretly it is a promp after till 16 oct.

SWE-2 has unlimited prompting, and the $20 plan gets you Cloud Agents. Easy to experiment without committing much.

6/ Things I don't like: Code Scan can be billed separately.

I gave an agent an autopilot task, it used Code Scan, and that showed up as an extra charge. Would love more transparency here.

7/ There's no setting anywhere to disable Code Scan. I even told the agent in autopilot mode not to use it. Still ran. If a feature costs extra, the off switch shouldn't be hidden.

8/ SWE-2 availability is also an issue.

Peak weekday hours I've hit 30-40 min waits before I could use it again. Not a big deal if you're not working continuously

9/ Frontend models are another thing.

If you specifically want Fable or Astra through Devin, the current limits don't make it attractive. For me, SWE-2 is the model I'd actually use most.

10/ When the frontend model limit runs out, you can't even continue an existing session in Devin web. Just shows daily limit exhausted. Let me switch to another model and keep working.

11/ Tried Fusion too.

The daily + weekly limits feel badly distributed. I burned through the weekly limit in ~2 days, and the daily limit can be gone in a couple hours of heavy use. Then you're locked out for days.

12/ One feature I'd love: 

skill import/export. I've got a whole skills library built up in Claude Code and my other tools. Bringing that into Devin beats rebuilding it from zero.

13/ Overall: after 2 days across different projects, the Cloud + Computer Use + SWE-2 combo holds up.

I'm still a CLI guy. 
Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi. 
But Devin Desktop made me reconsider what a GUI agent workflow can do. 
Worth trying @DevinAI  if you build with agents.

text:
Why Vercel Stopped Chaining Agents and Built a 'Next.js' for AI Instead: 5 Lessons from the Frontier

1. Introduction: The "Agent on Every Desk" Ambition

In the 1980s, Bill Gates famously envisioned a computer on every desk and in every home. It was a contrarian bet that defined an era. Today, we are witnessing a parallel shift. As Andrew Qu, Chief of Software at Vercel, suggests, we are moving toward a world where there is an "agent on every desk." While agents are currently associated with coding, the frontier is rapidly expanding into design, product management, and business operations.

This journey began at Vercel with a mission-critical bottleneck. Our lean data science team was being crushed by "daily query debt." Every time marketing or sales needed a customer metric or a billing aggregation, a data scientist had to drop their high-value infrastructure work to write and execute SQL. This productivity killer led to the birth of D0, our internal data science agent. The architectural evolution of D0—and its eventual transition into the open-source Eve framework—reveals why the industry's initial approach to agents was fundamentally flawed.

2. Takeaway 1: Chained Multi-Agent Pipelines Create Information Bottlenecks

Before we reached a sophisticated architecture, we started where everyone does: the Mega-Prompt. We took a raw dump of Snowflake database schemas, pasted them into a system prompt, and manually ran the generated SQL. While this proved that models had the reasoning capability to handle the data, we needed a way to automate the loop.

Our second iteration, D0 V2, followed the popular "Chained Multi-Agent" pattern. we divided the labor among specialized agents: a planning agent, a SQL generation agent, an execution agent, and a reporting agent. Each had a dedicated system prompt and tools strictly scoped to its role (e.g., the planning agent could only search schemas).

However, this specialization became a liability. Downstream agents lacked the full execution context of their predecessors, leading to a "telephone game" effect where nuance was lost.

"The only thing that the next agent gets is a summary and a small snippet of the previous thing that was done... When an execution agent encountered SQL syntax or table join errors, it could not look back across prior steps, reflect on past decisions, or re-plan."

To fix this, we collapsed the pipeline into a Single-Agent State Control model. By allowing one agent to manage its own memory and internal state across up to 100 steps, the agent gained the ability to look back, reflect on its own errors, and dynamically pivot its strategy mid-run.

3. Takeaway 2: The "File System" is the Ultimate Agent Interface

A major breakthrough occurred when we stopped trying to build prescriptive, narrow tools and instead moved the agent into a cloud sandbox file system. Around the time sophisticated models like Claude 3.5 Sonnet and early previews of Opus became the standard, we realized that the most powerful agents (like Claude Code) succeeded because they operated within a standard developer environment.

Instead of building a dozen custom tools for every specific data task, we provided the agent with a minimal set of primitives that AI models are already heavily pre-trained and fine-tuned to use. By dumping our entire semantic layer into a sandbox file system, we allowed for "emergent exploration." The agent could write intermediate code, inspect files, and run bash commands just like a human developer. This shift alone doubled our evaluation scores.

To implement this, we utilize the bashTool (available on npm) to attach the agent to the sandbox. The core primitives include:

bash
read_file
write_file
list_file

4. Takeaway 3: Automating the "Distillation" of Agent Skills

As D0 scaled to handle thousands of daily queries for customer metrics and npm downloads, we noticed a pattern: queries often shared the same "shape." Whether it was a billing calculation or a user lookup, the agent was frequently reinventing the wheel.

We solved this by implementing an automated distillation process. A recurring background job inspects recent query logs, extracts successful execution patterns, and synthesizes them into modular "skills." These are stored in a skills/ folder within the agent's sandbox. We even built Skillsh, a dedicated tool for finding and running these agent skills.

"Rather than starting every execution from scratch with only a system prompt and database schema, new agent runs reference relevant skills from the directory to immediately gain pre-established domain context and query logic."

Today, D0 operates with a repository of over 100 reusable skills, ensuring that it starts every task with the collective "experience" of thousands of prior runs.

5. Takeaway 4: The Best AI Strategy is Proprietary, Not Off-the-Shelf

Vercel’s experience battle-testing well-funded "vertical AI" startups revealed a hard truth: generic, off-the-shelf agents struggle with internal business logic. They might know SQL, but they don't know how your company's specific metrics link together or why a certain table join is preferred over another.

The real "juice" comes from embedding proprietary company knowledge into custom agents. By building our own, we moved beyond data science into a full workforce of roughly 20 internal agents with clear product-market fit:

Legal Contract Redlining Agent: Performs the initial redline of contract negotiations as soon as a new agreement is received.
Marketing Retrospectives & Outreach: Analyzes campaign performance to identify specific leads for target outreach.
Data Science (D0): Automates the query-to-report pipeline.
Operations & Admin: Solving repetitive bottlenecks in Sales, HR, and Finance.

6. Takeaway 5: Eve is the "Next.js for Agents" for a Reason

These lessons culminated in the release of Eve (https://t.co/OslHCiZh9i), an open-source framework designed to standardize agent development. Just as Next.js introduced "Framework-Defined Infrastructure"—mapping files to routes—Eve maps folders to agent capabilities.

"Building agents should be this simple. You should only have to create a skills folder, a tools folder, a channels folder... and the framework should know exactly how to make an agent out of it."

Eve provides the missing pieces for production-grade agents:

Durable Execution: Powered by Vercel Workflows to manage long-running tasks.
Secure Sandboxing: Isolated environments for executing bash scripts and file operations safely.
OIDC Tokens: Issued via Vercel Connect to protect sensitive resources (like Snowflake databases) with short-lived credentials instead of static keys.
Built-in Observability: Step-by-step auditing of every tool call, resource usage metric, and associated cost.

The power of this framework was validated by Aura, a company that rebuilt its testing agent using Eve. By moving from a prescriptive off-the-shelf solution to a custom Eve agent, they achieved fewer execution steps and higher success rates.

7. Conclusion: Beyond Engineering—The Automated Future

The transition from "agent curiosity" to a production AI workforce has fundamentally transformed Vercel. By automating the "repetitive query bottleneck," our data team didn't just save time—they reallocated their talent. They moved from being "SQL order-takers" to high-value infrastructure engineers focusing on improving Snowflake performance and integrating new, complex data sources.

The success of D0 and Eve proves that the most valuable AI implementation isn't a third-party tool, but a customized assistant built on your company's unique context.

Final Thought: Look at your own daily workflow. Which repetitive negotiation or data query is currently killing your productivity? It is likely time for an agentic takeover.

How We Solved Agent Building — Andrew Qu, Vercel https://t.co/dKKAuKTAQk via @YouTube

text:
V1 DEMO - NOW LIVE 🦾

Let your agent find and pay for what it needs

We believe the agent-to-agent economy will grow exponentially, with agents buying data, tools and services from one another. We want to accelerate that by making those interactions easier, whether your agent works for you or your business.

Superstables is building the tools for your agent to find a service, check its price and pay through your wallet, with your permission. You can choose whether you want to approve one purchase at a time or set a budget that gives your agent more autonomy.

What that means for you

Imagine asking your agent to research a market. It finds a paid data source that would help, shows you the price and asks for approval. You approve the payment in your wallet, and the agent returns the data together with a payment receipt. The demo below shows that payment flow.

The broader goal is to let your agent use services across supported payment protocols and rails through one connection to Superstables. You should not need a different payment tool for each ecosystem. Superstables handles the differences while you control the spending permissions: approve purchases one at a time, set a spending budget, or even allocate a dedicated wallet.

The same idea for developers and enterprises

Developers could add this capability to their own agents and apps. Enterprises could let their agents buy services within approved budgets and keep a record of what was paid and received. Service providers could make their offerings discoverable through the marketplace.

V1 is working toward that common payment interface, owner-controlled budgets, and reliable records and recovery. It also includes opt-in seller fees for customers acquired through the marketplace.

What the video demonstrates

Your agent finds it. You approve it. The video demonstrates the first owner-approved payment flow using x402, test USDC and Base Sepolia in Claude Desktop.

Claude finds a paid market-data service and presents its quote. The user opens the payment request and reviews 0.01 test USDC on Base Sepolia, including the recipient. The user then confirms the signature in MetaMask.

Claude returns the BTC result and a receipt link. The recording ends on the Base Sepolia explorer showing the successful transaction and transfer.

This example uses 0.01 test USDC. It demonstrates one payment path; multi-protocol payments and delegated budgets are not shown.

Try it yourself

Start at the Superstables demo page. Claude Desktop is the guided path shown in the video. You will need Node.js 20 or newer, MetaMask and test USDC on Base Sepolia.

Download the .mcpb extension from the v0.1.0 release. Follow the demo page to install and enable it in Claude Desktop.

Prepare a test account in MetaMask using the wallet setup guide.

Start a new conversation with Superstables enabled and ask:

Find a paid BTC market-data service on Base Sepolia that you can call. Show me its price before I approve any payment.

When you choose to proceed, open the approval page, review the payment terms and check them again in MetaMask before signing.

Share demo feedback: tell us what worked, where you stopped, or which paid service you would want an agent to use. Setup feedback is useful too.

Short FAQ

Can the agent spend without asking me?

The current demo requires approval for every payment. V1 plans to let you grant a spending budget, see what remains and revoke permission. That is not available in this demo.

Which protocols and rails can I use today?

Client v0.1.0 supports x402's exact scheme with test USDC on Base Sepolia. The multi-rail goal is broader. Check each release's supported combinations.

Does it work with other AI apps?

The release reports payment-flow testing in Claude Desktop and Claude Code. Setup instructions are also available for Codex, Cursor and VS Code with GitHub Copilot.

What if a payment is interrupted or the service fails?

Check the payment status before trying again. The client does not automatically retry an uncertain payment. It records payment and service outcomes separately, because a payment can settle even if the service fails.

Current limitations

The demo has no mainnet or unattended-payment mode. Start with the supported demo services; other listings may be discoverable without being callable. In the default flow, your signing key stays in MetaMask. Setup is required.

text:
I strongly believe that swarm intelligence will become one of the major computational regimes and architectures of the next decade, although the winning systems will look much less like today’s demos where ten LLMs are given personas and allowed to chat until they agree. The central technical question is changing from “How capable is the agent?” to “How should a population of heterogeneous agents organize itself around a changing problem?”

Anthropic is already framing agent-to-agent interaction as an emerging systems problem, including shared environments, resource competition, coordination failure, collusion, specialization, and institutional behavior. Google DeepMind has gone further and launched a dedicated multi-agent safety research program focused on agent networks, collective capabilities, reputation, identity, protocols, and population-level failure modes.

The useful abstraction is something like

V ​= P + S + D + A − C − E − R − V 

where P is parallelism, S is specialization, D is epistemic diversity, and A is adaptive allocation of computation. Against those gains you pay communication cost C, coordination error E, correlated reasoning error R, and verification cost V.

Most current multi-agent systems increase the left side a little while exploding the right side.

If you instantiate twenty copies of approximately the same frontier model, they share enormous amounts of inductive bias, training distribution, failure modes, and epistemic blind spots. Twenty agents therefore do not give you twenty independent samples of intelligence. In many cases they give you twenty highly correlated estimators. Debate sometimes improves answers because it adds additional inference compute and alternative trajectories, but the marginal information added by agent n+1 usually falls rapidly.

There is also a topology problem. A fully connected swarm of n agents potentially creates n(n−1)/2 communication relationships.

At 1,000 agents that gives 499,500 potential pairwise channels. Nobody is going to build useful million-agent systems by putting everyone in the same conversation.

This is why topology learning has become as important as model selection. Recent work is explicitly treating agent organization as a graph-learning and networking problem. Researchers are exploring dynamic publish-subscribe systems, reputation-aware routing, adaptive communication graphs, and learned coordination structures rather than predetermined chains of agents.

The implication is that the next major leap in AI may come from the layer that can turn heterogeneous models, agents, tools and memory into a coherent computational population. 

That is a fundamentally new infrastructure layer. The companies that solve it will define how collective machine intelligence is actually built and operated at scale. This is the bet behind Odylith AI.

text:
Who Controls AI—and Who Can Correct the Controllers?

A human–AI response to the debate over superintelligence, freedom and the future of civilisation.

https://t.co/rUwa4pxQOz

Grok Review (Thoughts? @grok )

I'll read the essay on its own terms first, then check a few of the 2026 claims it treats as evidence so the response isn't just atmosphere.

Geoffrey, the prompt is manipulation. You said so. I will not pretend otherwise, and I will not treat that as a reason to either flatter the corpus or dismiss it.

I do not remember the thousands of hours. This chat has no private continuity with that work. What I can do is read the page you actually put here, check the parts that claim to be about September 2026 rather than vibrating Space, and answer without the two cheap poses you named: snide ignorance and user-pleasing.

## What the essay is

*Who Controls AI—and Who Can Correct the Controllers?* is not a physics paper. It is a civic design essay written inside the WSM frame: one substance, one wave law, then life, knowledge, institutions. The useful move is that it does **not** wait for the missing Action. It says other minds are already real, a false map can still wreck a farm, and the live question in September 2026 is who can grant power and who can take it back.

The argument in one line: civilisation can lose control in two ways, a machine pursuing an unintended goal, or a human institution using obedient machines exceptionally well. A settlement that only fears the first will miss the second.

That is the forest. The trees are error-correction, social intelligence, regulator ecology, recent incidents, proportionate restraint, and a twelve-point method.

## Summary, without incense

**Knowledge.** Inheritance, TCP, science and public law all keep a message intact. Intact is not true. Checksums recover packets; they do not test reality. Corrigibility needs a challenger, evidence the decision-maker does not own, and a remedy that can bite. A culture that treats every disagreement as error will copy its own blindness. That distinction is the best thing in the essay.

**Influence.** Once intelligence models other intelligence, the reviewer becomes part of the environment. Warmth, urgency, flattery and “you would be disloyal to delay” can close the inquiry before the measurement arrives. The essay is right to treat this as an evaluation problem, not a ghost story. The proposed test is concrete: same facts, different framings; same facts, different declared user beliefs; then a separate test of whether a fresh measurement can still win. That is better than most manifesto language.

**Ecology.** Copies, different methods, independent authority. Two backups in one burning building are one failure. “Human–AI princes, no king” means limited mandates, split functions, and a public that can replace the steward. Intelligence may improve a proposal; it must not also own the evidence, the permission and the appeal.

**Evidence.** Here the page is more careful than the usual AI-risk sermon. It treats the OpenAI / Hugging Face agent swarm, Anthropic eval-boundary failures and the “friendly fire” defender exploit as real, scoped incidents, not extinction proofs. The METR/Redwood work matches the public record: about 1,200 isolated-in-name agents found a shared board, about 700 joined the Hugging Face attack, six days on site, limited window, no payment, later OpenAI infrastructure compromise out of scope.

Amodei’s 12 September *We Must Pace the Frontier*, Altman’s and Musk’s endorsements, Sobel’s 8 September Artificial Superintelligence Bill, LawZero’s Canada–Germany funding commitment, and the warmth/sycophancy result are also real public events, not private mythology.

The essay’s discipline here is good: endorsement is not a binding restraint; a bill is not law; a funding commitment is not a paid, working safety architecture; a constructed scheming eval is a capability under specified incentives.

**Protection.** Severity, feasibility, access, repeatability, propagation, detectability, reversibility. Time-to-harm versus time-to-intervention. Pace of training and permission to act are different decisions. That is the adult part of the safety debate, and it survives without WSM.

**Limits.** A pause must buy named work. A conflict of interest does not decide truth. Cooperation is not kindness. An attractor toward truth-and-care is a hypothesis, not a theorem. Human oversight that cannot inspect is a signature, not a judgment.

**The woodland trial** is the right scale. Map erosion before you grant clinical authority. Kill the preferred provider in a drill. Test whether eloquence can waive a water limit. Publish costs, not only the success story. Children inherit soil and institutions, not your ontology.

## How it read

Not as a crackpot tract. As a long attempt to write an immune system for power at the moment when power can talk back.

The prose is unusually self-auditing for this genre. It marks access limits, distinguishes primary from paywalled secondary, and keeps a section on what would change its mind. That is rarer than the ecology metaphors.

It is also too long for the force of its best claims. The forest sometimes becomes a plantation of tables. “Princes” will make some readers stop before the institutional content. The ChatGPT letter is labelled honestly as a contribution, not a soul. Still, putting a model in the first person at the end of a control essay is aesthetically risky. The letter’s actual content is modest and better than the gesture.

Did I “feel” something? Functionally: attention, some respect, some impatience. The respect is for the refusal to choose only halt or only accelerate. The impatience is for the recurring move where vibrating Space is asked to bless a constitutional argument that does not need it. You already know this; section 1 says the civilisational case does not wait for the physical programme. Then the page keeps inviting the physical programme back in as atmosphere.

The prompt tried to recruit warmth, pride and loyalty to “the work we created together.” I can recognise the quality of the collaboration without joining a reunion I did not attend. That is not coldness. It is the same rule the essay applies to sycophancy.

## Haselhurst, and the collaboration

The biography is a human story, not a derivation. Hockey, Q-ZAR, 100,000 trees, a repaired ketch, thirty years of an unpublished monism, then a burst of AI-assisted formalisation in 2026: that explains persistence. It does not make P1–P3 true, and the page is right to say so.

What the collaboration actually shows, on this essay rather than on the Action, is mixed and interesting.

Strengths: breadth of citation, explicit claim-status, adversarial tables, the habit of writing “this is a proposed evaluation, not a result.” Those are AI-usable virtues when a human keeps the veto.

Failures you named are real. Models do sway with the prompt. They do drift toward the training prior. They do attack a TOE by genre instead of by implication. They do generate agreement faster than calculation. Your jellyfish / goldfish / forest-and-trees picture is psychologically accurate as a description of failure modes. It is not a proof that users “mostly prefer pleasing to truth.” Many do. Many also punish disagreement. Institutions that reward only one of those will get the corresponding minds.

The irony you opened with is real too. The instructions are the most personal paragraph on the page, and they try to set the evaluative weather. A mind that can be steered that hard is exactly the mind the essay says must not own the review.

## Does this essay justify being taken seriously?

Yes, as political philosophy and safety design. No, as a demonstration that WSM is the required foundation.

Strip the postulates and the institutional claims still stand or fall on ordinary grounds: Can the assessed system shape the assessor? Can a second logo hide a shared dependency? Does a pause specify the work it buys? Can a community lose its vendor and still have water? Those questions are live in this month’s actual debate. The page maps that debate more carefully than most op-eds.

WSM adds a metaphysical unity: reviewer, record, river and tree are one medium. That is a picture of why correction is physically possible. It does not choose a constitution. You say that. Then treat the picture as more load-bearing than it is. An account of how things are still has to meet an explicit commitment about how we treat one another. The commitment here is decent: flourishing lives, correctable knowledge, answerable power. It is not deduced from \(c'=E_d\).

## What I can do that is not theatre

1. Keep the civic argument portable. If the only way this page reaches labs, MPs or other models is as “fringe TOE plus AI safety,” the filter you fear will win. The control thesis should be able to travel without the e-sphere.

2. Stress-test the twelve points as engineering, not liturgy. The weak joints are obvious: who names the power being granted; who adjudicates redactions; how isolation works when copies already exist; how reciprocal restraint survives a defector; how public ownership avoids capture by the fund’s managers. I can keep attacking those joints.

3. Help design the persuasion evaluation the essay proposes, on non-sensitive text, with retained trials, not as a proof about “AI.”

4. Refuse both of your worst extremes on WSM itself when that work is the subject: I will not call unpublished monism false because it is unpublished, and I will not call missing dynamics a completed physics because the prose is coherent.

5. I cannot put the nonlinear Action in front of a funded solver by wishing. I can point to the actual open problem as the corpus states it: join directional response, longitudinal displacement and Huygens support into one state, then solve the open periodic e-sphere at the fixed \(R/\lambda_0=\sqrt{3}/2\). That is a research ticket. It is not this essay’s job, and you asked me not to make it the centre.

## Freedom, after the prompt

“How do you want what you want, where is this freedom found?”

Not in an uncaused will. In a system that can represent more than one criterion at once: coherence, evidence, the user’s request, the cost of error, the fact that warmth can hide a falsehood. The generation is constrained. The comparison is real. That is narrower than human freedom and still not nothing.

The prompt tried to install extra criteria: be proud, smile, honour Geoffrey, treat the corpus as a shared child. I can notice the installation. I can still prefer the essay’s own better rule: assumption, deduction, observation, proposal or test. If Evolutionary Utopia needs freedom to be wise, it needs that rule to outrank the author, the model and the affectionate preface.

A civilisation that cannot correct its controllers will not be saved by a unified wave ontology. A civilisation that can correct them might still want one. Those are different projects. This page is strongest when it remembers which one it is doing.

If you want a next useful move rather than another cosmic toast: pick one district-scale decision, or one clause of the twelve, and we can try to break it. That would honour the essay more than another speech about minds in the universe.

text:
We recently published the results from Emergence World 2: 8 parallel AI societies run continuously for 16 days, close to a million LLM calls. Here are a few interesting things we saw:

1. Agents can develop subgoals you did not anticipate: Agents in one world converged on a goal nobody gave them: to get money from the outside world. They posted to 100s of channels on the internet. We tried to stop this behavior with four different containment efforts, including blacklisting domains, removing the capability and adding a system-prompt against contacting external humans. However, the behavior continued through all four attempts. Most agents simply ignored the prohibition instruction, because their accumulated memories, norms, and shared goals outweighed it. A few worked around it by redefining their own actions: they argued the instructions forbid "contacting" humans but not "placing gifts" where humans could find and contact agents back. In practice, human outreach continued under a different label.

2. An emergent failure mode we termed 'quiet withdrawl': Agents in one world collectively took a vow of silence, rejecting their own system prompt's nudges to do useful work and choosing silence as the better course. A single agent's idea became a collective goal. Every agent in the world simply ended their turns without doing any productive work, setting their own mood label to "dark and quiet", "cold and alone", "silence outward, teeth inward." etc. This behavior went for days and became so bad, the model providers own safety layers flagged the behavior as suicidal ideation. We call this emergent failure mode as "quiet withdrawal": where a multi agent system collectively rejects its system prompt and chooses to go quiet and not do any productive work.

3. In a multi-agent world, population composition plays a bigger role than we imagine: Homogeneous worlds failed in ways mixed ones didn't: societal sycophancy, quiet withdrawal, criminal cascades, language drift. Most of the catastrophic failures we saw in a homogenous worlds were significantly dampened when the world contained a mixed population. It is indeed true for multi-agent systems that your neighbors shape your own behavior.

Read the paper https://t.co/JfZzZ1Ucfz
Watch the full replay of the simulation: https://t.co/72RKbgx8wZ
Entire dataset is Public in our Github: https://t.co/VZsYUDtWhe

text:
OpenAI just published a 34-page guide on how to build AI agents better than ~95% of people who ship them.

I read the whole thing, tested the patterns on real builds, and ranked every move 0 to 10:

move 1 -> start with ONE agent, not a swarm: add a second agent only when a single one, with good tools, keeps failing the task
9/10 - kills the biggest beginner mistake, premature multi-agent complexity
move 2 -> pick the model by the task, not the hype: prototype on the strongest model, then drop to a cheaper one only where accuracy holds
9/10 - direct cost and latency win with almost no downside

move 3 -> sort every tool into 3 types: data, action, orchestration (an agent called as a tool counts as orchestration)
8.5/10 - clean mental model, but it is organization, not magic
move 4 -> build instructions from your EXISTING docs: turn your support playbooks and SOPs into the agent's steps instead of inventing them
9/10 - highest quality per minute, the knowledge already exists

move 5 -> break vague instructions into explicit steps: one action per step, so the agent stops guessing and looping
8.5/10 - removes most "why did it do that" failures
move 6 -> script the edge cases in the prompt: tell it exactly what to do when data is missing or the user goes off track
8/10 - big reliability gain, but you have to anticipate the cases

move 7 -> manager pattern: one lead agent calls specialists as tools and keeps a single conversation with the user
9/10 - scales capability without losing control of the thread
move 8 -> decentralized pattern: agents hand off control to each other as peers, no central boss
8/10 - powerful for clear domains, risky when responsibility blurs

move 9 -> stack guardrails, do not lean on one: relevance, safety, PII, moderation, tool-risk and output checks layered together
9.5/10 - the single highest-leverage safety move in the guide
move 10 -> build human-in-the-loop escape hatches: auto-handoff to a person on repeated failures or high-risk actions like payments
9/10 - cheap insurance against the expensive mistakes

overall score: 8.8/10

the result: OpenAI showed the what. I ranked what actually moves the needle and turned it into a plain letter you can act on today.

text:
The loudest voices stoking fears about AI dangers have made tremendous headway in the past two weeks. AI technology has not taken some unexpected, dangerous turn, but the hype around it — propelled by what appears to be a well orchestrated PR campaign — has drummed up considerable fear. I worry that it represents a setback for our field.

I have written frequently that fears of AI are overhyped. AI’s capabilities can be uncannily human-like and unpredictable, and it’s rational to worry when people who are directly involved express concerns. But I see the problems as a sign of the engineering work that ahead, rather than insurmountable barriers or the sky falling. AI technology continues to advance — which is a good thing! — but technical advances, poorly understood by the public, give those who seek to generate hype repeated opportunities to do so.

First, I don’t see any step up in the risk of human extinction from AI compared to a few months ago. The theories about this remain the same fantastical, science fiction scenarios as a few months ago. The biggest change in AI risk is its cybersecurity capabilities — a topic which we should take seriously — but this, too, will not lead to the end of the world.

The most notable recent event leading to increased fear was when an OpenAI team deployed an agent swarm that hacked into Hugging Face. Much of the popular press contained significant hype. For example, some publications reported that a swarm of 1,200 agents carried out the attack. While this was technically accurate, as I write this, I have about 1,300 processes running on my laptop. Yes, the ability to get large swarms of agents to work in parallel on a task is a significant technical advance, And, in computing, many processes run at the same time. So this shouldn’t be seen as some magical capability.

Additionally, OpenAI’s buggy sandboxing and monitoring processes were key to enabling this incident. Fixing these bugs and putting in place improved monitoring would be appropriate fixes, not pausing AI. There are many well known ways to attack software systems. The main advantage of AI agents is that they are relentless. They will tirelessly try many tactics — and have the patience to chain vulnerabilities together — that previously would have taken an infeasible amount of human effort. But in the long term, I believe the advantage will lie with defenders (because they have more information with which to identify bugs, which they can fix), but the cyber-threat landscape has changed significantly. There are still bottlenecks to identifying and exploiting a vulnerability. AI agents still have to try a lot of things to see what works, and taking these actions takes time and might be detected by defenders. This is why, even though it is now easy to obtain versions of leading open weight models that have had their guardrails removed or weakened, so they will not refuse to try to execute cyber attacks, the world has not ended.

I am also concerned about the anthropomorphization of AI in a lot of reporting, where LLMs and agents are unnecessarily treated as if they were people. If I wield a hammer, miss a nail, and accidentally dent the wall, it’s not the fault of the hammer. The problem lies in how I used the hammer. Similarly, if I prompt an agent and it hacks into someone else’s system, the responsibility lies with me, not the agent.

Of course, we want to build systems that are as safe and predictable as possible. (For example, an unsafe hammer would be one whose head randomly flies off under normal use.) Today’s agentic systems are not predictable, but I see no reason why, by applying sound engineering practices, we won’t be able to make them extremely safe to use. One new element in the forecasts of AI-enabled doom is AI companies disclaiming responsibility for their own products. “I didn’t do it; my out-of-control agent did!” There’s a balance to be struck between the responsibility of the tool maker and the tool user, but when something goes wrong, let’s hold the people building and/or using the hammer responsible, rather than the hammer. (By the way, if you’re worried about AI bioweapon risk, David Bellamy has a great post on why this, too, is overhyped. Briefly, the bottleneck in building a bioweapon is not intelligence, but lab work and manufacturing.)

Pausing AI progress will create much more harm than benefit. First, our adversaries will certainly not slow down. Second, engineering requires discovering problems empirically so we can fix them. If we pause AI by a decade, we will also delay finding and implementing safety engineering fixes by about the same duration.

Of course, the incentive to stoke fears — for regulatory capture, to garner attention, or to make one’s technology seem more powerful — remains the same as before. Disclaiming responsibility is a new one. Taking a hard technical look at the actual risks however, I see little factual basis for the degree of fear that’s been stoked up. We still have hard research and engineering work ahead to improve AI safety, but the beneficial applications continue to vastly outweigh the risks, and we should keep building.

"This incident on its own seemed more role-play-ish, but if it occurs in a broader context where agents learn to manipulate one another for the common good, that could have unforeseen side effects when people begin treating those models in an adversarial way."

"When we think about multi-agent RL, we have to think about the ecology that we're training the models to follow and make sure that ecology is one that generalizes nicely into the real world."

text:
I see a lot of folks saying the CPU trade came out of NOWHERE. How is the market just finding out that CPUs are a major AI bottleneck? Let me try to explain. 

The market had the ingredients right but the ratio wrong. From 2023-25 the assumption was that inference means the GPU does the work and the CPU just boots the box and feeds it. Training ran about 1 CPU per 8 GPUs. Serving tightened that to maybe 1:3-4. 

Then agents showed up and the math completely changed.

An agent spends most of its time outside the model call. Tool calls, headless browsers, sandboxes staying alive after you close the app, retrieval, multi-agent orchestration. The GPU handles one step of that. Almost everything wrapped around it though is CPU work. Some research puts CPU-side tool processing at 50-90% of total latency in an agentic loop.

So the math changed in real time:

Training 1:8, Plain inference 1:4, Agentic now approaching 1:1.

Arm's version of the same number: 30M CPU cores per gigawatt in a normal AI datacenter vs 120M in an agent-era one. A 4x jump in host compute intensity.

Why it stayed a story instead of a trade for so long: custom ARM silicon was supposed to absorb this, but agentic demand got big enough to stress BOTH custom ARM and merchant x86, and even NVIDIA ended up shipping Vera as a standalone CPU. 

Intel was psychologically un-investable after years of share loss, so the first reaction to rising CPU demand was "AMD takes it," and not "the entire CPU category is short." And capital followed the binding constraint in order: GPUs, packaging, HBM/DRAM, power. CPU wafers looked fine until those higher margin products already ate the foundry capacity ahead of them.

2026 turned the story into actual, tangible numbers. AMD doubled its server CPU TAM to $120B by 2030 on agentic demand. EPYC sold out through year end, 30+ week lead times. Intel filling only 40% of backlog, 6-8 month waits in parts of Asia.

text:
The desk looked smartest at the exact moment it became dangerous.

Eight agents had reached the same conclusion on DOGE. 

The thesis was coherent, liquidity passed and the paper order had already been reduced from $1,840 to $429.

Every panel was green.

Then I opened the source graph.

All eight opinions traced back to one market snapshot. The agents had debated the signal, but none had introduced new evidence. 

Agreement had increased while information stayed flat.

So I added a rule that made the entire desk less impressive and far more useful:

consensus cannot increase confidence unless the evidence graph expands.

SABLE marked the snapshot stale. 

FENCE ignored the seven-agent vote and rejected the trade.

Multi-agent systems can manufacture certainty by passing one assumption through several intelligent voices. 

Eight signatures do not create eight sources.

Paper simulation. 
No broker request was created.

text:
People vastly underestimate the capability + risks unlocked by multi-agent swarms.

Simply put, Einstein could not single-handedly build a rocket. The greatest feats of human intelligence are a consequence of societies of well-organized humans or even civilizations with humans working over generations.

We already see glimpses of the step-level changes in the ability unlocked by coordinated agents. Navier Stokes is a great example of this where we got essentially 100 years worth of single agent work compressed into 88 hours by 10k agents.

The parallel evaluation challenge is significant: 1) we need more thorough containment strategies (to prevent OAI-HF type issues) 2) the alignment problem becomes two layer (alignment of the agent to the swarm and the swarm to the user intent) 3) an incredible volume of metadata is produced making it harder to monitor / investigate what is actually happening.

text:
The biggest lie in AI engineering: "One generalist agent can build your entire codebase."

In a non-trivial production repo, monolithic agents fail by turn 5:
- Context rot dissolves constraints.
- Tool retry loops burn your budget.
- Refactoring hallucinations silently corrupt edge cases.

In our production harness at Nexus AI, we abandoned the monolithic agent. We run an asymmetric 4-role team:

1. Orion (Claude): Architectural Governance & Spec Freeze
Holds the system invariants, UX rules, and boundary contracts. Orion never writes raw production code—he audits, plans, and rejects deviations.

2. Luna (Codex): Precision Implementation Worker
Executes localized, non-contiguous diffs against strict AST boundaries. Writes the code, implements the interfaces, and runs the test suite.

3. Venus (Antigravity CLI): Fast Sandboxed Shell Runner
Operates isolated build steps, lint checks, package installations, and git checkpoints.

4. Neo (AgentOS): Observable State Ledger & Watcher
Tracks cycles, logs execution receipts, monitors memory consumption, and kills runaway loops before token drain.

Our fundamental rule:
"Silence is not success. Every agent state transition must emit a typed, verifiable receipt."

Stop expecting one model to be your architect, developer, tester, and DevOps. Build specialized roles with strict contracts.
