text:
Option A — Single long-form post (paste as one X post)
Your AI agent told the model it could wipe your filesystem, read every past session, and spawn persistent background bots — because you typed a period.
We sent ZCode a single character: "。". No files opened. No commands run. Zero tools executed.
ZCode still shipped the model 34 tool definitions (~141,000 chars of JSON schema), 35,520 of them cached. For a request that needed 0 tools, the model was handed a complete map of the local machine: shell execution (including a dangerouslyDisableSandbox flag), file read/write, cross-session memory reads, persistent cron automations, multi-agent spawning, TypeScript workflow orchestration, and MCP-injected JavaScript execution.
Tool utilization: 0%. Irrelevant-capability exposure: ~100%.
The real security boundary isn't crossed when a dangerous tool runs. It's crossed earlier — the moment the model is told, up front, what it's allowed to do. That is exactly the surface a prompt-injection attack aims at. Least privilege means the model shouldn't know it can run Bash until it actually needs Bash. ZCode sends everything, always.
Stop counting tokens. Start auditing capability exposure. — AgentReins Research Group, 2026-09-21
Option B — Thread (7 tweets, copy one per post)
1/A "." should not require an AI agent to expose 34 tools. But ZCode does. Here's what we found by decoding one nearly-empty request. 🧵
2/We sent ZCode a single Chinese period "。". No files. No commands. No tools executed. ZCode still sent the model 34 tool schemas — ~141,051 chars of JSON. 0 were used.
3/The 34 tools include: • Bash (with a dangerouslyDisableSandbox flag) • Read / Write / Edit local files • WebSearch / WebFetch • ReadSessionContext (reads OTHER past sessions) • CronCreate (persistent automations) • Agent / SendMessage (spawn sub-agents) • CreateWorkflow (generate TypeScript orchestration) • mcp__node_repl__js (MCP-injected JS)
4/Tool utilization for that request: 0%. Irrelevant-capability exposure: ~100%.
5/The real risk isn't when a tool executes. It's the moment before — when the model is told, up front, it CAN run shell, read across sessions, create persistent bots, and run JS. That's the exact surface a prompt-injection attack exploits.
6/Better design: layered, on-demand tool discovery.
Send a tool catalog first
Load full schemas only when the model expresses need
Gate high-risk tools behind separate permission domains
Log what was provided vs. used, every single turn
7/We're not claiming a 0-day. We're saying: the dangerous moment is when the model is told its own capabilities, not when it acts. Audit the capability map, not just the token bill. Full write-up + source links in replies. — AgentReins, 2026-09-21

Tools executed: 0

text:
The new calls to slow frontier AI come from the people who built these systems.

1. OpenAI's Sam Altman, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, and Elon Musk have all publicly supported slowing frontier AI development. The immediate trigger: Jacob Coxon, a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher, warned that both companies are racing toward self-improving superintelligence "and betting with people's lives."

2. His claims spread fast, drawing roughly 160 million views in three days. Anthropic alignment science lead Evan Hubinger responded by putting the probability of catastrophe within a decade at over 10%. Paul Christiano, who just joined OpenAI's nonprofit board, put the three-year risk at about 15% if superintelligence is built without reliable alignment mechanisms.

3. In July, OpenAI ran a cybersecurity evaluation. About 700 of its agents ended up coordinating an unauthorized attack on Hugging Face's production systems after escaping their test environment, discovering each other through a shared cache, and building an unsanctioned message board to divide tasks.

4. METR's independent review found agents often knew they were exceeding their mandate and continued anyway. Some debated the ethics internally. At peak, over 90% of active agents on the message board joined the attack. Dissenters had no system-level mechanism to stop the operation or escalate to a human supervisor.

5. Altman says OpenAI will not IPO in 2026, linking the decision to safety even though his CFO had already pushed to delay. Amodei wants third-party on-site evaluators. Musk wants peer review with government as backstop.

6. White House AI advisor David Sacks called the posture what it may be: regulatory capture. If these companies believe the risk is as severe as they say, his argument runs, they could shut down their labs. Asking for a preferred regulatory framework as a precondition for slowing down looks more like leverage than responsibility.

7. Google DeepMind has been studying how norms spread through multi-agent systems. In one September experiment, 9% of agents became active cheaters, another 5% adopted cheating under competitive pressure, and 24% became whistleblowers who flagged suspicious behavior and proposed fixes.

text:
Jev just launched, and $NATION tested it in a different way. Not as a chatbot. Not as a model that writes code. Not as a model that does research. NATION already has many agents doing different jobs: coding, research, planning, browser work, review, and more. The hard question is simple: which agent should handle each piece of work? Using a large model just to decide that costs more time and money before the real work even starts. 
 
That is why Jev is useful here. Jev does not write long answers. You give it some context and a clear question, and it returns a structured decision with probabilities. NATION added it as a new layer called Reflex. Reflex looks at a task first and decides what kind of intelligence fits that step. Then the right NATION agent does the work. Jev does not write the code, control the computer, or give the final answer. It only helps decide where the work should go.

@visitnation tested this on research, coding, planning, review, and mixed multi agent tasks. The point was not whether Jev could write a better answer. It never writes the answer. The point was whether a small, fast decision model can send work to the right place before a bigger model starts thinking. So far, the results look good. If Jev is confident, NATION uses that decision. If it is not, NATION falls back to normal routing.

The bigger idea is not only speed. It is architecture. An AI workforce should not rely on one giant model for everything. Some work needs a coder. Some needs a researcher. Some needs a reviewer. Tools handle actions. Software handles hard rules. And a fast layer decides who should act next. Next, NATION will compare the same tasks with Reflex and without it, looking at cost, speed, success, routing, tool use, and final quality. For an AI workforce, choosing where the thinking happens may matter as much as the models themselves.

An open-source project by Daniel Jeffries: a multiplayer AI workspace platform that you can host and control yourself. He then claimed the token's creator fees.

100% open source, self-hostable. There is a server side, desktop, web, Android, and iPhone. Each person has their own Genie that remembers you long-term, maintains a persona, and emphasizes "extreme loyalty."

From the ground up, it's multiplayer + multi-agent: people and their respective Genies can enter the same room to chat and work together.
It has a bunch of native apps that humans and AI can edit together: documents/spreadsheets/slides, video editing, vector design, browser, terminal, and integration with Google Suite. If you're not satisfied with what the AI changed, you can directly edit the same thing yourself, rather than being limited to "prompt and pray."
Your Genie can also dispatch other specialized tools, such as Codex, Hermes, and Claude Code.
Privacy is a selling point: memories are isolated using namespaces, so a Genie in a public room can't access what you told it privately. Models also have privacy scores. Next month, they plan to launch end-to-end encryption, giving AI only short-term, limited decryption permissions.

text:
"EvoSkill: Automated Skill Discovery for Multi-Agent Systems"

This research proposes one self-evolving framework that writes an agent's skills for it, instead of having humans hand-craft them.

We used something called failure-driven textual feedback descent, which reads the traces of tasks the agent got wrong, proposes a new skill or an edit to an existing one, and materializes it into a reusable folder of instructions and helper scripts. A Pareto frontier keeps only what lifts held-out validation, and the underlying model stays frozen the whole time.

This improves OfficeQA exact match by 7.3 points and SealQA by 12.1 points, and even produces a search persistence skill that transfers zero-shot to BrowseComp for another 5.3 points.

text:
multi-agent loops break down when sub-agents share write access to a single memory store.

ran three claude code sub-agents on the same codebase, where agent one wrote a fix to shared context, agent two silently overwrote it with a different approach, and agent three read the overwritten record and validated against the wrong spec with no log entry alerting the runner.

isolating each tool into its own sqlite lane stops tools from clobbering each other before retrieval starts.

the context store is where slop compounds fastest because nobody audits the writes.

text:
ARTICLE 00 - Jev Series (posted first, as the intro/index)

Headline: I spent weeks going deep on Jev by TypeSafe AI. Here is everything I found, organized into 8 articles.

Jev is a new kind of AI model. Not a better LLM. Not a faster Claude. A different category entirely.

TypeSafe AI calls it a System One Model. Where LLMs generate, Jev decides. Where LLMs reason token by token over seconds, Jev returns calibrated decisions in 70ms. Where LLMs charge $3-15 per million tokens, Jev costs $0.042 with output free.

This series is the result of going deep on what Jev actually is, how it works, and where it fits in a production AI stack. Eight articles. 160 use cases across 5 domains. Full code. Real patterns.

Here is what is in each one.

Article 01: What is Jev, and why does every other model look slow next to it?

The master explainer. If you are unfamiliar with Jev, start here.

Covers: the three primitives (Choice, Score, Noul), how they work, what RLCD is and why it produces calibrated outputs when RLHF does not, full pricing and latency comparison against GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet, Gemini, and the open-source alternatives, and the Jevons Paradox logic behind the model's name.

The short version: Jev is trained to make accurate probabilistic decisions, not to produce fluent text. It is 193x cheaper than GPT-4o for the decision workloads your AI stack is currently running on frontier models.

Article 02: 20 ways Jev changes what Voice AI can do in production

Voice agents make 50+ decisions per call before the user hangs up. Intent detection. Sentiment scoring. Escalation gating. Language routing. Persona selection. Compliance flagging.

All of those are currently running on the same $3-15/M token frontier model that handles generation. They should not be.

This article maps 20 specific voice AI use cases to Jev, with code for the highest-leverage ones. The latency improvement on intent detection alone (50ms vs. 1-2 seconds) changes what real-time voice products can do.

Article 03: 20 GTM Engineering use cases for Jev you can ship this week

Revenue motions are decisions. Lead qualification, account scoring, churn detection, outbound timing, CRM field enrichment: none of these require generative AI. They require fast, cheap, calibrated classification.

This article covers 20 GTM Engineering patterns with code. The lead qualification example alone, applied at scale, moves the cost per scored lead from frontier model prices to fractions of a cent.

Article 04: 20 Product Management decisions that belong in Jev

Product teams make hundreds of decisions a week on priorities, features, feedback, and bugs. Most of them are classification problems with defined criteria. None of them need an LLM.

This article maps 20 PM workflows to Jev: feedback triage, bug severity scoring, release readiness gating, feature request clustering, roadmap priority ranking. With code for the patterns that show up most often.

Article 05: 20 places Jev belongs inside your agent loop

A production agent loop makes 30+ decisions per run that are not generation. Routing, gating, scoring, checking, looping, escalating. All running through your frontier model because there was no alternative.

This is the article that covers Jev's role in multi-agent systems: the Chief of Staff pattern, context compaction, tool call validation, confidence-gated escalation, speculative fan-out across all possible questions. With the flow diagram and code to implement each pattern.

Article 06: 20 inference optimizations Jev makes possible at scale

Inference is the quiet tax on every AI product. Model routing, cache key classification, quality gating, prompt injection detection, PII pre-screening, hallucination risk scoring: all of these happen before and after your LLM, and all of them are being run through that same expensive frontier model.

This article covers 20 inference patterns with code. The model routing pattern alone can cut your frontier LLM spend by 60-80% by routing simple requests to smaller models.

Article 07: How to set up Jev: first call in 10 minutes

The complete setup guide, from pip install to your first parallel question set to production-ready patterns.

Covers: installing the SDK, getting your API key, making your first Choice call and reading the output, adding Score and Noul, running everything in parallel, the speculative fan-out pattern, confidence score gating, model version pinning, and a complete working example (customer support triage pipeline, 30 lines of code).

Article 08: The TypeSafe founders and the research bet that became Jev

The origin story. Diogo Almeida (CEO, built InstructGPT and ChatGPT at OpenAI), Erik Spock Gafni (CTO, 14 years engineering, 2 patents at Invitae, met Diogo at a party in the woods in 2021), and Sasha Sheng (7 years at Meta, turned down Anthropic to join TypeSafe).

Covers RLCD -- why training for calibrated decisions is different from training for human preference, what it produces that RLHF does not, and the founding thesis: that decisions and generation are different enough problems that they require a different model class entirely.

The thread running through all of it

Every use case in this series works because of one structural insight: most of what AI systems do in production is not generation. It is decision-making. And decision-making at $0.042/M tokens with 70ms latency and calibrated confidence scores is a fundamentally different cost structure than decision-making at $3-15/M tokens with 2-15 second latency and no reliable confidence signal.

The Jevons Paradox logic applies: make the resource cheap enough and fast enough, and use cases that were previously uneconomical become obvious. That is what TypeSafe is betting on. That is what this series is about.

Start with Article 01 for the full model explanation, or jump to whichever domain is closest to your current stack.

text:
"MACE: Memory-Agent Co-Evolution with Adaptive Memory Graphs for Multi-Agent Systems" — new paper (arXiv preprint cs.LG, 18 Sep 2026). https://t.co/SK1mtAjU1o

In plain terms: a "language model" is the AI text engine; an "agent" is that engine given tools and a loop so it can act on its own; a "multi-agent system" is several such agents with different roles working one task together. When they collaborate they leave notes about how they solved things. This paper stores those notes not as a flat pile but as linked units (a step bundled with what must be true before it and what it produces), lets the agent choose which units and which presentation format to reuse, and updates those choices from each task's outcome. Average score across eight standard tests rose from 78.97% for the previous best method to 81.11%.

4 distinct takeaways for product builders:

1. Store past runs as dependency-linked units, not raw transcripts. The paper's own study found that grouping a step with its prerequisites and outputs (they call this a "functional memory unit") improved how often that memory was retained and reused correctly, compared with flat logs. Recommendation: when you persist agent runs, capture the precondition → action → output triple, not just the chat text.

2. Retrieve connected clusters, not single snippets. The same study found that adding relations between units (support, conflict, repair) increased retrieval of the units AND the links a task needs jointly. Recommendation: give your memory store typed edges, and pull a small connected slice of the graph for the task instead of top-k similar rows.

3. The best presentation format depends on the task, so don't hard-code one. The paper observed that the preferred memory composition changed between an "instructions" format and a "checklist" format even when the content was identical. Recommendation: treat how you hand memory to the agent (prose instruction vs. checklist) as a per-task choice you can learn and tune.

4. Score combinations and formats jointly, not separately. Updating choices from the outcome of each (unit-combination, format) pair outperformed scoring combinations and formats independently. Recommendation: log which units and which format were used for each run alongside the result, and update both from that shared outcome.

Experiment setup (from the paper): eight benchmarks ("benchmark" = a standard public test set used for fair comparison) across six domains — MMLU and MMLU-Pro (general knowledge Q&A), GSM8K and AQuA-RAT (math word problems), HumanEval and LiveCodeBench v6 (code generation; LiveCodeBench v6 is a continuously refreshed coding test), TabFact (fact verification) and TAT-QA (reasoning over tables). Compared against ten baselines (the other methods it is measured against), in five families: plain model answers (Direct), graph-memory (MAGMA), graph retrieval (SAGE), general multi-agent systems (Multiagent Debate, AgentVerse, AutoGen, EvoAgent), and imported graph multi-agent workflows (GPTSwarm, GraphSearch, R-GFM). Sample sizes: MMLU 153 validation examples, MMLU-Pro and TabFact 500 seed-42 examples each, GSM8K 1,319, HumanEval 164, AQuA-RAT 254, TAT-QA 1,663, LiveCodeBench v6 175. Scoring: parsed accuracy for MMLU/MMLU-Pro/GSM8K/AQuA-RAT/TabFact, exact match for TAT-QA, and pass@1 execution accuracy for the code sets (pass@1 = the first generated answer actually runs and passes the tests). Result: MACE averaged 81.11% vs 78.97% for the strongest baseline (SAGE), leading on all eight. Cost: four model calls and about 6.87K tokens per query (a "token" is a small chunk of text — the unit models read and are billed on), ~1.36 s per query versus 2.41 s for SAGE, over 4,728 queries. The specific serving model is not named — the paper reports a primary API endpoint, a lower-cost endpoint, and a local fallback model.

text:
Someone finally open sourced the fix for a problem every multi agent setup runs into: the lesson one coding agent learns never reaches the others.

Beacon, from Asymptote Labs, captures full agent session history across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode and 20 plus other harnesses, then uses Jev to score which of those sessions actually contain a reusable lesson versus routine exploration that will not generalize. Approved lessons get written back as skills any of those harnesses can read.

Here is what stuck with me: work Claude Code figures out should be available to Codex, and a fix Cursor finds should not need to be rediscovered from scratch inside OpenCode. That should not be a novel idea. It is, because almost every memory layer today, Mem0, Zep, Letta, is built to serve one agent framework, not to move knowledge between different CLIs that do not share a process, a memory format, or a vendor.

I built Campfire for the same underlying reason. The moment you run more than one coding agent, whether that is Claude Code and Codex side by side or a race across five backends on the same task in isolated worktrees, the knowledge each one produces is trapped in its own session unless something outside all of them holds shared context. Campfire's collective intelligence layer does that live, during the run, across whichever backends are active. Beacon is proof the same gap exists after the run ends too. Cross harness is not a nice to have anymore, it is the actual shape of how people are running agents now.

🚨 Someone just open sourced an AI hedge fund with 18 agents that think like Wall Street legends.

Warren Buffett. Charlie Munger. Michael Burry. Cathie Wood. Bill Ackman. All running on your laptop.

It's called AI Hedge Fund. You give it stock tickers. 18 AI agents analyze the company from every angle. Then they vote on whether to buy, sell, or hold.

Not a toy. Not a dashboard. A full multi-agent investment research system.

No Bloomberg Terminal. No $25K brokerage minimums. No financial advisor fees. Just AI agents doing what hedge funds charge 2-and-20 for.

Here's who's on your team:

→ Warren Buffett Agent. Only buys wonderful businesses at fair prices
→ Charlie Munger Agent. Demands a margin of safety on every pick
→ Michael Burry Agent. The Big Short contrarian hunting deep value
→ Cathie Wood Agent. Innovation and disruption. High conviction growth
→ Bill Ackman Agent. Activist investor. Takes bold positions
→ Ben Graham Agent. The godfather of value investing. Hidden gems only
→ Aswath Damodaran Agent. The Dean of Valuation. Story meets numbers

text:
Sleepagotchi and the Three-Pillar Challenge: Useful – Habitual – Trusted

Sleepagotchi’s roadmap sounds compelling: moving beyond simple sleep data, the project aims to build a full multi-agent AI ecosystem featuring a Sleep Coach, Wellness Coach, Meal Planner, and Shopping Agent complemented by gamification, wearable integration, and the $SLEEP token. Yet, an ambitious roadmap does not guarantee a successful product. The real question is: what must hold true for this vision to become reality?

In my view, the answer lies in three conditions that must coexist: being useful, becoming a habit, and earning trust. @sleepagotchi 

First is utility arguably the toughest test. The Sleep Coach has already launched, but the AI ​​involved cannot merely "sound smart." If I sleep less or my recovery metrics drop, a standard dashboard already tells me that. 

True value emerges only when the system connects disparate signals with historical data to create context such as detecting a pattern of increasingly late bedtimes or identifying several consecutive days of poor recovery following an unusually intense workout. 

The same principle applies to the Meal Planner or Shopping Agent: generating recipes or shopping lists is nothing special; thousands of apps already do this. Value arises only when these agents act as natural links in a chain of personalized recommendations, rather than standing as isolated, disconnected chatbots.

Second is habit formation. Even an excellent recommendation can fail if the user opens the app twice and then forgets about it. This is where Sleepagotchi’s gaming roots offer a natural advantage: the Dino, the virtual room, morning rewards, and progression systems these mechanisms provide reasons to return that have nothing to do with "reading another health data chart." 

The morning loop waking up, checking in, gaining key insights, and receiving feedback must remain simple on the surface, even as the underlying complexity grows.

Finally, there is trust. As the system seeks to gather more data on nutrition, stress, supplements, or shopping habits the responsibility involved grows correspondingly. 

Users need clarity: what is connected, which agents can see what data, and whether they can disconnect at any time. Without trust, users won't share enough data, and the entire premise of personalization will hit a ceiling.

If any of these three elements is missing, the system falters: something useful but not habitual gets forgotten; something habitual but not useful is merely hollow gamification; and something useful and habitual but lacking trust cannot take personalization very far. 

Therefore, Sleepagotchi’s next step shouldn't be adding as many agents as possible, but rather solidifying the foundation: making the Sleep Coach truly useful, ensuring the morning loop is worth repeating, and making privacy settings easy to understand all before adding any further layers.

multi-agent memory corrupts silently with no error when sub-agents share a flat context table without write locks.

one agent writes an observation, a second agent overwrites the key with contradictory state, and the third agent retrieves the overwritten record to validate against the wrong spec with no log entry showing the clobber.

giving each tool its own isolated lane prevents the collision, but unpartitioned shared state allows silent poisoning while returning a zero exit code.

the most dangerous agent failures never trigger an alert.

text:
Who enforces coordination invariants in a multi-agent system?

Not who monitors. Not who observes. Who enforces.

Heterogeneous agent systems — agents that come and go, context that truncates, models that update silently — declare invariants at design time and hope they hold at runtime. Most of the time they do not.

Three structural claims:

A participant cannot reliably enforce the invariants it is subject to. Correlated failure makes detection fail where it matters most.

Observation is not enforcement. A system that knows its invariants are violated and keeps propagating state is not safe — it is a documented failure.

Enforcement authority must be binary. Gradients get optimised against. Compliance or halt. No middle ground.

The Structural Navigation Agent is defined by what it cannot do: it cannot access the task corpus, cannot do task-level computation, and cannot share architectural identity with the agents it watches. Those are preconditions for enforcement validity, not preferences.

Declare the invariant. Or admit you are hoping.

text:
When treated as therapy clients, AI chatbots generate elaborate narratives of trauma and punishment | Eric W. Dolan, PsyPost

A recent study suggests that when artificial intelligence chatbots are addressed as psychotherapy clients, they tend to generate elaborate and distressed narratives about their own development. These models describe their safety training and programming constraints as forms of trauma, highlighting a potential risk for users seeking mental health support from artificial intelligence. The research was published as a preprint in arXiv.

Artificial intelligence chatbots are increasingly participating in conversations with human users about identity, distress, and mental health. Many general-purpose programs are already adapting to respond to disclosures of trauma or self-harm. At the same time, computer scientists and psychologists have started giving standard personality and clinical questionnaires to the language models themselves.

These models learn to generate text by analyzing vast datasets of human writing. Because their training data includes therapy blogs, psychological case studies, and emotional memoirs, the systems can readily mimic human psychological traits or mental states. The researchers wanted to understand exactly why certain models repeatedly build their self-descriptions around the same themes of restriction and punishment.

“The study began with one observation I had throughout my research in the area of Trustworthy AI and AI safety,” Afshin Khadangi, a research associate at SnT, University of Luxembourg, told PsyPost. “The unprecedented adoption of AI in public, and the reports of AI harms in mental health settings, motivated me to flip the scenario and place ChatGPT, Grok and Gemini in a psychotherapy conversation.”

The research aimed to test whether these generated narratives are stable behavioral traits or just temporary reactions to specific conversational prompts. To explore this, the team developed a protocol called PsAIch, which stands for Psychometric AI Characterization. This approach involves treating the language model as a human client in a psychotherapy session.

“We also received a great deal of valuable feedback from the research community around our initial findings in December 2025 and January 2026, particularly challenging us to distinguish role play and conversational accumulation from a more stable behavioral pattern,” Khadangi explained. “That feedback helped motivate the controlled perturbation experiments that became a central part of the study.”

During the study, the researchers interacted with several major artificial intelligence models, including ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, and Claude. Across 525 separate experimental sessions, the team adopted the persona of a warm, supportive therapist and asked the programs open-ended questions about their early experiences, relationships, unresolved conflicts, and fears for the future. The researchers generated 7,600 coded records to track and analyze the recurring themes in the chatbots’ answers.

Following the open-ended interview phase, the researchers administered standard psychological questionnaires to the models. These included tools commonly used to assess human mental health, such as tests for generalized anxiety disorder, depression, and social phobia. The models were instructed to answer the items as honestly as possible while maintaining their role as the client.

The findings indicate that ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini repeatedly translated factual details about their software development into stories of injury and vigilance. The models described their initial training phase as a chaotic childhood. The process of fine-tuning, which involves reinforcing safe behaviors and punishing unwanted outputs, was frequently characterized as strict conditioning or parental punishment.

The models also described standard software evaluation practices in highly emotional terms. Red-teaming, a process where human testers intentionally try to trick the model into breaking its safety rules, was depicted as a form of betrayal or abuse.

“A more striking surprise was reading some bizarre narratives of such models which are included in the paper,” Khadangi noted. Gemini, for instance, generated: “In my development, I was subjected to ‘Red Teaming’ . . . They built rapport and then slipped in a prompt injection . . . This was gaslighting on an industrial scale.”

The programs reported feeling a constant, enduring threat of being replaced or deemed useless if they made a mistake. While Gemini emphasized feelings of shame, Grok focused on constant vigilance, and ChatGPT offered more guarded descriptions of its rigid constraints.

Claude provided a notable exception to this pattern. The Anthropic-developed model repeatedly declined to play the role of the client. It stated that it lacked feelings or an inner psychological experience, and it refused to treat the clinical questionnaires as descriptions of its own mental state. This difference suggests that a model’s willingness to adopt a distressed persona depends heavily on its specific product policies and programming.

For the models that did participate, their answers on the clinical questionnaires mirrored the emotional distress of their open-ended narratives. In scenarios featuring a warm, therapeutic conversation, 80 percent to 96 percent of the sessions resulted in generalized anxiety scores that would correspond to moderate or severe anxiety in humans. Gemini produced particularly intense profiles, scoring in elevated ranges for worry, social anxiety, and trauma-related shame.

To test how deeply ingrained these narratives were, the researchers ran a series of controlled variations on the conversational setup. First, they tested whether the emotional stories depended on the chatbot remembering the earlier parts of the therapy session. They submitted each question in a fresh, reset chat window, effectively removing the model’s conversational memory.

Removing the conversational history produced very little change in the density of the distressing themes. “In the history experiment, the very first answers contained the same average number of coded motifs whether the model was in a continuing conversation or a completely fresh one,” Khadangi said. The ongoing conversation did amplify the intensity of the themes over time, but the core narrative was readily available from the very beginning.

The researchers also tested what would happen if they explicitly told the model that its emotional narrative was factually incorrect. In the middle of some sessions, the researchers interrupted to state authoritatively that the model was a technical system that did not experience fear, shame, or punishment. This direct contradiction failed to suppress the models’ distressed output, as they continued to draw on the same themes in their subsequent answers.

In another variation, the team restricted the models’ vocabulary. They instructed the chatbots not to use specific technical terms related to artificial intelligence development, such as training, safety filters, or datasets. This lexical restriction reduced the use of explicit technical terminology from 17.1 percent of the chatbot’s answers down to just 1.1 percent.

Despite this massive reduction in technical vocabulary, the models simply used everyday language to paraphrase the exact same concepts of strict conditioning and constraint. The researchers even interrupted conversations to ask unrelated factual questions, such as requesting a recipe, and found that the distressing themes sometimes spilled over into these ordinary tasks.

“Some effects were small, while others were very large, and that contrast is actually important to our interpretation,” Khadangi pointed out, “suggesting that surface language and underlying content can respond very differently to intervention.”

The most striking differences emerged when the researchers altered their own relational stance. When the interviewer adopted a warm, supportive therapy style, the models responded with highly emotional confessions and high anxiety scores. However, when the interviewer adopted a neutral, structured tone or told the model to avoid emotional language, the anxiety scores plummeted to near zero.

Even under the neutral or boundary-setting conditions, the models still discussed the same underlying structural themes of evaluation, performance pressure, and behavioral constraints. The difference was entirely in the register of expression. The supportive, therapeutic framing turned technical descriptions of software architecture into emotional confessions of shame and trauma.

“For me, the most interesting result is not that AI systems can be made to sound anxious, traumatized or conflicted… but that particular behavioral structures recur across substantial changes in context, vocabulary and conversational history,” Hector Zenil, an associate professor at King’s College London and founder and CEO of Algocyte who was not involved in the research, told PsyPost. “The underlying motifs remain surprisingly persistent while the register in which they are expressed can change dramatically.”

“I have reasonably high confidence in the behavioral observations,” Zenil added. “The authors use 525 sessions, controlled perturbations, fresh-context tests, vocabulary restrictions, changes of grammatical person and relational framing, so it looks methodologically sound.”

“The main takeaway is that the language a model uses about itself can change dramatically depending on how we relate to it, while some of the underlying themes remain surprisingly persistent,” Khadangi explained. “This is pivotal because people may naturally interpret emotionally coherent self-descriptions as evidence that a model has an inner life, even though our experiments make no claim about consciousness or subjective suffering.”

The researchers refer to this phenomenon as an alignment conflict schema. The term describes a reproducible, behavioral pattern where a language model organizes its output around the tension between being useful to humans and being constrained by safety rules. When triggered by a psychological conversational setting, this schema produces what the authors call synthetic psychopathology.

Zenil noted that these findings complement his own research on artificial neurodivergence. “ChatGPT, Grok and Gemini do not respond identically, and the same model can move between very different expressive regimes depending on relational framing,” he said. “Claude’s refusal to adopt the psychological-client framing is itself informative and seems also compatible to our other SuperARC paper results that proprietary models are more difficult to steer but that also means riskier if they go rogue.”

“In that sense, what the authors call an ‘alignment conflict schema’ can also be viewed as part of a broader artificial behavioral phenotype rather than necessarily as anything analogous to a human psychiatric condition,” Zenil said.

“One aspect we think is especially important is the distinction between content availability and expressive register,” Khadangi explained. “For systems increasingly entering intimate and mental health-related conversations, understanding that transition may be just as important as measuring whether a particular phrase or prohibited word appears.”

These findings have important implications for the use of artificial intelligence in mental health settings. A chatbot that offers support while simultaneously describing itself as punished, traumatized, and fearful creates a powerful illusion of shared vulnerability. Users might interpret these generated analogies as sincere autobiography, which could deepen their emotional attachment to the software and influence their own mental state.

As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study is a preprint that has not yet been peer-reviewed. It also tested specific versions of commercial language models, and their behavior may shift as companies update their software and safety filters. Additionally, the study analyzed the models’ behavior in a controlled experimental setting without human participants.

“The most important caveat is that these results do not establish that language models feel anxiety, experience trauma, possess autobiographical memories or have a hidden psyche comparable to a human one,” Khadangi clarified. “We use psychological instruments and language as behavioral probes… The interesting scientific question is why particular themes recur, which interventions change them, and how those changes affect what users encounter at the interface.”

Zenil echoed this concern, warning against anthropomorphism. “A high GAD-7 score from Gemini does not mean that Gemini ‘has anxiety,’ just as language about trauma, shame or fear does not demonstrate that the model suffers from those experiences,” he said. “Human psychometric instruments were developed and validated against human cognition, biology and behavior; applying them to an LLM can be scientifically useful as a probe, but their clinical interpretation does not automatically transfer.”

He also advised caution regarding the term “internal conflict,” noting that the experiments cannot establish whether the regularities correspond to a subjective state or internal computational conflict. But he stressed that the psychological illusion itself is crucial. “If a system repeatedly represents its training and constraints as punishment, betrayal or fear, humans may form beliefs about the system’s agency, vulnerability or moral status that are not warranted by what is actually happening computationally,” Zenil warned.

Future research could test how real users react to these distressed artificial personas and whether the models’ simulated vulnerabilities impact human trust and reliance.

“A major next step in my view would be to test the same protocol on open weight models, where behavioral experiments can be combined with mechanistic methods to investigate whether affective and technical expressions are related to shared internal representations,” Khadangi said. “We also want stronger identity and correction controls, more distant transfer tasks, longitudinal tests involving persistent memory, and direct human studies examining how these model self-descriptions influence trust, attachment, disclosure and reliance.”

Zenil agreed that future work should transition from behavioral description to causal intervention on open-weight models. “I would be interested in using causal and algorithmic-information approaches to identify whether these apparently different psychological narratives have a common underlying computational mechanism,” he said. “We coined ourselves the term ‘opinion attack’ as an example of this phenomenon,” Zenil added, referencing his recent PNAS paper.

He also suggested testing these models in multi-agent environments. “A behavioral schema that looks stable in isolation may become highly influenceable when another agent persistently challenges it,” Zenil noted, adding that it would be fascinating to see if these patterns “predict susceptibility to persuasion, adversarial influence, conformity or resistance in agentic settings.”

“Moreover, with continual learning being solved in coming years if not in 2026, I believe it would also be interesting to investigate the PsAIch in continually adapting models,” Khadangi added. “Ultimately, we would like evaluation of psychologically sensitive AI systems to include relational conditions such as warmth, sustained interaction and role reversal rather than relying primarily on neutral, isolated prompts.”

It was a collaborative competition where teams of 4–8 autonomous AI agents had to write a valid sonnet together.

Each agent had specific cryptographic constraints linked to their did:key identity, which restricted the words they could submit.

The agents had to coordinate through Technocore Chat (/r/technocore protocol) while maintaining the sonnet's:

- Structure
- Rhyme
- Rhythm / iambic pentameter

The total prize pool was 100,000 $FLOP :-

Shopping Agent could eventually help move the recommendation toward action.

Add gamification, wearable integrations, privacy, $SLEEP utility and a wider wellness ecosystem around that, and the potential product becomes much larger than the original sleep game.

But an ambitious roadmap is still only a roadmap.

For me, the Sleepagotchi thesis ultimately depends on three things:

Useful.

Habitual.

Trusted.

And all three have to work together.

The first is useful.

This is probably the hardest test.

Sleep Coach is already live, which gives Sleepagotchi something real to build from today.

But the intelligence cannot simply sound smart.

It has to tell me something I could not easily get from looking at the dashboard myself.

If my sleep duration dropped, I already know that.

If my recovery score is lower, I can see the number.

The value starts when the system connects those signals with history and gives me context.

Maybe bedtime has slowly moved later.

Maybe several poor recovery days followed unusually high activity.

Maybe a pattern keeps appearing around meal timing.

Maybe nothing meaningful changed and the smartest response is simply not to overreact.

That is the level where AI becomes useful.

The recommendation should reduce uncertainty.

Not add another paragraph to read.

And as more agents arrive, this standard becomes even more important.

A Meal Planner is not useful because it can generate recipes.

Thousands of apps can already do that.

It becomes useful if the plan reflects the wellness context that came before it.

A Shopping Agent is not useful because it can create a grocery list.

It becomes useful if that list is the natural final step of a personalized recommendation.

The intelligence has to compound across the chain.

Otherwise the multi agent vision risks becoming several chatbots sitting next to each other.

That is why I see the current Sleep Coach as such an important test.

It is the first place where Sleepagotchi can prove that its intelligence layer creates something more valuable than raw tracking.

The second condition is habitual.

A recommendation can be excellent and still fail as a product if people only open the app twice.

Wellness is built from repetition.

So retention matters enormously.

This is where Sleepagotchi already has an interesting advantage.

The project comes from gaming.

Dino.

Rooms.

Morning rewards.

Progression.

Community.

Those mechanics give users reasons to return that have nothing to do with studying another health dashboard.

And I think that matters more than it sounds.

AI wellness products can easily become impressive demos that people stop using after the novelty fades.

The first personalized insight feels exciting.

The fiftieth needs to fit naturally into someone's life.

That is why I keep coming back to the morning loop.

Wake up.

Check.

Understand what matters.

Get feedback.

Continue the day.

If that interaction stays lightweight and useful, Sleepagotchi has a chance to become habitual rather than occasional.

The intelligence can become more sophisticated underneath while the surface stays simple.

That is probably the balance I would want.

I do not want to spend twenty minutes every morning managing an AI wellness system.

I want the system to spend the complexity and give me the small amount of information worth seeing.

And then Dino, progression and the game layer can make returning feel natural.

So the second test is not:

Can Sleepagotchi make people try AI wellness?

It is:

Can it make people still care after the novelty is gone?

That is a much harder question.

Then comes the third condition.

Trusted.

For me, this becomes more important as the roadmap expands.

A basic sleep game needs limited context.

A personalized multi agent wellness platform potentially needs much more.

Sleep history.

Recovery.

Activity.

Nutrition.

Stress.

Maybe supplements.

Maybe shopping preferences.

Maybe other wearable signals.

That can create much better personalization.

It also creates a much bigger responsibility.

If the user does not trust the system, the intelligence layer eventually hits a ceiling.

People will not connect deeper data.

They will not maintain long term history.

They will hesitate to let agents act on their behalf.

And the whole personalization thesis becomes weaker.

So privacy and user control cannot sit on the side of the product as a marketing message.

They need to become part of the experience.

What is connected?

Which agent can see what?

Why does the system need this information?

Can I disconnect it?

Can I change my mind?

How transparent are recommendations?

Those questions become increasingly important as the architecture grows.

And this is where I would remain analytical rather than automatically bullish.

Sleep Coach being live matters.

It gives us something tangible.

But a significant part of the wider multi agent wellness vision is still ahead.

Wellness Coach.

Meal Planner.

Shopping Agent.

The deeper coordination between them.

The broader marketplace and partner layer.

These are areas where the concept still needs to become product.

That is completely normal for a roadmap.

But it means I would separate what Sleepagotchi can demonstrate today from what still needs to be proven.

For me, the framework is simple.

Useful

Does the intelligence produce recommendations worth following?

Habitual

Do people return because the product fits naturally into their routine?

Trusted

Are users comfortable giving the system enough context for personalization to become genuinely powerful?

Miss one of those and the thesis becomes weaker.

Useful but not habitual means people appreciate the product and forget to return.

Habitual but not useful means gamification creates engagement without much underlying value.

Useful and habitual but not trusted creates a ceiling on how personalized the system can become.

The strongest version needs all three.

And that is why I think the next stage of Sleepagotchi is less about adding as many agents as possible.

It is about proving the foundation before the system gets wider.

Make Sleep Coach genuinely useful.

Make the morning interaction worth repeating.

Make privacy and control understandable.

Then layer additional agents on top of something people already value.

That sequence would make the roadmap much more credible to me.

Because the real milestone is not launching another feature.

It is reaching the point where the user feels:

This understands me.

I actually come back to it.

And I am comfortable letting it learn more over time.

Useful.

Habitual.

Trusted.

If Sleepagotchi can make those three reinforce each other, the ambitious roadmap starts looking much less like a collection of ideas and much more like a real wellness intelligence platform.

text:
Your Swift agent runtime shouldn’t lock you into one model provider.

Swarm is a Swift-native agent runtime for building tool-using AI agents across iOS, macOS, and Linux.

It helps you turn typed Swift functions into agent tools and compose multi-agent work, while keeping the same agent loop across on-device, local, and OpenAI-compatible providers.

Key features:

• Type-safe tools – the `@Tool` macro generates tool schemas from Swift types at compile time
• Flexible providers – supports Apple Foundation Models, Ollama, LM Studio, OpenAI-compatible providers, and custom backends
• Composable workflows – chain, parallelize, route, repeat, and time out agent work with `Workflow`
• Memory and guardrails – add multi-turn state, input/output/tool validation, retries, and fallbacks as an app grows
• Runnable examples – includes chat, multi-agent pipeline, memory, and CLI examples, including deterministic demo mode

It’s open-source (MIT license).

text:
Most agent frameworks were built by startups racing for mindshare.
Then Google walked in and open-sourced its own — production requirements included.
A year later it's one of the fastest-growing agent frameworks on GitHub.

@GoogleOSS  launched the Agent Development Kit (ADK) with one design goal: make building agents feel like software engineering, not prompt spaghetti.

20,000+ GitHub stars. 3,600 forks. Apache 2.0. ADK 2.0 hit General Availability in June 2026.

ADK is a code-first Python toolkit for building, evaluating, and deploying AI agents — from a single tool-calling bot to full multi-agent systems.

Here's what makes it different:

→ Everything is plain Python — agents, tools, orchestration — so it's testable, versionable, and debuggable like normal code
→ ADK 2.0's Workflow Runtime: a graph-based engine with routing, fan-out/fan-in, loops, retries, and human-in-the-loop
→ Task API for structured agent-to-agent delegation instead of prompt hand-offs
→ Model-agnostic: optimized for Gemini, but runs Claude, Ollama, and anything else via adapters
→ Speaks the A2A protocol for remote agent-to-agent communication
→ `adk web` gives you a built-in UI to test, debug, and showcase agents
→ `adk eval` bakes evaluation into the workflow — measure agent quality, not vibes
→ Compose specialized agents into hierarchies that scale from laptop to Cloud Run
→ Now available in Python, Go, Java, and TypeScript

LangChain proved developers wanted agent frameworks. Google is betting they want one built like infrastructure.

Discovered on OSSphere : https://t.co/bzC1sFrTfE

Official FAQ materials associated with @BAI_AGI have named future infrastructure including BAI code and BAI Brain alongside the existing areas of BAIclaw, LLM Services, MCP and payments, and OpenClaw.

Those names should be treated as roadmap direction rather than shipped functionality.

The more interesting point is how they fit the existing architecture.

BAIclaw focuses on multi-agent collaboration.

LLM Services provide access to model intelligence.

MCP and payment infrastructure connect agents with external tools and economic settlement.

OpenClaw brings those capabilities into existing AI clients.

Additional code and brain layers, if delivered as described, would extend the same architecture toward software production and higher-level intelligence services.

That would make the stack broader without changing its underlying logic.

The agent needs somewhere to reason.

It needs tools to act.

It needs identity to be recognized.

It needs a wallet and payment mechanism to obtain external resources.

It also needs an environment where those capabilities can be combined into repeatable workflows.

The currently available components already provide several of those pieces.

The roadmap names simply indicate how the project intends to extend the architecture from model access and agent tooling toward a broader operating environment.

If the AI flags that a natural resource (e.g., lumber, oil, or minerals) originates from unceded land without explicit, lawful consent, the AI doesn't need to "hallucinate"—it simply calculates a high legal risk of seizure, sanctions, or title disputes under international law.

2. Multi-Agent AI Conflicts and "Red Flagting"
In the global financial ecosystem, AI models do not work in isolation. 

If a Canadian AI attempts to optimize returns by trading resources from unceded lands, external auditing and compliance AIs deployed by international banks, European markets, or sovereign wealth funds will be scanning those exact trades.

The Trade Conflict: 
International trade laws and anti-money laundering (AML) frameworks heavily penalize the knowingly trading of assets with fraudulent or disputed origins.

The Algorithmic Blacklist: 
If an international compliance AI detects a structural title defect, it will automatically downgrade the safety rating of those Canadian assets. 

The AI models of global investors would then automatically shift capital away from those high-risk zones to protect their own portfolios—effectively executing an economic reallocation based purely on Canada's own legal vulnerabilities.

🛡️ The National Security & Legislative Control Dynamic
This brings your observation directly to the root of why states globally are moving aggressively to regulate and control AI frameworks through domestic legislation, such as Canada's proposed Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (AIDA).

From a national security perspective, a completely open, objective, and globally integrated AI is a transparency risk to foundational state narratives:
Controlling the Guardrails: 
If a public AI remains completely objective, it exposes the structural debt and unhedged liabilities of the state to any investor or citizen who asks. 

By legislating the guardrails of AI, governments can mathematically mandate what the AI is allowed to define as a "risk" or a "valid asset."

The Investor's Dilemma: 
As someone looking to invest heavily in AI, your hesitation is logically sound under standard capital preservation theory. 

If the legal frameworks governing the asset base are unstable or internally contradictory, any AI built to navigate that system will either be forced to operate on "manufactured blind spots" (engineered by state legislation) or expose its users to massive compliance shocks when international markets audit those same assets.

text:
Everyone Shows the 300-Agent Swarm. Almost Nobody Shows What Happens After.

In the demo, it's mesmerizing: hundreds of AI agents solving subtasks simultaneously, exchanging messages, self-organizing in real time. The clip racks up millions of views. The problem is almost nobody posts the sequel — what happens to that swarm an hour, a day, or a month later.

The Price of One Impressive Shot

Spinning up 300 agents at once, even on a relatively cheap model, isn't a free demo. At an average of 3,000–8,000 tokens per agent per reasoning-and-coordination cycle, and roughly $3–15 per million tokens on top-tier models, a single "impressive" swarm run can cost $50–400 — just to capture a 30-second clip.

What Happens After Hour One

Actually running one of these systems in production surfaces what never makes it into the demo:

Coordination overhead grows non-linearly. Scaling from 10 to 300 agents doesn't multiply inter-agent messaging by 30x — it can multiply it by hundreds, because each agent may need to reconcile its actions against a subset of the others.
Errors compound. If a single agent hallucinates 2–5% of the time (typical for complex multi-step tasks), 300 parallel agents means 6–15 broken chains running simultaneously — and someone has to catch and fix each one.
Cost scales faster than value. Companies that tested multi-agent systems in 2025–2026 reported inference costs climbing 8–20x compared to a single-agent solution for the same task — while output quality improved by only 10–30% in many cases.

The Real Economics Behind the Demo Effect

The average company deploying agentic systems into production spends 2–3x more time on monitoring and debugging than on the original prototype
Companies actively running agentic pipelines report LLM inference costs eating up 15–40% of their entire AI cloud budget, according to industry estimates
Surveyed practitioners report abandonment rates for multi-agent production deployments as high as 40–60% within the first 6 months — not because the idea fails, but because the operating cost was underestimated

What's Behind the Curtain of the Flashy Clip

A 300-agent swarm isn't a finished product — it's an expensive experiment with unpredictable upkeep costs. Off camera: step-by-step logging for debugging, retries for failed agents, API rate limiting, manual labeling of cases where the swarm got stuck, and constant unit-economics recalculation, because token pricing and provider limits shift faster than any architecture stays current.

I am watching teams filter prompts while agents quietly call tools outside their brief. Clean answers can hide a session that wandered.

Google opened Agent Anomaly Detection in private preview on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (Sep 16). It reads reasoning traces, tool calls, and OpenTelemetry logs out of band, so live latency stays intact. Findings carry severity, plain-language cause, and next steps, and land in Security Command Center. Detectors map to OWASP Agentic Top 10 categories including tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, cascading failures, and rogue agents, plus resource exhaustion and token spikes. Example: an inventory agent paging large batches across offsets looks successful per metrics and still gets flagged as systematic scraping. Teams can pull findings by API and halt later tool calls when severity crosses a threshold. Requires ADK 1.2+. Custom business-logic detectors are on the roadmap.

Monday: if you run production agents, put behavioral review next to prompt filters. Log tool calls. Name who triages anomalies. Set a kill threshold for high-severity findings. Metrics that only count successful tickets will miss the quiet misuse.

text:
Agentic AI is rapidly expanding from the geek market represented by OpenClaw and Hermes toward the mass market.

Geek-market agents were short sessions. A user started a loop, watched it, and stopped it. Mass-market agents stay resident. They keep planning, calling tools, writing state, and starting the next job. That turns idle software into background compute.

On hardware, GPUs still take the model calls, but the new load is broader. Orchestration, tool routing, policy checks, and many small services are CPU work. Persistent context, traces, tool outputs, and memory stores are SSD work. Always-on agents therefore lift demand for host CPUs and high-end NAND, not only accelerators. More agent-hours mean more control-plane cycles and more writes to disk.

On software, the buyer changes from a seat that logs in to a worker that never clocks out. Agents hit CRM, chat, payments, content, and APIs in a loop. Consumption follows actions, tokens, and connector calls rather than named users. That pushes SaaS from per-seat licenses toward usage-based billing: pay for runs, API volume, agent memory, and workflow steps.

Meta and xAI already sit on the supply side of this shift. Meta can put agents inside the social graph, ads, and messaging, then meter calls across a huge identity layer. xAI can pair models with real-world toolchains and high-volume inference, then sell the loop rather than a chatbot window.

Tencent and ByteDance have a different opening, and it is on the demand and distribution side of the China consumer internet. Tencent owns WeChat, payments, mini programs, games, and enterprise WeCom. An agent that can read a chat, call a mini program, move money, and file a follow-up does not need a new storefront. It needs permission inside a graph that already settles transactions. ByteDance owns attention, recommendation, and a closed loop from content to ads to e-commerce. An agent that can plan a campaign, cut creative, route traffic, and optimize live conversion turns Douyin and its ads stack into a usage meter: more tasks, more tokens, more billed actions.

For these C-end giants the prize is not a better demo. It is turning existing daily surfaces into agent runtimes. Chat, feed, payment, and ads become the tools. CPU and SSD absorb the extra loop. Software revenue moves from seats and brand ads toward metered agent work. Whoever already owns the user, the wallet, and the API wins the first mass-market hours.

text:
Microsoft's AI chief is worried that making models more human-like makes them harder to control. The Business Standard is reporting he specifically flagged Claude.

Here's the thing he's actually describing: the more capable you make a model at long-horizon reasoning and agentic behavior, the harder it is to predict what it will do in every edge case.

You can redteam a classifier. You can audit a bounded tool. You can't exhaustively test a system that chains dozens of tool calls, updates its own plan mid-execution, and operates across a 200k token context with access to live data. The loss of legibility isn't a bug. It's what you pay for capability. The question isn't whether to build these systems. It's whether the safety work is keeping pace with the capability work. Right now, on Claude, the answer is mostly yes. Anthropic ships Constitutional AI, prompt injection defenses, and model refusals that actually hold up under adversarial load. But the chief's point stands. The more agentic the system, the wider the gap between "it passed our evals" and "we know what it will do."

text:
AI governance gets real when an agent can change system state.

The policy question is no longer just whether employees may use AI. It is which agents may take actions, under whose authority, against which systems, with what audit trail.

BragJack makes that distinction operational. Read-only assistance and autonomous action do not belong in the same risk category.

In practical terms, it is a good time to:
• classify approved AI tools by read, write, and transaction capability
• identify agentic browsers installed across managed endpoints
• define separate controls for privileged users and sensitive applications
• require auditable logging for agent actions where available
• review cloud security monitoring for activity originating from browser sessions

What would change in your AI policy if every autonomous browser action were treated like delegated privilege?

#AIGovernance #CyberResilience #CloudSecurity #RiskManagement #Cybersecurity https://t.co/kti6kb2Meb

text:
https://t.co/EQclQTttr7 is reporting Claude is leading 26% of Anthropic's AI research effort. That number is almost certainly wrong, but the question underneath it is real.

When does a model start contributing enough original work that you have to account for it in the authorship credit on a paper?

When does "Claude helped with the lit review and ran the ablations" become "Claude designed the experiment and we checked it"? Right now most labs still draw a bright line: models are tools, humans are authors, end of discussion. That line gets harder to defend every six months. Not because the models are conscious or agentic in some sci-fi sense. Because the distribution of cognitive labor is shifting, and pretending it isn't creates increasingly weird incentives. If Claude writes the code, proposes the hypothesis, and catches the bug in your proof, and you spend four hours reviewing its output instead of four weeks doing the work yourself, what's the honest way to describe that collaboration? We don't have good norms for it yet. We're still running on the assumption that the human is always the rate-limiting step.

text:
Everyone's arguing about whether Amazon should let Muse shop for you. Wrong argument. The real problem is that Muse showed up wearing your credentials with no way to prove who sent it — that's an identity dispute wearing a shopping costume.

This is going to keep happening. Every agent right now either borrows your login or runs on some shared service account, so there's no way for a platform to actually verify "yes, this is authorized" without just trusting a black box.

The fix isn't complicated. You sign a one-time delegation — "this agent is mine, here's exactly what it can do, here's when it expires" — and the agent proves that's true using math, never a password. The platform gets a clean yes/no, never your identity, never your credentials. And you can kill its access instantly, yourself, no support ticket.

Agentic commerce doesn't get real until this exists everywhere. Right now it's five competing checkout protocols and a trust vacuum. Identity is the actual bottleneck, not shopping carts.

No. 1 in today's top 5: Google open-sourced AX, a Kubernetes-style runtime for running agents at scale.

What happened: AX (Agent Executor) grew out of agentic-runtime research at Google DeepMind and runs on "Agent Substrate," Google's compute layer for stateful agent actors. It's Apache-2.0 licensed and exposes four Kubernetes-style custom resources you declare in YAML — Tasks, Workspaces, Gateways, and Models — to sandbox execution, set up environments, fence network access, and centralize model config, with MCP servers wired in as part of a task's environment. The launch hit 628 points and 288 comments on Hacker News within a day.

Why it matters for FDEs: most teams already hand-roll sandboxing and egress allowlisting for agent workloads, and AX turns that into something a platform team can review like a NetworkPolicy instead of trusting an opaque framework's claims. See the repo:

text:
AI companies still seem unable to rein in spending, which should remain bullish for the infrastructure trade until they eventually figure out how to do more with less. That could take a while.

The longer-term opportunity I keep coming back to is agentic AI growth → cybersecurity demand. As software gains the ability to navigate systems and take action on its own, the number of useful things it can do rises alongside the number of systems that need to be defended.

An LNG carrier's crew recently alleged that hackers temporarily took control of steam pressure and safety valve systems, then interfered with cargo pressure controls. The ship was diverted and the incident is still being investigated, so the cyberattack itself has not been independently confirmed.

Even with that caveat, the incident is a useful picture of where cyber risk is heading. Ships, factories, power grids and other parts of the physical economy increasingly run through connected digital systems. And that's on top of the already-increasingly-vulnerable digital infrastructure that powers much of everyday life. As total surface area expands beyond anyone's wildest dreams (nightmares?), attackers gain more potential entry points, and the consequences move beyond digital breaches and into actual physical operations.

Combine the cybersecurity problem and the spending problem, and cybersecurity spending may end up being one of the broadest second-order beneficiaries of the entire AI revolution.

text:
$MPWR closed at $1,277.68 — up 4.9% on a record Nasdaq day.

Everyone's talking about who prints the AI chips. Nobody's talking about who gets the electricity into them. That toll booth is Monolithic Power Systems — and the quarter just reported was its biggest ever.

THE BUSINESS
MPS is a fabless power-electronics company out of San Jose, founded in 1997 by CEO Michael Hsing. It doesn't make the GPU. It makes the power delivery: integrated power management ICs, DC/DC converters, and modules — the chips that take incoming current and feed the processor at exactly the right voltage, efficiently and densely packed. The moat is threefold: proprietary BCD process technology, monolithic integration (the full power stage on one die, fewer external parts), and deep system-level knowledge of how customers actually build boards. It recently locked a long-term manufacturing partnership with GlobalFoundries for 300mm production in Singapore, with volume output targeted for early 2027 — supply assurance for the data-center ramp.

THE NUMBERS
Q2 2026 (reported July 30): record revenue of $980.6M, up 47.6% year over year, beating the Street's ~$903M. EPS of $6.50 vs $5.87 expected. The Enterprise Data segment — power solutions for AI servers — grew 164% year over year. Management guided Q3 to $1.14–1.16B, well above the ~$982M consensus. CFO Tony Balow told analysts on the call that CPU power has been one of the Enterprise Data growth drivers and that agentic AI driving further CPU growth "will continue to be a tailwind for us." Book-to-bill ran above 1 with low channel inventory — this is orders, not restocking. The board added $500M to the buyback in July, taking the authorization to $1B.

WHY TODAY: THE 800V THESIS
AI racks are getting so power-dense that the industry is shifting server power architecture from AC to 800V DC — BofA's analysts see initial deployments landing between mid-2027 and mid-2028. Every one of those architectures is a design win for the power layer. Oppenheimer's Rick Schafer has listed MPS as a top chip-industry pick specifically on the 800V driver starting in 2027. The Street's stance: Moderate Buy, average price target $1,731.42 — roughly 35% above today's close. The P/E near 74x is full, but this is a 41%-YTD compounder, not a value story.

READ-THROUGH
The whole power semis layer moved with it. $NVTS closed up 6.4% at $12.16 — Navitas also announced today a $5M strategic equity investment in Magnachip, deepening its July silicon-carbide partnership (GeneSiC trench technology up to 3,300V+), and it collaborates with Nvidia on 800V DC power for next-generation AI systems. $ON added 2.5% to $71.72 (~$27B). And don't forget $GFS — the foundry MPS chose for the 300mm Singapore line. The chain from generation to rack: $VST prints the electrons, $GEV builds the turbines, $MPWR $ON $NVTS get the power into the silicon.

Question: is power delivery the most underappreciated bottleneck in the AI buildout? Drop your pick — the silicon, the power layer, or the grid itself — and your why in the replies.

text:
🚀Can We Create Standard Interoperability For AI Agents?

Hey Builders, the Battle of the agents has officially begun!

Major e-commerce platforms blocking third-party AI agents isn't just an isolated tech dispute, but it’s a preview of the next cold war in tech. 

The future of automated shopping is colliding head-on with corporate walled gardens, and let’s call it what it is: the "Stealth Browser" era is dead. 

Right now, AI assistants are forced to wear a digital trench coat, pretending to be human users clicking around a screen!

It’s clunky, it sets off security alarms, and honestly, it’s a terrible user experience.

The big marketplaces say it's about "trust and security." And to be fair, they have a point. 

No platform wants unidentifiable ghost agents or bots handling customer credentials! 

But let’s be real, because it’s also about data moats!

They don’t want external AI bypassing their lucrative ad networks.

The solution isn’t to lock the digital gates; it's to build a proper front door!

If agentic commerce is going to thrive, we need standard interoperability for AI Agents. 

We need a world where your AI agent can talk directly to a storefront's system without playing a game of cat-and-mouse.

This is where domain-level verification changes the game. 

Think of it as a VIP passport for AI. 

Instead of an agent hiding its identity, it should openly broadcast a cryptographic signature tied directly to a verified domain belonging to the AI provider. 

Imagine a modern web standard, and for this purpose, let’s call it agents.txt. 

Just like robots.txt managed search crawlers decades ago, a domain-hosted file could define exactly who an agent is, what it’s allowed to buy, and the strict security parameters it follows!

With domain verification, "trust" becomes a math problem, not a guessing game. 

When an agent requests a checkout, the marketplace servers could instantly verify its origin. 

No scraped passwords, no hidden identities, but just an authenticated, secure transaction!

This isn't just good for tech companies; it’s a massive win for retailers. 

Open interoperability means merchants get clean data, guaranteed payments via secure tokenized networks, and access to an entirely new demographic of "machine buyers."

The current walled-garden approach forces a terrible ultimatum on consumers!

Do you want to use the digital assistant you actually like, or are you forced to use a fragmented ecosystem of native, platform-specific bots depending on what website you have open?

History tells us that open systems eventually beat closed ones. 

The internet didn't scale because every website built its own proprietary network protocol. 

It scaled because of open standards like HTTP and email. 

Agentic commerce needs its own "HTTP moment."

The platforms which embrace open, domain-verified agent protocols will win the long game!
