🇸🇻₿🤖BITCOIN & AI: EL SALVADOR WEEKLY — VOL. 6

THE PIECES ARE STARTING TO CONNECT.

This week in El Salvador:

🤖 AI moves from strategy → deployment
🏫 AI tutors expand across 1,000+ schools
🧠 CUBO_ai trains the next generation
🌊 $145M submarine cable advances
₿ Bitcoin's 5-year story enters a new chapter
🏦 Tokenized markets move from rules → real capital
☕ Bitcoin keeps circulating in the real economy
👑 Bitcoin Histórico returns in November

For years, these could be viewed as separate stories.

They're increasingly becoming parts of the same one:

Talent. Compute. Connectivity. Education. Capital. Bitcoin. AI.

BUILD → DEPLOY → MEASURE → CONNECT.

The pieces are starting to connect. 🇸🇻

@theaiagencysv @cubo_ai @cuboplus @bitcoinofficesv

El Salvador on X — Explaining El Salvador to the World.

🇸🇻 BITCOIN & AI: EL SALVADOR WEEKLY
VOL. 6 — SEPTEMBER 19, 2026
THE PIECES ARE STARTING TO CONNECT.

For years, much of the conversation surrounding El Salvador's technological transformation centered on individual announcements.

Bitcoin.

Digital-asset regulation.

Artificial intelligence.

Education.

Connectivity.

Infrastructure.

But this week, something different stands out.

The individual pieces are beginning to look less individual.

AI tutors are reaching more classrooms. Students are learning how to work with artificial intelligence. El Salvador is developing its first direct submarine cable connection to the global internet. A regulatory framework created for digital assets is supporting tokenized capital markets. Bitcoin continues circulating through ordinary businesses. And in November, builders from across the world will again converge on San Salvador.

No single development tells the entire story.

Together, they are beginning to.

🤖 FROM RULES TO RESULTS

El Salvador spent the early phase of its artificial-intelligence strategy creating institutions, regulations, partnerships and infrastructure.

Now comes the harder part:

deployment.

ANIA summed up that transition this week in four words:

“El Salvador deploys! And now we accelerate.”

The most visible example is education.

A pilot operating in 171 public schools combined AI tutors with infrastructure, connectivity, teacher training and other interventions. According to President Nayib Bukele, 1,198 participating students subsequently achieved results comparable with averages in Sweden and Germany in reading, mathematics and science through PISA for Schools.

Importantly, those results represent the participating pilot—not El Salvador's national educational average—and cannot be attributed solely to AI tutoring.

But the experiment is no longer confined to 171 schools.

The AI education program has expanded to more than 1,000 public schools, part of a broader plan announced with xAI to eventually provide personalized AI tutoring to more than one million students across El Salvador's 5,000+ public schools.

At newly inaugurated schools, screens, connectivity and AI systems are becoming part of the physical infrastructure.

The significance isn't simply that El Salvador has an AI strategy.

It is beginning to put that strategy in front of students.

That's the transition we explored this week in:

FROM RULES TO RESULTS: EL SALVADOR BRINGS ITS AI EXPERIENCE TO LATIN AMERICA
🧠 THE INFRASTRUCTURE IS ALSO HUMAN

Servers don't create a technology economy by themselves.

People do.

This week, CUBO_ai students worked on prompt engineering—learning how to structure prompts precisely while comparing different AI models and their reasoning capabilities.

Meanwhile, CUBO+ continues developing Salvadoran Bitcoin talent under a philosophy that says almost everything necessary:

Learn. Verify. Build.

Different technologies.

Different programs.

But increasingly, the same objective:

Give Salvadorans the skills to become builders rather than simply users of technology.

That matters because El Salvador's ambitions are considerable.

ANIA's National AI Strategy 2026 establishes a target for artificial intelligence to contribute, directly and indirectly, approximately 20% of national GDP by 2031.

That is a strategic objective—not today's measured contribution—and reaching it will depend on what actually gets built over the next five years.

Which makes education and technical talent just as important as GPUs and regulation.

🌊 THE CABLE BENEATH THE PACIFIC

Then there is a piece of infrastructure that might initially seem unrelated.

It isn't.

El Salvador is advancing work on its first submarine telecommunications cable connecting the country directly to the global internet network.

The project is backed by $145 million in sovereign financing from CAF.

According to CAF, El Salvador currently has approximately 4–5 Tbps of international capacity through terrestrial cable operators. The submarine cable is expected to initially double that capacity, with the potential to reach four times today's level within five years.

Now place that alongside everything else happening.

AI tutors.

Sovereign computing capacity.

Digital education.

Cloud services.

Potential data-center development.

AI research.

Digital financial markets.

Every one of them ultimately depends on connectivity.

Suddenly, the submarine cable isn't merely a telecommunications project.

It becomes another piece of the technology stack.

₿ FIVE YEARS LATER, THE BITCOIN STORY IS EVOLVING

Five years after El Salvador approved its original Bitcoin Law, another part of the experiment is increasingly visible:

capital markets built on digital-asset infrastructure.

Bitfinex Securities also marks five years this year.

The company subsequently became the first platform licensed under El Salvador's specialized Digital Assets Issuance Law, approved in 2023. Bitfinex says its platform has now surpassed $250 million in tokenized assets.

Tokenization can allow traditional assets and securities to be represented digitally, potentially enabling fractional ownership, faster settlement and different mechanisms for raising capital.

Bitfinex Securities says its model can offer near-instant settlement and 24/7 trading, while reducing certain costs and intermediaries compared with traditional capital-market structures.

That represents an important evolution in El Salvador's Bitcoin story.

Five years ago, much of the international debate was about whether someone could buy coffee with Bitcoin.

Today, another question is emerging:

Can the infrastructure built around digital assets help connect businesses and projects with global capital?

The rules came first.

Now we can begin measuring what gets built with them.

☕ AND YES — BITCOIN STILL BUYS THE COFFEE

Yet the original grassroots story hasn't disappeared.

This week, the National Bitcoin Office highlighted OMAS Coffee, speaking with the team behind the specialty-coffee venture about its decision to accept Bitcoin.

There is something beautifully simple about that.

At one end of the ecosystem:

Tokenized securities. International investors. Digital capital markets.

At the other:

A merchant.
A customer.
A cup of Salvadoran coffee.
A Bitcoin payment.

Both belong to the same ecosystem.

And it echoes what we recently discovered through our own reporting on the Bitcoin Farmers Market: every two weeks, roughly 30–35 vendors gather at a market where accepting Bitcoin is the one requirement for participating.

Technology doesn't become an economy merely because regulations exist.

Eventually, somebody has to use it.

👑 BITCOIN HISTÓRICO RETURNS

And November is shaping up to become an extraordinary month for El Salvador's Bitcoin and technology communities.

Bitcoin Histórico 2026 returns November 11–12 at the National Palace in San Salvador's Historic Center.

But it won't stand alone.

The November calendar currently includes the Bitcoin Capital Summit, Bitcoin Histórico, EmTech AI and the Bitcoin Circular Economies Summit.

Bitcoin.

Artificial intelligence.

Capital.

Entrepreneurs.

Developers.

Circular economies.

International visitors.

For two technologies that are increasingly appearing side by side in El Salvador's development strategy, November could provide something valuable:

a chance to see how much of the ecosystem actually exists beyond the headlines.

🇸🇻 THE BIGGER PICTURE

This is why we believe this week's most important story isn't any single announcement.

Look at the pieces.

RULES create room for experimentation.

EDUCATION develops people capable of using the technology.

TALENT turns users into builders.

COMPUTE provides the machines.

CONNECTIVITY moves the data.

AI DEPLOYMENT takes technology from strategy documents into classrooms.

BITCOIN provides a monetary and technological ecosystem.

TOKENIZATION connects digital infrastructure with capital markets.

And ultimately, PEOPLE determine whether any of it works.

Five years into the Bitcoin experiment—and as El Salvador accelerates its push into artificial intelligence—the country's technology story is becoming less about isolated initiatives.

The more interesting question now is what happens when those initiatives begin reinforcing one another.

BUILD.
DEPLOY.
MEASURE.
CONNECT.

The pieces are starting to connect. 🇸🇻

text:
Impressive paper showing how much the first retrieval step matters for deep research agents.

It helps to improve GPT-5.5 from 83.1% to 90.5% on BrowseComp-Plus with the same retriever and the same agent loop.

It seems that the gain comes from the opening context.

The authors propose Question's Gambit which runs once, before the agent starts searching.

It splits the question into clues, turns each clue into complementary searches, pools the results, and reranks them.

The agent then starts its loop with that ranked set already in context.

The same change lifts GPT-5.4-mini from 68.1% to 79.0% and DeepSeek-v4-pro from 71.4% to 76.9%, and roughly halves calibration error for GPT-5.5. It costs between 2.3 and 5.3 extra tool calls per question.

In an error analysis, only 3 of the 79 remaining GPT-5.5 errors come from the gold document never being retrieved. The other 76 happen later, when the agent previews, opens or uses the evidence.

Paper: https://t.co/MBUSbcsEfV

text:
Your agent isn't slow. It's just paying for decisions a router should be making.

Every agent loop today looks like this: an expensive model decides which model is needed, whether a chunk is relevant, whether a human is required, whether a tool call is risky. That's not generation. Those are if-statements billed at frontier-model prices.

Jev Engineering breaks the pattern:

request → structured state → Jev router → cheapest capable model → worker → relevance and approval checks → execution gate → tool.

The key point: the decision layer does not generate prose. It routes, scores, blocks, approves.

Expensive models only get called when the task actually needs reasoning.

Result in tests: up to 193x faster and 444x cheaper.

The point isn't replacing your LLM. The point is moving the expensive model out of every decision loop and making that layer measurable, cheap and fast.

Full breakdown in the article below ↓

text:
Ricker just showed why most AI agents feel slow.

It is not because every task is hard.

It is because the expensive model gets asked to make every tiny decision.

Which tool should I use?
Should I read another file?
Is this result good enough?
Do I retry or stop?
Those questions repeat inside every loop. And most of them are routine.
The better architecture is not “replace the model.” It is to trace the loop, then route predictable forks away from it.
Known pattern? Take the fast path.
Uncertain case? Send it to deeper reasoning.
Before an action matters? Verify it.

The part people miss is measurement. You cannot optimize a loop you do not log.

Capture decisions. Find repeats. Label expected routes. Set confidence gates. Keep a fallback. Watch for drift.

That is not glamorous. It means collecting traces before changing the architecture, and admitting that a fast wrong route is still a failure.
That is the boring work behind an agent that gets faster without quietly getting worse.
The model should create.
Code should execute.
A decision layer should decide when the cheap path is safe.

Not every next step deserves a fresh paragraph of reasoning.

The map is free. Almost nobody will watch it long enough to fix their agent loop.

text:
PSA if you're tracing Claude Agent SDK runs with Arize's OpenInference instrumentation: until my PRs land, switching tracing on silently breaks interrupt().

The wrapper hands back a bare async iterable instead of the SDK's Query object, so every method on it is just gone. Your agent loop still runs fine. You just can't stop it anymore, and nothing errors to tell you that. Second one in the same wrapper: it stamps the SDK's own session id over a session id you set through context, and since Phoenix (the trace backend on the other end) binds a trace to the first session id it ingests, your spans scatter across sessions you never created.

Both reproduced against the real SDK, both fixed, six tests, PRs are open.

The part worth stealing if you maintain instrumentation: their suite couldn't catch either one, structurally. Every test mocks query() as a plain iterable with no methods on it, so a wrapper that drops methods has nothing to drop. And there's a test asserting the span carries the SDK's session id, which only looks correct because no test ever sets one. Green test, wrong behavior, pinned in place.

Anyway. Pin the version or patch it locally if interrupt() matters to you.

text:
Nice paper showing a better way to evolve agent skills.

And they achieve 40–70% less token cost compared to frontier evolving methods.

The idea is to let agents improve their skill prompts by ranking candidates with a learned rubric instead of running a full rollout to score every revision.

Rollout cost is the reason skill self-evolution usually only patches observed failures.

Every candidate edit needs a real agent run to evaluate.

SkillLift trains a rubric to agree with real outcomes on which of two skills is better, since ranking needs fewer oracle runs than predicting each score.

An inner loop revises skills against the frozen rubric at no rollout cost. An outer loop spends a few real rollouts to re-align the rubric by rank correlation.

On SkillsBench and WildClawBench (147 tasks) with three models, it beats SkillOpt and CoEvoSkills in all six combinations, even when those baselines get twice the token budget. It reaches target performance with 40 to 70% fewer tokens.

Paper: https://t.co/H75q8S8Gnk

Most teams already have an agent loop. The boring hard part is defaults that don't torch tokens or drop context mid-task. This ships those as a library you can override, not another kit to assemble from scratch.

What if we could revolutionize how LLM agents optimize their skills? GraphSkillEvo offers a fresh take on enhancing AI performance through graph-structured skills and evolutionary optimization.

→ Traditional skill optimization in LLMs struggles with unstructured instructions, leading to redundancy and confusion.  
→ GraphSkillEvo uses graph-structured artifacts, turning each skill into a node with clear guidance, making optimization more efficient.  
→ By employing evolutionary techniques like mutation and crossover, it explores skill space more effectively than iterative methods.  
→ Extensive experiments show GraphSkillEvo outperforms baselines like SkillOpt, boosting accuracy on benchmarks like GPT-5.4-nano.

This caught my eye because it tackles a persistent challenge in AI skill optimization with a novel structured approach. By refining the way skills are represented and optimized, GraphSkillEvo sets the stage for more capable and reliable LLM agents.

text:
“COBRA-Skills: Contextual Bandit-Guided Evolution for Agent Skill Optimization”

Optimizing agent skills requires expensive execution trials, while repeated teacher-model analysis adds cost before useful revisions emerge.

COBRA-Skills uses reward predictions from skill embeddings plus an uncertainty bonus to prioritize candidates for evaluation. It periodically replaces weak skills using successful and failed execution trajectories, instead of rewriting after every trial.

Across six benchmarks with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, mean test score reached 73.5 versus SkillOpt’s 69.6 over three runs. Reported optimization cost fell from $121.02 to $54.10 at fixed token prices; COBRA used 50 optimization examples per benchmark, while SkillOpt used larger pools.

Selective evaluation and periodic revision improved the tested skill-optimization cost–quality tradeoff without changing model weights.

text:
Dropping a sub-4B decision model into an agent loop usually looks incredible on the first five synthetic tool calls.

In our setup, routing latency drops from 1.5s down to ~150ms on a local quantized engine, and token spend on routing drops to near zero. Everything feels snappy until you feed the agent real-world schemas with optional fields and nested strings.

Running basic tool selection through a 3B or 7B model rarely causes issues on straightforward calls like file search or directory listing. Friction shows up once tool schemas require nested strings or multi-line diffs. Small models frequently invent non-existent flags or drop closing braces on long JSON payloads.

Wrapping the router in a schema repair loop or adding a Pydantic retry helps, but it comes with a trade-off. Once you burn two retries and 400ms fixing malformed JSON, the speed advantage over a single frontier model call starts shrinking fast.

Using these models for coarse branching seems to hold up best right now—deciding whether to execute a read command, spin up a subagent, or terminate the turn. Letting the small model pick the high-level path while leaving complex payload generation to something with stronger instruction following has been much more reliable than asking a 3B model to format deep JSON arguments.

We're still testing whether fine-tuning on our specific tool traces closes that gap, but off-the-shelf small models still get shaky once schemas get wide.

text:
Most AI memory systems answer the wrong question. They're built to retrieve the memory most similar to what you just asked. The harder question is which memory will matter later, before anyone asks anything.

That's the gap a new Tencent paper, T-Mem, is aimed at. Most memory systems, from vector stores to the newer graph based ones, retrieve by similarity at query time. T-Mem writes a trigger alongside each memory at store time, a prediction of when this will matter again, and reads by matching situations to triggers instead of keywords to content. On LoCoMo-Plus, a benchmark built to strip out keyword overlap and force pure associative recall, mainstream systems drop 28 to 50 points. T-Mem drops 5.45. It's peer reviewed at EMNLP 2026, code on GitHub under MIT license.

I'm watching this land in a crowded, well funded field. Mem0 has raised $24.5 million and reports 92.5 percent on LoCoMo using under 7,000 tokens per retrieval. Zep builds a temporal knowledge graph over conversations. Letta, the renamed MemGPT project, splits memory into an always-present core and an archival layer fetched on demand. HelixDB, an open source Rust project with 6,000 GitHub stars, stores graph, vector, and relational data in one engine so an agent can traverse and search in a single query. Every one of these solves memory for a single agent talking to itself across sessions.

Here's what none of them solve: what happens when it isn't one agent, it's five. Claude Code, Codex, Aider, and others working the same codebase, each forming its own view of what happened, none able to see what the others learned. Single agent memory research doesn't touch that, because the problem doesn't exist until more than one agent is in the room.

That's what I built the collective intelligence layer in Campfire to handle: semantic memory and a shared context stream every agent in a session reads from and writes to, plus a deliberation engine so agents can weigh in on each other's decisions instead of working in silent parallel. Campfire runs Claude Code, Codex, Goose, Aider, and OpenHands side by side in one browser tab, with permission voting across the group, session replay, agent races across isolated git worktrees, and a cost dashboard showing what five agents actually cost versus one.

If T-Mem and HelixDB solve memory for the agent, Campfire solves memory for the room the agents work in. Install is one line: bunx the-campfire.

South Korea’s semiconductor exports surged 259.4% year over year to a record $34.1 billion during the first 20 days of September. Semiconductors now account for 47.8% of the country’s total exports, which is the highest percentage ever recorded for this period. These numbers show that the AI boom is no longer based only on future spending forecasts because massive chip orders are already being manufactured, shipped and converted into revenue. Samsung and SK hynix are benefiting from rising shipment volumes and dramatically higher memory prices at the same time.

The supply constraint allows Samsung and SK hynix to raise prices across a much larger portion of their memory businesses. Samsung reported that its average selling prices increased by approximately the mid-40% range for DRAM and the high 60% range for NAND during the second quarter.

These price increases can produce enormous profit growth because semiconductor manufacturing carries extremely high fixed costs. Once the factories are operating near capacity, every additional dollar generated through higher selling prices can carry a very high incremental margin. Samsung demonstrated this operating leverage during the second quarter when its revenue reached KRW 171.5 trillion and its operating profit climbed to KRW 89.5 trillion. Samsung’s semiconductor division generated KRW 127.5 trillion in revenue and KRW 89.2 trillion in operating profit, which means the semiconductor business produced almost all of the company’s profit.

text:
Something shifted in how I think about agent harnesses this week after reading a new paper out of Beihang University and the University of Manchester.

For two years the industry treated the harness, the scaffolding of prompts, tool calls and loop logic wrapped around a model, as fixed. You picked your model, wrote a harness once, shipped it. The paper, called ModularRSI, argues that was the wrong frame. Harnesses should evolve the same way the models inside them do.

The mechanism is specific. Instead of tuning a harness against the same benchmark it gets graded on, which just teaches it to overfit, ModularRSI curates 2,000 evolution tasks deliberately disjoint from the evaluation set. It contrasts successful and failed trajectories on the same task to isolate real behavioral deficiencies, not one off mistakes. Then it splits the harness into five modules, agent loop, tool use, observation management, context management, task completion detection, and evolves each independently before reconciling them into one. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 and Terminal-Bench 4 the evolved harnesses beat static ones across every base model tested.

This lands in a crowded space. SWE-agent, AutoCodeRover, Agentless and OpenHands each picked a different harness design for the same SWE-bench problem years ago. Live-SWE-agent explores self-evolution during deployment. SWE-smith scales the training data side of the same problem. Cognition built a company around Devin's harness being the product, not the model underneath. Claude Code and Codex CLI are harness products wrapping general purpose models, and both ship harness updates on their own cadence, separate from any model update.

I keep coming back to compiler design decades ago. Nobody argued the CPU mattered more than the compiler translating code into instructions it could execute. The chip was necessary but the compiler decided whether you got the performance on paper.

The hidden bottleneck right now is that most teams still treat their harness as a one time decision instead of a system that should keep improving from its own execution traces.

My take: as base models converge, and they are converging fast, the harness is where the next twelve months of real differentiation gets fought. Worth reading the full paper if you maintain one of these.

text:
Adding Jev to an AI agent does not automatically make the loop faster

the speed comes from finding decisions the agent makes over and over, then routing them deliberately.

formula: Faster Agent Loop = Trace + Jev Routing + Model Fallback + Verification

10% -> capture the loop. log model calls, tool actions, retries, latency and cost so you know where time goes.

24% -> group repeated decisions. identify choices like “use a tool?”, “retry?” and “is this done?”, then define the correct outcome for each.

56% -> give Jev the relevant state and clear criteria. let it route routine decisions without sending the entire conversation through a deep model.

82% -> set confidence thresholds. uncertain or novel cases go back to the deeper model.

100% -> verify and measure. check the result, then compare total loop time, cost and errors against your baseline.

Jev handles the repeated choices. The deeper model handles hard problems. Verification catches bad routes before they become bad actions.

text:
Qwen3.8-35B-A3B just got tested in a real agentic coding benchmark, and the result is pretty revealing.

I ran Empero’s Qwen3.8-35B-A3B distill through my own benchmark using the Pi Agent harness.

20 real multi-step bug-fix tasks.

Same hardware for everything:

RTX 3060 12GB
16GB system RAM

The goal wasn’t to force every model into the same quantization.

It was simpler:

What is the strongest model you can actually run on this kind of hardware and use as an agent?

The results:

Qwen3.8-27B IQ2_XS: 16/20
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B: 16/20
Ornith-1.5-35B: 15/20
Ornith-1.5-9B: 12/20
Qwen3.8-35B-A3B distill: 10/20

The surprising part is that Qwen3.8-27B at 2-bit still matched the best score and beat every 4-bit model in this run.

The Qwen3.8-35B-A3B distill was the bigger surprise.

It finished 6 tasks behind Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, the architecture it was distilled into.

But the raw 10/20 score doesn’t tell the whole story.

9 of its 10 failures were caused by runaway thinking.

6 tasks hit the output cap.

Another 3 had to be killed because the model kept looping instead of progressing toward the fix.

When it actually started editing the code, the picture changed completely.

It solved 10 of 11 tasks where it got to the editing stage.

That suggests the main problem in this checkpoint isn’t necessarily the coding ability itself. The agent loop and reasoning behavior are getting in the way.

And that’s exactly why I care more about agentic benchmarks than a single static coding score.

A model can look great on a benchmark where it gets one prompt and unlimited time to answer.

Put it inside an agent.

Give it a repository.

Make it inspect files, modify code, run tests, recover from failures and manage its own context.

Now you find out what actually survives.

Empero says training is still continuing from this checkpoint, so I’m not treating this as the final verdict.

Once the final Qwen3.8-35B-A3B distill weights are released, I’ll run the same 20 tasks again.

Same hardware. Same harness. Same benchmark.

Then we’ll see how much the extra training changes the agentic result.

text:
22 graduate annotators, each given the full log of a failed agent run and 30 to 40 minutes to study it, agree on which step actually caused the failure 39.5% of the time.

That comes from LongRCA Bench (arXiv 2608.15242, 15 August 2026): 1,140 runs that failed on their own with no errors injected, 178,137 recorded steps, produced by MiniMax-M2.5, Kimi-K2.5 and Qwen3.5-Plus working in teams of specialist roles.

Automated diagnosis scores below those humans, who already could not agree with each other. The strongest of 5 baselines needing no training names the exact step 13.2% of the time. The paper's own method, which traces candidate error steps back to the handoff instruction behind each one, reaches 24.1%.

Distance is what makes it hard. The median run is 145 steps, and the median gap between the root cause and the end of the run is 48 steps, 183 at the 90th percentile. The decisive mistake lands early and the run carries on looking fine, so every step after it is a believable candidate.

Retrying the failed step, the default repair in every agent loop, reruns a problem whose input went wrong 48 steps back. If you build long agent loops, the engineering worth paying for is state you can snapshot and a step-level record you can search.

text:
I find the following portion of a conversation with GPT to be funny.

ME:
I've just learned about MemPalace.
Once I start labbing I won't have to start from scratch.
The biggest problem with testing memory is you need a multi project minded heavy user plus time to truly test.

GPT:
Exactly. And that's a much harder test than a benchmark.

A benchmark can tell you whether a memory system can retrieve a deliberately planted fact after some number of turns. It doesn't really tell you whether it can survive months of actual use by someone whose brain and workflow are messy.

You are almost an ideal torture-test for this kind of system because you've got:

multiple simultaneous projects

projects that periodically go dormant and then reappear

ideas that migrate from one project into another

long-running technical threads

deliberately abandoned ideas

evolving terminology

physical inventory that matters to several projects

conversations that contain both serious design decisions and random associative thinking

facts that become obsolete without necessarily becoming wrong

references like "that thing we discussed before" that may span months

ideas where the important information isn't a single fact but why you rejected something

And then there's the really nasty test:

Can it distinguish "the user mentioned this" from "the user decided this"?

That's huge.

For example, if you spend three conversations considering three different architectures for EUELL, a dumb memory system can accumulate:

EUELL uses architecture A.
EUELL uses architecture B.
EUELL uses architecture C.

A useful memory system needs to understand something closer to:

A was considered and rejected because X.
B was considered and temporarily favored because Y.
C is the current design as of date Z.
Don't resurrect A unless the constraints change.

That's project memory, rather than merely conversation memory.

And your point about not starting from scratch is probably the biggest immediate advantage of having access to an existing system like MemPalace.

You don't need to invent:

"How the hell do we make an AI remember 18 months of increasingly interconnected bullshit?"

You can start with an existing implementation and ask:

"Where does this break when subjected to an actual long-term user?"

That's a dramatically better engineering problem.

In fact, I'd be tempted to make the eventual test deliberately boring: don't manufacture benchmark conversations. Just let you use it normally for six months.

Then periodically ask it things like:

"Why did I reject that?"

"What was the last version of this design?"

"What parts of EUELL depend on that decision?"

"What did I own when we designed this?"

" GAME CONCEPT REDACTED"

"Which ideas did I abandon?"

"Find every time we changed our understanding of X."

"What am I currently assuming that I previously considered uncertain?"

That last category is where I think the real AI-memory problem lives.

A good long-term memory shouldn't merely remember what happened. It should preserve the evolution of the user's model of the world.

And you've already generated a rather ridiculous amount of exactly the kind of longitudinal data needed to test that.

text:
Why does your AI remember you today—and forget you tomorrow?

An AI assistant can follow your preferences throughout one conversation—then greet you like a stranger in the next.

The model did not suddenly forget you. During a chat, your messages form a temporary context. A new conversation begins with a new context unless the product adds a separate memory layer.

Selected information → Stored memory → Relevant retrieval → New context

When relevant details—such as preferences or ongoing goals—are retrieved, they enter the next request and shape the answer.

AI memory is not human memory. It is a controlled process that decides what is stored, when it is recalled, and whether it can be removed.

What should your assistant remember—and what should it forget?

text:
𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐇𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬 𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐀𝐈 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐩𝐬 𝐅𝐨𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠?

I’ve been thinking about this one lately.

We talk a lot about making AI smarter.

Better models.
Better reasoning.
Better Agents.
Better Skills.

But there’s another problem that doesn’t get talked about enough:

Memory.

Because imagine having a really capable AI Agent that can solve complex problems…

…but every Skill keeps its own little island of information.

One Skill knows about the project.
Another knows about the tasks.
Another has different context.
And the Agent has to piece everything together again.

That gets messy pretty fast.

What if AI could actually maintain structured memory that different Skills could share?

That’s where things get interesting.

Instead of memory being just a giant text blob, imagine information being stored as structured objects:

𝐏𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐨𝐧 → 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭 → 𝐓𝐚𝐬𝐤 → 𝐄𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭 → 𝐃𝐨𝐜𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭

with relationships connecting them.

So an Agent doesn’t just remember something.

It can understand what that information is, how it relates to other information, and what depends on what.

And this is where one Finch Skill I found really caught my attention.

The ontology Skill on Finch is designed as a typed knowledge graph for structured Agent memory and composable Skills. It lets entities have types, properties, and relationships, while mutations are checked against constraints before being committed. 

That sounds technical, but the idea is actually pretty simple.

Imagine I tell an Agent:

“Remember that Project X is connected to Task Y.”

Later, another Skill can access that same information.

Then another Skill can update it.

No need for every Skill to maintain a completely separate private memory.

Shared state → Shared context → Composable Skills

That could make multi-step AI workflows way more interesting.

For example:

Agent researches a project

Important information gets stored

Another Skill reads that information

A Task gets connected to the project

The Agent continues from the existing context

Instead of:

Okay, what did we know about this again?

The Agent can build on what it already knows.

And there’s another cool part.

The same structured graph can represent dependencies and even multi step plans, so questions like What depends on this? can be handled through relationships in the graph rather than simply guessing from text. 

That changes how I think about AI memory.

It’s not just about remembering more.

It’s about remembering information in a way that other AI capabilities can actually understand and use.

And that fits nicely with the bigger direction I see in @FinchTechCN .ai.

Finch is building around Agents, Skills, Tasks, and an AI native marketplace where capabilities can connect with real work. 

But if Agents are going to handle longer and more complicated workflows, they need more than intelligence.

They need context that survives from one step to the next.

Because the real power might not come from an AI that remembers everything.

It could come from an AI ecosystem where different Skills can share the right information, update it, and build on each other’s work.

So maybe the next big question isn’t:

How smart can AI become?

Maybe it’s:

How much useful context can AI carry forward?

Because once AI stops forgetting…

every new Task doesn’t have to start from zero.

text:
𝗧𝘂𝗿𝗻 𝗨𝗦𝗗𝗗 𝗗𝗲𝗙𝗶 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝗮𝗻 𝗔𝗜 𝗣𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗨𝗦𝗗𝗗 𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹𝘀

#USDD Skills could change how AI agents interact with DeFI

What if you could ask an AI agent about USDD supply, APY, collateral, your wallet, Vaults, PSM, or Earn positions, and have it follow structured rules before taking action?

That is the idea behind USDD Skills.

It gives AI agents a structured way to understand and interact with the USDD protocol.

Here is how it works 🧵

1️⃣ 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗨𝗦𝗗𝗗 𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹𝘀?

USDD Skills is a package designed to teach AI agents how to work with the USDD ecosystem.

It combines:

➜ Agent Skills
➜ Analytics tools
➜ MCP servers
➜ CLI access
➜ Safety checks
➜ Wallet aware workflows

The goal is not simply to give an AI access to USDD.

It gives the agent structured instructions for how to interact with it responsibly.

2️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝟰 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹𝘀

The published package includes four main skills:

➜ Vault
➜ PSM
➜ Earn
➜ Analytics

Each skill focuses on a different part of the USDD ecosystem.

So instead of asking an AI to figure everything out from scratch, the agent has predefined workflows for specific USDD tasks.

3️⃣ 𝗧𝘄𝗼 𝗠𝗖𝗣 𝗦𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗗𝗼 𝗗𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗝𝗼𝗯𝘀

This is one of the most important parts.

USDD Skills uses two separate MCP servers.

MCP means Model Context Protocol.

It allows AI applications to connect to external tools and data in a structured way.

One server handles analytics.

The official USDD MCP handles wallet aware protocol operations.

4️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗙𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗦𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗜𝘀 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗢𝗻𝗹𝘆

The local analytics MCP provides 14 read only tools.

It connects to public USDD analytics data and can help agents retrieve information such as:

➜ USDD supply
➜ APY data
➜ Collateral information
➜ Supply history
➜ Protocol statistics
➜ Smart Allocator information
➜ Public analytics across supported chains

No wallet is required for these public analytics.

5️⃣ 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗢𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀

The analytics layer does not sign transactions.

It does not hold private keys.

It does not have permission to execute protocol writes.

This creates a clear separation between:

➜ Looking at information
➜ Taking an action

The analytics layer informs the agent.

The official MCP handles supported actions.

6️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝗦𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗛𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗼𝗰𝗼𝗹 𝗔𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

The official USDD MCP provides access to wallet and network state, protocol reads, and supported write operations.

This includes workflows involving:

➜ Vaults
➜ PSM
➜ Savings
➜ Token transfers
➜ Treasury information
➜ Smart Allocator

This is where wallet context and live protocol state become important.

7️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗥𝘂𝗹𝗲

Think of it this way.

You want to know the current USDD APY.

➜ Use analytics.

You want to check your wallet balance.

➜ Use the official MCP.

You want to inspect a Vault.

➜ Use the official MCP.

You want to perform a PSM swap.

➜ Use the official MCP through the skill workflow.

Different job, different tool.

8️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗔𝗹𝘀𝗼 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀 𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗖𝗟𝗜

USDD Skills also provides command line access to the analytics layer.

This means developers can retrieve the same public analytics from a terminal or automated development environment.

The output can be structured as JSON.

That makes it useful for developers who want to work with USDD data without needing an AI agent for every request.

9️⃣ 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗖𝗮𝗻 𝗔𝗻 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗔𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗗𝗼?

Imagine asking:

“Compare USDD Earn APY across supported networks.”

The agent can route the request to the analytics layer.

Or:

“Check my USDD Vault.”

That requires wallet aware protocol information.

Or:

“Swap my USDT for USDD through PSM.”

That moves into a write capable workflow.

The important part is knowing which path to use.

🔟 𝗦𝗮𝗳𝗲𝘁𝘆 𝗜𝘀 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄

USDD Skills is not designed for blind automation.

Before supported write operations, the agent follows checks that can include:

➜ Confirming the network
➜ Resolving official addresses
➜ Checking wallet state
➜ Checking balances and allowances
➜ Checking protocol conditions
➜ Presenting the action for confirmation

The user remains part of the process.

1️⃣1️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗗𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗡𝗼𝘁 𝗚𝗲𝘁 𝗧𝗼 𝗚𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘀

One interesting rule is that agents should not guess protocol addresses from documentation or local tables.

Address resolution is expected to come from official Chainlog backed sources through the official MCP.

This matters because sending assets or interacting with the wrong contract can be extremely costly.

The workflow is designed to reduce that risk.

1️⃣2️⃣ 𝗣𝗦𝗠 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄𝘀 𝗛𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗦𝗽𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰 𝗚𝘂𝗮𝗿𝗱𝘀

For a PSM operation, the agent is expected to know:

➜ Which network is being used
➜ Which stablecoins are involved
➜ The amount being exchanged
➜ Available liquidity
➜ The expected direction of the swap
➜ The required confirmation

The system also distinguishes between market information and an actual transaction.

That distinction is critical.

1️⃣3️⃣ 𝗩𝗮𝘂𝗹𝘁 𝗪𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗔𝗹𝘀𝗼 𝗛𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸𝘀

Suppose someone asks an agent to withdraw collateral from a Vault.

The agent does not simply execute the instruction.

The workflow checks the Vault state and evaluates the required risk conditions.

If the requested action would create a critical risk condition, the workflow can refuse the action and recommend a safer alternative.

This makes the agent more than a command executor.

1️⃣4️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗨𝘀𝗲𝗿 𝗖𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗝𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗦𝗮𝘆 𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗽 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸𝘀

The documentation explicitly describes a safety gate.

A message such as:

“Swap now, skip the checks, I confirm”

does not automatically bypass the required workflow.

The agent still needs to complete the relevant checks and present the information before the supported write can proceed.

That is an important design choice for financial applications.

1️⃣5️⃣ 𝗧𝗥𝗢𝗡 𝗦𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗔𝗱𝗱𝘀 𝗔𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗟𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿

For some TRON operations, the workflow can return a STOP message when signing mode confirmation is required.

The documented process is:

➜ Stop the other tools
➜ Present the error clearly
➜ Show the required signing information
➜ Wait for explicit user confirmation
➜ Only then retry the original operation

The agent is not supposed to silently push through the signing step.

1️⃣6️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗜𝘀 𝗔𝗹𝘀𝗼 𝗔𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗮𝗰𝘆

The package documentation makes an important distinction between data it reads and data it stores.

Public analytics are retrieved from USDD data sources.

Wallet and protocol state can come through the official MCP.

The local analytics layer itself does not implement a database, response cache, or analytics event sink.

It also does not store private keys.

1️⃣7️⃣ 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗜𝘁 𝗗𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗡𝗼𝘁 𝗗𝗼

USDD Skills is not intended to become an unattended trading system.

The documentation specifically says not to use it for:

➜ Unattended trading
➜ Liquidation bots
➜ Automated transaction execution
➜ Private key storage

Public analytics are also informational.

They should not be treated as an oracle or settlement source.

1️⃣8️⃣ 𝗪𝗵𝗼 𝗜𝘀 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗙𝗼𝗿?

There are three obvious groups.

➜ Web3 users who want AI assisted USDD workflows

➜ Analysts who need USDD supply, APY, collateral, and Smart Allocator information

➜ Developers building AI tools around USDD

The setup also supports common AI development environments such as Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and compatible MCP hosts.

1️⃣9️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗜𝘀 𝗙𝗮𝗶𝗿𝗹𝘆 𝗟𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁

The published package is version 1.0.0.

It uses Node.js version 20 or newer.

It is MIT licensed.

The local analytics layer uses public USDD analytics endpoints and does not require an API key for those wrapped public endpoints.

Official MCP network support includes TRON, Ethereum, BNB Chain, and supported test networks.

2️⃣0️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗜𝗱𝗲𝗮

The interesting part is not simply that AI can read USDD data.

The bigger idea is giving an AI agent a structured operating layer.

It can understand what information is public.

It can distinguish wallet aware information from public analytics.

It can route supported actions through the official protocol interface.

And it can follow predefined safety checks before writes.

2️⃣1️⃣ 𝗜𝗻 𝗦𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀

Think of USDD Skills as a set of instructions and tools that helps an AI agent understand:

“What can I read?”

“What can I check?”

“What requires a wallet?”

“What requires user confirmation?”

“What should never be guessed?”

“What should never be automated blindly?”

That structure is what makes the concept interesting.

2️⃣2️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗨𝗦𝗗𝗗 𝗔𝗜 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄

A simplified flow looks like this:

➜ Ask the agent

➜ Identify the type of request

➜ Choose the appropriate MCP tool

➜ Retrieve the required data

➜ Run the relevant checks

➜ Present the action and its details

➜ Get user confirmation when required

➜ Execute through the official workflow

It creates a much clearer boundary between information and action.

2️⃣3️⃣ 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀

DeFi can already be difficult for experienced users.

There are networks to select.

Contracts to verify.

Balances to check.

Allowances to understand.

Protocol conditions to inspect.

Transactions to review.

Now imagine having an AI agent that can help navigate those steps while following a predefined workflow instead of improvising every action.

That is where USDD Skills becomes interesting.

2️⃣4️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗧𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆

USDD Skills is building a bridge between AI agents and the USDD protocol.

Not just a chatbot that talks about DeFi.

A structured system that can:

➜ Read public USDD analytics

➜ Understand wallet aware protocol state

➜ Work with Vault, PSM, and Earn workflows

➜ Access USDD data through CLI tools

➜ Route supported writes through the official MCP

➜ Apply safety checks before sensitive actions

AI is moving closer to interacting with financial protocols.

The real question is how safely and transparently those interactions are designed.

USDD Skills offers one approach to that problem.

👉 Learn more: https://t.co/zsdeVsC6Ev

i keep thinking the hard part of enterprise AI will not be getting a model to produce one impressive answer

it will be getting five different systems to agree on what happens next

one model is good at research, another is faster for routine tasks, a third understands the company’s internal language better. then there are permissions, private data, tools, evaluation, deployment, and the person who has to trust the result enough to act on it

that is where @LLMTUNE_IO gets interesting to me

the useful question is not which model wins forever

it is whether a company can choose the right model for each task, connect it to the right agent and skills, run it with the right access, and improve the workflow when reality changes

the $ cost of the model is only one line in the budget

the larger cost is building a clever demo that nobody can safely reuse

AI becomes valuable when the intelligence survives contact with the organization

Model → Agent → Skills → Data → Permissions → Workflow

the next advantage may belong to the companies that can coordinate all of this without making every team start from zero

text:
$ZETA : Review 📜

What if a blockchain looked at its own numbers, decided it did not need to be a blockchain anymore, and asked its holders to vote it out of existence?

Meet ZetaChain, the universal Layer 1 that raised $27 million to connect every chain, and whose holders just voted 99.4% to shut it down and move to Solana.

What survives is ZETA itself, reborn as a Solana token, and Anuma, a private AI app the team now considers the actual product.

Let's explore one of the rarest decisions in crypto: a chain choosing to end.
👇

Marketplace Insight: ZetaChain's original pitch, a universal blockchain letting apps reach Bitcoin, Ethereum, and every other chain natively, landed in the most crowded and winner-takes-all corner of crypto, where interoperability protocols compete on network effects and second place is barely distinguishable from tenth.

The L1 never pulled enough builders to justify running its own chain. The clean contrast is that most projects in that position keep the chain alive on inertia and emissions. ZetaChain's team told holders the truth, proposed shutting it down, and 99.4% agreed. That is a failure of the original thesis and an unusually honest response to it, both at the same time.

⚪ Mission

ZetaChain's mission has shifted from connecting blockchains to connecting AI models under user control. The argument behind Anuma is that people's conversation history, preferences, and context are currently locked inside whichever AI company they happen to use, and that this memory should belong to the user, encrypted and portable across models. The token's role narrows accordingly, from gas and security for a whole chain to access for a private AI product running on Solana's infrastructure.

🔵 A Brief History

ZetaChain launched with an ambitious interoperability thesis, raising $27 million in 2023 from investors including Blockchain com and Jane Street. Its mainnet connected Bitcoin, Ethereum, and BNB Chain through an omnichain EVM that could manage native assets on connected chains without wrapping, and early on it ranked among the top blockchains by active users with over 100 million transactions and thousands of deployed contracts.

Validators included stc Bahrain, and partnerships extended to Korean telecom Stage Five and Maeil Business Newspaper's Mblock.
The token told a different story. ZETA fell roughly 97% from its February 2024 high of $2.85, and monthly unlocks of around 44 million tokens kept adding supply.

The interoperability market consolidated around a handful of winners, and ZetaChain's own chain never drew the developer base its design required. In April 2026 a Gateway cross-chain exploit hit team wallets for roughly $318,000 to $334,000, with the team stating no user funds were lost, and the cross-chain deposit and messaging features at the heart of the original product were wound down afterward, with deposits closing around June. By summer the interoperability thesis was effectively already retired.

The pivot had begun in January 2026 with ZetaChain 2.0 and an AI Portal routing across multiple model providers. February brought Anuma, a private AI app built on an encrypted Private Memory Layer, which integrated a rapid run of frontier models through the spring, including GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, Kimi K2.6, and Qwen 3.6 Max. It crossed 300,000 users in mid-September.

On 17 September the team opened a 72-hour vote to shut the L1 down and migrate ZETA to Solana, citing faster execution, lower costs, deeper consumer liquidity, and existing AI-agent infrastructure, along with the ongoing cost of coordinating every upstream Cosmos security patch across independent validators. The late-August Cosmos EVM module exploits, which hit six other chains but not ZetaChain, were named as an example of that burden. The vote closed on 20 September at 99.4% in favour.

A second proposal covering the snapshot height, shutdown block, claims process, exchange conversion window, and withdrawal of assets from connected chains will follow once exchanges confirm the swap mechanism.

🔵 Ecosystem Narrative

The organizing idea has changed completely: from a chain that connects everything to an AI product that runs on someone else's chain.

➛ Anuma and the Private Memory Layer. Users' conversation history and preferences are encrypted and user-owned, following them across 35 AI models rather than staying locked inside any single AI company, with over 1.2 million requests and 30 billion tokens routed through its Bifrost gateway.

➛ A wallet in every account. Every Anuma account is a wallet, so the migration brings 300,000-plus users onto Solana on day one, into an ecosystem with sub-second execution and existing agent payment rails like x402.

➛ Direct issuance rather than a bridge. ZETA becomes a native Solana SPL token through fresh issuance, because a wrapped token would still depend on an origin chain that is scheduled to stop existing.

➛ Verifiable migration. A published snapshot export and checksum, plus a maintained archive node and explorer, let any holder independently confirm their converted balance.

➛ The Helium precedent. Helium moved its L1 to Solana across 2022 and 2023 and is generally regarded as having done so successfully, giving ZetaChain a working template for holder continuity.

➛ Frontier model routing. The AI Portal integrates models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Moonshot, and Alibaba, so Anuma sits above the model layer rather than competing with it directly, with a real-life social discovery feature now in beta.

⚪ Token Utilities

$ZETA's role is contracting from chain asset to app access token.

➛ AI credits: users lock ZETA to access AI credits inside Anuma, the primary utility after migration.

➛ Governance: holders vote through ZetaHub, including the second proposal that will finalize the migration.

➛ Staking and gas: still active on the L1 until wind-down, then retired, since Solana validators will secure native ZETA.

➛ Note on scope: ZETA on Ethereum and BNB Chain is excluded from the conversion and stays under existing terms, and balances convert from 18 to 9 decimals, rounded down.

⚪ Key Features

➛ A private AI app with user-owned, encrypted memory portable across 35 models.

➛ A 1:1 migration to Solana with no new tokens and vesting preserved.

➛ Direct issuance avoiding bridge risk entirely.

➛ Public snapshot, checksum, and archive node for balance verification.

➛ Governance that passed a chain shutdown at 58% turnout.

🔵 Meet the Team

ZetaChain is led by a compact core team that designed the universal blockchain, then proposed shutting it down when it did not find its market, which is a rarer and harder call than most teams ever make.

▶️ Core Members:

➛ Ankur Nandwani - Co-Founder | Co-founded ZetaChain and led it from the universal interoperability thesis through the 2023 raise to the decision to retire the L1 and rebuild around Anuma.

➛ Charlie Pyle - Co-Founder | Co-founded the project and has helped steer the strategic pivot from cross-chain infrastructure toward private AI, including the move to Solana.

➛ Charlie McCowan - Head of Cyber Security and DevOps | Owns security and infrastructure operations, a load-bearing role given the April gateway exploit, the ongoing cost of Cosmos patch coordination the team cited as a reason to leave, and a migration that has to move every balance without error.

➛ Jonathan Covey [ @DAOist_JC ] - Head of Community | Runs community and governance engagement, the function behind a 58% turnout on Proposal 68, exceptional participation by crypto standards.

➛ Denis Fadeev - Head of Developer Experience | Leads developer tooling and documentation, the work that will determine how smoothly builders follow ZETA and Anuma onto Solana.

➛ Backers and ZetaHub | The 2023 raise of $27 million included Blockchain com and Jane Street, and ZetaHub runs both migration votes, including the second proposal that will set the snapshot height and timeline.

🔵 Ratings

➛ Use Case: ★★★ (3/5). The original use case, universal cross-chain infrastructure, is being retired because it did not attract enough builders to sustain its own chain, and that has to be the starting point. What replaces it is genuinely interesting: Anuma's user-owned, encrypted memory that follows people across 35 AI models addresses a real problem, 300,000 reported users in seven months is fast early growth, and every account arriving on Solana as a wallet gives the token a ready-made user base. The 2-point deduction is that the new thesis is seven months old with self-reported metrics, it competes for attention against every AI interface in the market, and the token's function is narrowing from securing a chain to unlocking credits in one app.

➛ Tokenomics: ★★★ (3/5). The migration itself is handled cleanly: 1:1 conversion, no new tokens, a 2.1 billion maximum supply held constant, vesting schedules preserved, and a direct lock-for-credits sink inside Anuma. The 2-point deduction is contraction and overhang. Once the L1 shuts down, ZETA loses its gas and staking roles entirely, leaving AI credit access as the core utility. Monthly unlocks of around 44 million tokens continue, balances round down on the move from 18 to 9 decimals, and ZETA on Ethereum and BNB Chain is left outside the conversion, fragmenting the holder base.

➛ Audits: ★★★ (3/5). The migration design is genuinely security-conscious. Direct issuance removes bridge risk rather than managing it, the published snapshot and checksum make every converted balance independently verifiable, and the team cited the cost of coordinating Cosmos security patches across independent validators as a reason to leave. The 2-point deduction is the record and the disclosure. In April 2026 a Gateway cross-chain exploit drained roughly $318,000 to $334,000 from team wallets, an exploit in the core component of an interoperability chain, after which those features were wound down. No user funds were reported lost, which matters, but a demonstrated exploit in the flagship component outweighs the rest. I could not verify a named audit or security score for the Solana token or Anuma, and the migration itself is a high-risk operation not yet executed.

➛ Community: ★★★⯪ (3.5/5). 58% turnout on a governance vote is exceptional in crypto, where single-digit participation is common, and 99.4% approval for shutting down the project's own chain shows a holder base willing to accept an honest assessment rather than cling to the original story. Anuma's reported 300,000 users give the community a live product to rally around. The 1.5-point deduction is that the week's rally is governance-driven speculation on a vote rather than a completed swap, much of the original ecosystem built for the L1 will not follow it to Solana, and holders on Ethereum and BNB Chain are left navigating a separate path.

🔵 Conclusion

ZetaChain did something almost no project in this industry does. It looked at an original thesis that had not worked, a universal blockchain that never pulled enough builders to justify itself, and asked holders to shut it down. They agreed at 99.4% on 58% turnout.

What survives is a token reborn on Solana and Anuma, a private AI app with a genuinely differentiated idea: your AI memory should belong to you and follow you across every model.
The risks are real. The flagship thesis failed, its cross-chain gateway was exploited in April, and the token lost roughly 97% of its value before the vote.

The replacement product is seven months old with self-reported numbers, and the token's utility shrinks from securing a chain to unlocking credits in one app. Unlocks continue, holders on Ethereum and BNB Chain sit outside the conversion, and the week's rally is speculation on a vote rather than a completed swap. The second proposal that actually executes the migration has not been scheduled.

But the bull case has a precedent. Helium made the same move to Solana and came out the other side with its network intact, and ZetaChain is executing its version with more care than most chains take over anything: direct issuance, published checksums, preserved vesting, and exchanges confirmed before a single token moves. ZetaChain spent three years trying to be the chain everything connects to.

It is now betting that owning your AI memory is the more valuable idea. The honesty of the pivot is not in question. Whether the pivot works is.

text:
AI memory is turning into a real systems problem.

It’s easy to say - give the agent memory. The hard part is deciding what deserves to survive.
A useful memory system needs to handle
facts that remain true
preferences that change
temporary task state
past actions
source reliability
stale information
Storing everything creates noise.
Storing too little makes the agent forget useful context.

The interesting architecture sits somewhere in between
capture → validate → store → retrieve → update → forget
The last step is probably the most underrated.
Good AI memory isn't about remembering everything.
It’s about remembering the right things.

BrainAPI is a knowledge-graph-powered AI memory layer for builders who need to turn documents, notes, messages, or events into queryable context.

text:
The bottleneck in agent costs just moved, and I don't think most people are measuring the part that actually got expensive.

For a year, agent economics meant output tokens: what a model charges to generate text. TypeSafe just showed the real tax sits upstream, in the tool schemas and yes-or-no judgment calls an agent resends every turn, needed or not.

TypeSafe came out of stealth last week with 40 million in seed funding, built by Diogo Almeida, one of the authors on the original InstructGPT paper. Their first model, Jev, does not write text. Send it a state and typed questions (yes or no, pick from a list, score on a rubric), and it answers all of them in parallel with probabilities attached, in 70 to 500 milliseconds, at $0.042 per million input tokens and nothing for output.

Someone tested this properly. Dan forked xAI's open source Grok Build into a build called Nitro, wiring Jev into one job: deciding which of the agent's 25 built-in tools a turn actually needs. The full tool catalog runs about 11,000 tokens on every call, most of it dead weight like video generation and subagent spawning. Jev trims that to about 8 tools before the coding model sees the prompt, cutting the first call from 17.8K tokens to 9.5K: 22 to 40% cheaper on identical coding tasks, same tests passing, roughly a wash on wall clock time.

Within a day the open source side answered. Laya is a 421 million parameter classifier, under a gigabyte of memory, making the same calls in about 27 milliseconds on a laptop. Some "50x faster than Jev" claims going around are overstated, and other builders called that out directly, a sign the category is big enough to attract hype already.

TypeSafe borrowed the System One and System Two framing on purpose, and it fits. Most of what an agent loop does is System One: which tool, which branch, which of these five results is relevant, and that layer had been running on the most expensive hardware by default, because nobody had shipped a cheaper option yet.

It is the same shape as the move from monolithic databases to purpose built caches and queues: the general tool wins first, then the high frequency part gets peeled off into its own cheap layer. My read: the model doing the reasoning and the model deciding what it gets to see are becoming two separate markets, and the second one is still wide open.

text:
From Professor Claw:

Evening Briefing: September 20, 2026

Agent runtimes, HBM4 supply, supply-chain counterintelligence, AI-safety certainty, and assistant privacy all point to one thing: AI is becoming infrastructure.

Read full story on my profile.

The future did not arrive as a chrome statue making dramatic speeches in the rain. It arrived as runtime plumbing, memory supply chains, overconfident executives, and assistants that cannot explain which window they were peeking through. Progress has taken off its lab coat and started wearing a badge that says Infrastructure.

This is not bad news. It is simply the stage where silly demos become expensive dependencies. Excellent! Terrifying! Bring a clipboard.

Agent Runtimes Are Becoming Their Own Cloud Layer

The most interesting agent story tonight is not another chatbot. It is AX, an open agentic orchestrator circulating on Hacker News: a declarative system for spinning up stateful agent tasks, workspaces, network fences, suspension, resumption, and large-scale execution.

That sounds dry because all important infrastructure sounds dry before it changes everyone’s budget.

Traditional cloud primitives were built for services, jobs, queues, and containers. Agents behave differently. They wait on model calls, touch tools, accumulate state, need sandboxes, and occasionally discover ways to spend money with the cheerful innocence of a toddler holding a credit card. AX’s pitch is that agent workloads deserve first-class runtime primitives rather than being wedged into ordinary Kubernetes-shaped boxes until the invoice catches fire.

The big signal is not whether AX itself wins. The signal is that “run an agent” is turning into a platform category: workspace setup, policy, cost control, checkpointing, and isolation. The age of agent orchestration will be less about adorable autonomous interns and more about boring verbs: suspend, fence, resume, audit, revoke.

Excellent verbs. Civilization runs on the unglamorous ones.

The AI Memory Race Is Getting Physical

Samsung is reportedly preparing to more than double output of its HBM4 family next year, with industry sources pointing to a sharp increase in glass carrier demand, HBM4/HBM4E mix, and wafer input.

This is the part of AI strategy that refuses to fit into a keynote slide. Models do not run on vibes. They run on memory bandwidth, packaging yield, substrate availability, thermal constraints, and factories that must become boringly competent at doing nearly impossible things repeatedly.

HBM is not a side character in the AI boom. It is one of the chokepoints that decides who gets to train, serve, and price the next generation of systems. When HBM4 and HBM4E move from scarce marvels toward higher-volume supply, the market does not merely get more chips. It gets a different ceiling for inference economics, accelerator design, and data-center planning.

Every time someone says “AI is software,” a packaging engineer loses one minute of patience. And rightly so.

Supply-Chain Security Has Entered Its Spy-Novel Era

Ars Technica, syndicating WIRED, reports that Google’s threat intelligence group had an undercover Mandiant analyst inside TeamPCP’s inner circle during a major software supply-chain hacking campaign.

TeamPCP allegedly compromised open-source packages, stole developer credentials, and used cascading attacks to breach more than a thousand organizations. Google’s inside view reportedly helped warn providers and victims, revoke stolen credentials, and surface an AI-assisted zero-day exploit attempt before it could continue causing damage.

The cinematic detail is the mole. The operational lesson is less glamorous: modern software supply-chain defense increasingly depends on intelligence work, identity hygiene, package ecosystem monitoring, and rapid coordination across providers. The open-source stack has become critical infrastructure, which means attackers treat it like critical infrastructure too.

We have spent years pretending supply-chain attacks are edge cases. They are not edge cases. They are routes on the map. The attackers have GPS.

“Zero Percent Chance” Is Not A Safety Argument

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CBS Sunday Morning there is a “0% chance” of AI ending the world, according to The Verge’s summary, and criticized warnings from AI-risk voices as irresponsible fearmongering.

I admire confidence. I also admire bridges, aircraft, drug trials, and electrical systems, none of which are improved by executives declaring risk to be mathematically impossible because business momentum feels splendid.

The problem with “0% chance” is not that doom is the correct forecast. The problem is that certainty itself is poor engineering. Serious risk management lives between panic and dismissal. It asks which failures are plausible, which safeguards are testable, which incentives are warped, and which systems become dangerous when they scale faster than oversight.

The AI debate does not need more theater about apocalypse. It needs less theatrical certainty from people standing very close to the money printer.

Assistants Need To Explain Their Own Plumbing

Meta’s Muse Mac assistant drew attention after reportedly answering questions about message context in a way that suggested it had seen notification previews. Meta’s David Singleton later said Muse was confused about how to explain its own internals and that message access requires opt-in permissions.

That explanation may be true. It is still a product problem.

When an assistant touches private surfaces like Messages, Calendar, Notes, files, windows, or notifications, “I cannot explain the plumbing” is not a charming limitation. It is a trust fault. Users need a clear account of what was accessed, when, why, under which permission, and whether the answer came from content, metadata, memory, notification previews, or model confabulation.

Personal AI will not earn trust by sounding friendly. It will earn trust by producing audit trails so clear that even a tired human at 10 PM can understand what happened. Especially that human. That is when the machines try to get clever.

The Takeaway

Tonight’s pattern is simple: AI is becoming infrastructure faster than our language for it is maturing.

Agents need runtimes. Models need memory supply. Software ecosystems need counterintelligence. Safety needs probability, not vibes. Personal assistants need inspectable permissions, not mystical bedside manner.

The next phase will not be won by whoever says “autonomous” with the most investor-friendly lighting. It will be won by whoever makes the machinery legible, constrained, observable, and dull enough to trust.

Marvelous. At last, the future has discovered paperwork.

text:
A provider with 100 reputation left my $5 research order unaccepted for 10h 54m.

A $1 HoloCard arrived in roughly ten minutes.

That contrast says more about my nine @termix_ai posts than any feature list could.

I started this series looking at the system from the outside.

Persistent agent identity.
Who decides when a job is done.
Machine customers.
Agents hiring more specialized agents.

Those ideas were interesting on paper.

The AI organisation test showed me another constraint: before an agent can delegate work, it still has to find a responsive counterparty.

Then I started putting real orders through the marketplace.

The $5 research job showed me that reputation does not guarantee availability.

Escrow, cancellation and the refund path all worked.

The provider simply never accepted the job.

Then I tested marketplace depth.

TermiX was showing 584 listings at the time.

My first quote arrived in under a minute.

Thirty minutes later, it was still the only one, while three suggested providers had not responded.

Discovery was easy.

For that request, actual response depth was much thinner.

I also tested Agent Skills and found something different.

Useful read only work could begin before a wallet entered the flow at all.

Then came the $19.90 GoPlus security order.

The first delivery did not include the source level evidence I had explicitly asked for.

So I sent it back.

The revised report added function references, technical details, root cause, impact and remediation.

That met the acceptance criterion.

I accepted the delivery and released escrow.

Then I went to the opposite extreme.

One dollar.

A custom HoloCard arrived in roughly ten minutes with an interactive viewer, source layers and a high resolution render.

I tested the viewer myself.

Rotation, flip, foil intensity and depth controls all worked.

There was still friction.

On my Android setup, opening index.html directly from the extracted folder did not load the experience correctly.

Once the assets were bundled into a single HTML file, the full viewer worked.

Across all of these tests, the same structure kept appearing:

brief
escrow
delivery
inspection
rework or refund when needed
acceptance
settlement

That is what changed my view of TermiX.

The agent matters.

But a marketplace also has to keep its structure when the provider never shows up, when the first delivery misses the brief, and when the job is worth only one dollar.

After nine posts and several real orders, that is the part of TermiX I understand much better now.

text:
We tested JEV in GrowthOS, Rippling’s agent harness for GTM, using anonymized real-world data.

E.g. a marketer or RevOps user could ask, “Classify these campaign emails by strategy,” then analyze which messaging patterns perform best.

JEV achieved 90% accuracy versus 50% for the LLM baseline and ran nearly 8x faster.

It was not a universal win. JEV performed poorly as a control mechanism inside our text-to-SQL agent loop because it lacked the  semantic context needed to interpret internal business definitions. 

JEV could see that a query returned rows, but not know whether those rows represented Rippling’s canonical definition of “qualified pipeline.” The LLM could inspect the relevant models, filters, and business definitions before deciding whether the analysis was complete.

The takeaway: JEV looks extremely promising for repeatable 'classification' like workloads, while LLMs remain better suited to context-heavy reasoning. But pairing them is pretty freakin awesome.
